docs.title: Chapter 14: Adjectives
docs.text:
Les adjectifs

A French adjective is a chameleon: it changes its ending to match the noun it describes — masculine or feminine, singular or plural. And it usually comes after the noun: une voiture rouge, “a car red”. A small group comes before, and a few even change their meaning when they move. Here is the full system.

In one line

An adjective agrees with its noun (add -e for feminine, -s for plural) and usually goes after it: une robe noire, des livres intéressants.

docs.title: 14.1 Agreement: -e for feminine, -s for plural
docs.text:
Start with the masculine singular (the dictionary form). Add -e for feminine, -s for plural, and -es for feminine plural. Hindi speakers know this idea: achha ladka, achhi ladki, achhe ladke — the adjective follows the noun’s gender and number.

Singular Plural Masculine un livre vert des livres verts Feminine une robe verte des robes vertes
  • un ami grand → une amie grande — a tall friend — in the feminine, the silent d is heard [GRÃ → GRÃD]
  • un petit chat → une petite maison — a small cat, a small house [puh-TEE → puh-TEET]
  • Il est français, elle est française. — He is French, she is French. [frã-SEH → frã-SEZ]
  • Les fleurs sont jolies. — The flowers are pretty. (agreement also after être) [lay FLUHR sõ zho-LEE]

Hear the feminine

Adding -e often makes a silent final consonant sound: petit [puh-TEE] / petite [puh-TEET]. The plural -s stays silent.

docs.title: Three small rules
docs.text:
• un pull rouge, une jupe rouge — 1. Already ends in -e? No change for feminine: rouge, jeune, facile, rapide, calme.
  • un garçon heureux, des garçons heureux — 2. Already ends in -s or -x? No change for masculine plural: français, gris, heureux.
  • Ravi et Anita sont contents. — 3. A mixed group (one male, one female) takes the masculine plural: contents.

docs.title: 14.2 Irregular feminines: the patterns
docs.text:
Many adjectives do more than add -e. Most of them follow one of these patterns:

Pattern Masculine Feminine -eux → -euse heureux, sérieux heureuse, sérieuse -if → -ive sportif, actif, neuf sportive, active, neuve -er → -ère cher, premier, dernier chère, première, dernière double consonant + e bon, gentil, cruel, ancien bonne, gentille, cruelle, ancienne -et → -ète (some) complet, inquiet, secret complète, inquiète, secrète -eur → -euse travailleur, menteur travailleuse, menteuse

And a group of true irregulars to learn one by one:

Masculine Feminine English blanc blanche white frais fraîche fresh, cool sec sèche dry long longue long doux douce soft, gentle, mild faux fausse false, wrong gros grosse big, fat public · grec publique · grecque public · Greek favori favorite favourite
  • Ma sœur est très sportive. — My sister is very sporty. [spor-TEEV]
  • Elle est heureuse et gentille. — She is happy and kind. [uh-RUHZ ay zhã-TEEY]
  • une chemise blanche, une longue journée — a white shirt, a long day [BLÃSH … LÕG zhoor-NAY]
  • C’est une bonne idée ! — That’s a good idea! (bon → bonne: the nasal disappears) [ewn BON ee-DAY]
  • De l’eau fraîche, s’il vous plaît. — Some cool water, please. [duh loh FRESH]

docs.title: Irregular plurals
docs.text: Like nouns: -al → -aux (un problème national → des problèmes nationaux), and -eau → -eaux (beaux, nouveaux). The feminine plural is regular: nationales. Exceptions in -als: banals, finals, fatals.

docs.title: 14.3 Beau, vieux, nouveau: the special trio
docs.text:
These three very common adjectives have a third masculine form, used before a masculine noun that starts with a vowel or silent h. It sounds like the feminine — so the words flow without a gap.

Masc. + consonant Masc. + vowel Feminine Plural (m / f) beau bel belle beaux / belles vieux vieil vieille vieux / vieilles nouveau nouvel nouvelle nouveaux / nouvelles
  • un beau jardin, un bel arbre, une belle vue — a beautiful garden, a beautiful tree, a beautiful view [BOH · beh-LARBR · BEL VEW]
  • un vieux livre, un vieil ami, une vieille ville — an old book, an old friend, an old town [VYUH · vyeh-ya-MEE · VYEY VEEL]
  • mon nouveau travail, mon nouvel appartement, ma nouvelle voiture — my new job, my new flat, my new car [noo-VOH · noo-veh-la-par-tuh-MÃ · noo-VEL]
  • de beaux enfants, de vieux amis — beautiful children, old friends — in the plural, no special form; liaison with z [duh boh-zã-FÃ · duh vyuh-za-MEE]

bel, vieil, nouvel

Before a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or silent h, use bel, vieil, nouvel: un bel homme, un vieil ami, un nouvel hôtel.

docs.title: 14.4 Position: after the noun — except BAGS
docs.text:
Most French adjectives come after the noun: colours, nationalities, shapes, long adjectives, and participles. A short list of very common adjectives goes before. Remember them with BAGS: Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size.

Figure 14.1. BAGS adjectives are short, common and “subjective”. Also before: autre, premier, dernier (in a series), and numbers.
  • une jolie fille, un jeune homme — a pretty girl, a young man [zho-LEE FEEY · zhuh-NOM]
  • un bon restaurant, un mauvais film — a good restaurant, a bad film
  • une voiture rouge, un chanteur américain — a red car, an American singer
  • un livre intéressant, une question difficile — an interesting book, a difficult question
  • un grand appartement moderne — a big modern flat — one before, one after (liaison: grand‿appartement with a t sound) [ɛ̃ grã-ta-par-tuh-MÃ mo-DERN]
  • C’est mon premier voyage en France. — It’s my first trip to France. [mõ pruh-MYAY vwa-YAZH]

BAGS before, the rest after

Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size go before the noun (une jolie petite maison); colours, nationalities and most others go after (une maison blanche).

docs.title: 14.5 Adjectives that change meaning with position
docs.text:
A few adjectives mean one thing before the noun (often figurative, personal) and another after it (literal, objective). These are favourite exam questions.

Figure 14.2. Before = how you feel about it; after = what it objectively is. Also: le seul ami (the only friend) / un homme seul (a man alone).
  • C’est mon ancien patron. — He’s my former boss. [mõ-nã-SYɛ̃ pa-TRÕ]
  • Ce restaurant est trop cher. — This restaurant is too expensive. [troh SHEHR]
  • Chers amis, bienvenue ! — Dear friends, welcome! [shehr-za-MEE byɛ̃-vuh-NEW]
  • Gandhi était un grand homme. — Gandhi was a great man. (était = was)
  • la semaine dernière / la dernière semaine des vacances — last week (the one just gone) / the last week of the holidays (final in a series)

docs.title: 14.6 Colours: mostly agree, some never change
docs.text:
Most colour adjectives agree like any other adjective, and they always go after the noun:

Masc. Fem. Masc. pl. Fem. pl. noir noire noirs noires vert verte verts vertes bleu bleue bleus bleues blanc blanche blancs blanches violet violette violets violettes rouge · jaune · rose rouge · jaune · rose rouges · jaunes · roses rouges · jaunes · roses

But two groups are invariable — they never take -e or -s:

  • des chaussures marron, des chemises orange — brown shoes, orange shirts — colours named after a thing (marron = chestnut, orange = the fruit) do not change. Also: kaki, crème, turquoise. [ma-RÕ · o-RÃZH]
  • des yeux bleu clair, une robe vert foncé — light blue eyes, a dark green dress — compound colours never change [bluh KLEHR · vehr fõ-SAY]

Note the exceptions: rose, mauve and fauve come from nouns but do agree: des fleurs roses.

Invariable colours

Colours that are also nouns (marron, orange) and compound colours (bleu clair, vert foncé) never change: des sacs marron, des yeux bleu clair.

docs.title: 14.7 Mistakes learners really make
docs.text:
Adjective traps

  • Wrong: une rouge voiture
  • Right: une voiture rouge

  • Why: Colours always go after the noun. English order does not work.

  • Wrong: Ma mère est très gentil.

  • Right: Ma mère est très gentille.

  • Why: The adjective agrees with mère (feminine): gentil → gentille.

  • Wrong: un beau homme / un nouveau ami

  • Right: un bel homme / un nouvel ami

  • Why: Before a masculine vowel sound: bel, vieil, nouvel.

  • Wrong: un film bon

  • Right: un bon film

  • Why: bon is a BAGS adjective (goodness): before the noun.

  • Wrong: des chaussures marrons

  • Right: des chaussures marron

  • Why: marron (from the chestnut) is invariable.

  • Wrong: Les filles sont heureux.

  • Right: Les filles sont heureuses.

  • Why: -eux → -euse in the feminine, + s in the plural.

  • Wrong: une chemise blanque

  • Right: une chemise blanche
  • Why: blanc → blanche (and franc → franche, sec → sèche).

docs.title: 14.8 In real life — describing a flat and a flatmate
docs.text:
• — Alors, ton nouvel appartement, il est comment ? — So, what’s your new flat like?
  • — Il est petit mais très lumineux. Il y a une belle cuisine moderne. — It’s small but very bright. There’s a beautiful modern kitchen.
  • — Et ta colocataire ? Elle est sympa ? — And your flatmate? Is she nice?
  • — Oui, elle est italienne, très drôle et un peu bavarde. Elle a les cheveux longs et les yeux verts. — Yes, she’s Italian, very funny and a bit chatty. She has long hair and green eyes.
  • — Et le quartier ? — C’est un vieux quartier calme, avec de jolies petites rues. — And the area? — It’s a quiet old area, with pretty little streets. (de before a plural adjective)

À retenir

  • An adjective agrees with its noun (add -e for feminine, -s for plural) and usually goes after it: une robe noire, des livres intéressants.
  • Adding -e often makes a silent final consonant sound: petit [puh-TEE] / petite [puh-TEET]. The plural -s stays silent.
  • Before a masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or silent h, use bel, vieil, nouvel: un bel homme, un vieil ami, un nouvel hôtel.
  • Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size go before the noun (une jolie petite maison); colours, nationalities and most others go after (une maison blanche).
  • Colours that are also nouns (marron, orange) and compound colours (bleu clair, vert foncé) never change: des sacs marron, des yeux bleu clair.
  • Adjectives describe; possessives and demonstratives point — my, your, this, that — in My, your, this, that. Today, describe your room in five adjectives, checking each agreement.

docs.title: 14.9 Practice — Adjectives
docs.text:
Exercise 1

une maison ___ (blanc)

  • blanc
  • blanche
  • blanque
  • blance
Answer

blanche

blanc → blanche in the feminine.

Exercise 2

un ___ hôtel (nouveau)

  • nouveau
  • nouvel
  • nouvelle
  • nouveaux

Hint: silent h = vowel sound

Answer

nouvel

Before a masculine vowel sound: nouvel.

Exercise 3

Which order is correct?

  • une rouge petite voiture
  • une petite voiture rouge
  • une voiture petite rouge
  • une rouge voiture petite
Answer

une petite voiture rouge

Size (BAGS) before, colour after.

Exercise 4

'my former teacher'

  • mon professeur ancien
  • mon ancien professeur
  • ma ancienne professeur
  • mon professeur vieux
Answer

mon ancien professeur

ancien before the noun = former.

Exercise 5

des sacs ___ (brown)

  • marrons
  • marron
  • marronnes
  • brun
Answer

marron

marron is invariable.

Exercise 6

Elle est très ___ (sportif).

Answer

sportive

-if → -ive.

Exercise 7

Mes sœurs sont ___ (heureux).

Answer

heureuses

-eux → -euse, plus -s for plural.

Exercise 8

un ___ ami (vieux)

Hint: before a vowel

Answer

vieil

vieux → vieil before a masculine vowel.

Exercise 9

C'est une ___ idée ! (bon)

Answer

bonne

bon → bonne (double n).

Exercise 10

des problèmes ___ (national)

Answer

nationaux

-al → -aux in the masculine plural.

Exercise 11

Pick the wrong word.

Ma grand-mère est très gentil.

Answer

Wrong word: gentil.

Corrected: Ma grand-mère est très gentille.

Feminine: gentille.

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

J'ai acheté une bleue robe.

Answer

Wrong word: bleue.

Corrected: J'ai acheté une robe bleue.

Colours go after the noun.

Exercise 13

Match the phrase to its meaning.

A B un grand homme my own room un homme grand a clean room ma propre chambre a great man une chambre propre a tall man Answer

un grand homme — a great man; un homme grand — a tall man; ma propre chambre — my own room; une chambre propre — a clean room

Before = figurative, after = literal.

Exercise 14

Put the words in order.

Words: a / noire / belle / Elle / une / voiture

Answer

Elle a une belle voiture noire

belle (beauty) before, noire (colour) after.

Exercise 15

Put the words in order.

Words: bon / restaurant / indien / un / C'est

Answer

C'est un bon restaurant indien

bon before, indien (nationality) after.

Exercise 16

Say it aloud — make the bel flow into the noun.

C'est un bel appartement

Answer

bel before a vowel: bel‿appartement [beh-la-par-tuh-MÃ].

Exercise 17

Describe a friend.

Mon amie est grande et très gentille

Answer

Feminine agreement: grande, gentille.

Next step

Adjectives describe; possessives and demonstratives point — my, your, this, that — in My, your, this, that. Today, describe your room in five adjectives, checking each agreement.

docs.title: Chapter 30: Advanced compound tenses
docs.text:
Plus-que-parfait, futur antérieur…

I had done, I will have done, I would have done: these tenses let you place one action before another, in the past, the future or the imagination. They sound advanced, but they are all built with one rule you already know from the passé composé. Learn the rule, see the timeline, and you can tell any story in the right order.

One rule builds them all

Compound tense = avoir / être in a simple tense + past participle. The auxiliary’s tense decides the name, and the result always means "one step before" that simple tense.

docs.title: 30.1 The auxiliary decides the tense
docs.text:
Everything you learned in The past: passé composé still applies: the same verbs take être, the same agreement rules apply. Only the tense of the auxiliary changes.

Auxiliary in the… Compound tense Example présent passé composé j’ai fini · je suis parti imparfait plus-que-parfait j’avais fini · j’étais parti futur futur antérieur j’aurai fini · je serai parti conditionnel conditionnel passé j’aurais fini · je serais parti passé simple passé antérieur j’eus fini · je fus parti subjonctif présent subjonctif passé que j’aie fini · que je sois parti
  • Elle était déjà partie. — She had already left. (être → agreement: partie)
  • Nous nous serions perdus sans GPS. — We would have got lost without GPS. (reflexive → être)
  • Ils auront fini avant ce soir. — They will have finished before this evening.
  • Je suis heureux que vous ayez aimé le spectacle. — I’m happy you liked the show. (subjonctif passé — see The subjunctive)

docs.title: 30.2 The plus-que-parfait — "had done"
docs.text:
imparfait of avoir/être + past participle. It describes an action completed before another past moment. Think of it as the past of the past.

manger (avoir) arriver (être) je / j’ avais mangé étais arrivé(e) tu avais mangé étais arrivé(e) il / elle avait mangé était arrivé / arrivée nous avions mangé étions arrivé(e)s vous aviez mangé étiez arrivé(e)(s) ils / elles avaient mangé étaient arrivés / arrivées
  • Quand je suis arrivé, le film avait déjà commencé. — When I arrived, the film had already started.
  • Il était épuisé : il n’avait pas dormi de la nuit. — He was exhausted: he hadn’t slept all night. (the cause, further back)
  • J’ai perdu les clés qu’il m’avait données. — I lost the keys he had given me.
  • Si seulement j’avais su ! — If only I had known! (regret)
  • Elle s’était levée à cinq heures pour prendre le train. — She had got up at five to catch the train.

You will also meet it after si in the third conditional pattern (si j’avais su, je serais venu — see Conditional & si clauses) and in reported speech (il a dit qu’il avait fini — see Passive & reported speech).

Careful

  • Wrong: Quand je suis arrivé à la gare, le train est déjà parti.
  • Right: Quand je suis arrivé à la gare, le train était déjà parti.
  • Why: The train left before I arrived — that earlier action needs the plus-que-parfait. déjà is a strong signal.

docs.title: 30.3 The futur antérieur — "will have done"
docs.text:
future of avoir/être + past participle. It describes an action that will be finished before another future moment.

finir (avoir) partir (être) je / j’ aurai fini serai parti(e) tu auras fini seras parti(e) il / elle aura fini sera parti / partie nous aurons fini serons parti(e)s vous aurez fini serez parti(e)(s) ils / elles auront fini seront partis / parties

docs.title: Use 1 — after quand, dès que, une fois que…
docs.text:
This is where English and French differ most. English says "when you have finished" (present perfect). French, logically, says "when you will have finished" — because it is in the future.

Figure 30.1. Both actions are in the future; the one that is finished first takes the futur antérieur.
  • Quand tu auras fini, tu pourras sortir. — When you have finished, you can go out.
  • Dès que j’aurai reçu ton message, je t’appellerai. — As soon as I’ve received your message, I’ll call you.
  • Une fois que les invités seront partis, on rangera. — Once the guests have left, we’ll tidy up.

docs.title: Use 2 — deadlines
docs.text:
• D’ici vendredi, j’aurai terminé le rapport. — By Friday, I will have finished the report.
  • Dans dix ans, nous aurons remboursé la maison. — In ten years, we will have paid off the house.

docs.title: Use 3 — a guess about the past
docs.text:
A very French use: the futur antérieur can express a probable explanation of something that already happened — English "must have".

  • Paul n’est pas là ? Il aura raté son bus. — Paul isn’t here? He must have missed his bus.
  • Je ne trouve plus mes lunettes. Je les aurai laissées au bureau. — I can’t find my glasses. I must have left them at the office.

The English trap

"When / as soon as / once I have done" (future meaning) = quand / dès que / une fois que + futur antérieur. Never the passé composé.

Careful

  • Wrong: Quand j’ai fini mes études, je voyagerai.
  • Right: Quand j’aurai fini mes études, je voyagerai.
  • Why: Both actions are in the future; finishing comes first → futur antérieur.

docs.title: 30.4 The conditionnel passé — "would have done"
docs.text:
conditional of avoir/être + past participle. It talks about a past that did not happen: regrets, reproaches, missed chances.

faire (avoir) venir (être) je / j’ aurais fait serais venu(e) tu aurais fait serais venu(e) il / elle aurait fait serait venu / venue nous aurions fait serions venu(e)s vous auriez fait seriez venu(e)(s) ils / elles auraient fait seraient venus / venues

docs.title: The four regret phrases
docs.text:
French English Example j’aurais dû + inf. I should have J’aurais dû accepter. j’aurais pu + inf. I could have J’aurais pu gagner. j’aurais aimé / voulu + inf. I would have liked J’aurais aimé te voir. il aurait fallu + inf. we should have; it was necessary Il aurait fallu partir plus tôt.
  • J’aurais dû t’écouter. — I should have listened to you.
  • Tu aurais pu me prévenir ! — You could have warned me! (a reproach)
  • Sans ton aide, je ne serais jamais arrivé jusqu’ici. — Without your help, I would never have got this far.
  • Si tu m’avais demandé, je t’aurais aidé. — If you had asked me, I would have helped you.
  • Selon les médias, l’avion aurait décollé avec deux heures de retard. — According to the media, the plane reportedly took off two hours late.

It also works as a "future perfect seen from the past": Il a promis qu’il aurait fini avant midi. (He promised he would have finished before noon.)

Careful

  • Wrong: J’aurais dû de venir.
  • Right: J’aurais dû venir.
  • Why: devoir and pouvoir take a bare infinitive — no de. Note also: it is j’aurais dû, never "j’aurais devoir".

docs.title: The passé antérieur — recognise it
docs.text:
passé simple of avoir/être + past participle: il eut fini, elle fut partie. It lives only in written narratives that use the passé simple (novels, history books, fairy tales), almost always after quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, après que or à peine… que. It marks an action finished just before the next one. You need to recognise it, not to use it.

avoir verbs être verbs je / j’ eus fini fus parti(e) il / elle eut fini fut parti / partie nous eûmes fini fûmes parti(e)s ils / elles eurent fini furent partis / parties
  • Dès qu’il eut fini son repas, il sortit. — As soon as he had finished his meal, he went out.
  • Lorsqu’elle fut partie, le silence retomba sur la maison. — When she had gone, silence fell over the house again.

docs.title: The passé surcomposé — the spoken cousin
docs.text:
Speech has no passé simple, so to say the same thing out loud some speakers use a "double" compound: avoir in the passé composé + past participle — il a eu fini. It is especially common in the south of France and in Switzerland. Understand it; in standard French you can simply say quand il a fini or après avoir fini.

  • Quand il a eu fini de manger, il est parti. — When he had finished eating, he left.

Same idea, three registers

Literary: Dès qu’il eut fini, il partit. Spoken (regional): Dès qu’il a eu fini, il est parti. Neutral: Après avoir fini, il est parti. — see Gérondif & participles.

docs.title: 30.6 The full timeline
docs.text:
Here is every indicative tense on one line. The compound tenses always sit just before the simple tense whose auxiliary they borrow.

Figure 30.2. Top: the tenses seen from today. Bottom: the same logic one step back — from a past moment, the conditional plays the role of the future, and the conditionnel passé the role of the futur antérieur.

Read the timeline in pairs

plus-que-parfait comes before the passé composé; futur antérieur before the futur simple; conditionnel passé before the conditionnel présent. Each compound is the "earlier" partner of its simple tense.

docs.title: 30.7 Sequencing a story
docs.text:
In a real story the tenses work as a team. The passé composé moves the plot forward, the imparfait paints the scene, and the plus-que-parfait flashes back. Read this short story and look at the tense of each verb.

  • Ce matin-là, il pleuvait et j’étais en retard. — That morning it was raining and I was late. (imparfait: the scene)
  • La veille, j’avais oublié de régler mon réveil. — The night before, I had forgotten to set my alarm. (plus-que-parfait: flashback)
  • J’ai couru jusqu’à la gare, mais le train était déjà parti. — I ran to the station, but the train had already left. (event + earlier event)
  • Si j’avais pris un taxi, je l’aurais eu. — If I had taken a taxi, I would have caught it. (unreal past)
  • Maintenant, j’ai une règle : quand j’aurai réglé mon réveil, j’irai me coucher. — Now I have a rule: once I’ve set my alarm, I’ll go to bed. (futur antérieur → futur)

Narrative roles

passé composé = what happened next · imparfait = the scene · plus-que-parfait = what had happened before · conditionnel passé = what could have happened.

docs.title: 30.8 Mistakes to avoid
docs.text:
Careful

  • Wrong: Elle avait parti avant midi.
  • Right: Elle était partie avant midi.
  • Why: The auxiliary choice never changes between tenses: partir takes être in every compound tense, with agreement.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je te rendrai ton livre quand je l’ai lu.
  • Right: Je te rendrai ton livre quand je l’aurai lu.
  • Why: Reading will be finished before giving back, and both are in the future → futur antérieur after quand.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je serais venu si tu m’aurais invité.
  • Right: Je serais venu si tu m’avais invité.
  • Why: The conditionnel passé goes in the result; after si use the plus-que-parfait.
  • À ta place, j’aurais tout de suite dit oui. — In your place, I would have said yes straight away.
  • Ils auront sûrement oublié le rendez-vous. — They must surely have forgotten the appointment.

À retenir

  • Compound tense = avoir / être in a simple tense + past participle. The auxiliary’s tense decides the name, and the result always means "one step before" that simple tense.
  • "When / as soon as / once I have done" (future meaning) = quand / dès que / une fois que + futur antérieur. Never the passé composé.
  • plus-que-parfait comes before the passé composé; futur antérieur before the futur simple; conditionnel passé before the conditionnel présent. Each compound is the "earlier" partner of its simple tense.
  • passé composé = what happened next · imparfait = the scene · plus-que-parfait = what had happened before · conditionnel passé = what could have happened.
  • Tell the story of your worst journey in six sentences, using at least one plus-que-parfait and one conditionnel passé. Then continue with Passive & reported speech, where these tenses shift.

docs.title: 30.9 Practice — Compound tenses
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Quand nous sommes arrivés, ils ___ déjà dîné.

  • ont
  • avaient
  • auront
  • auraient

Hint: Before a past moment

Answer

avaient

An action before another past action → plus-que-parfait: ils avaient dîné.

Exercise 2

Appelle-moi dès que tu ___ ton examen.

  • as passé
  • passes
  • auras passé
  • avais passé

Hint: Finished before a future/command

Answer

auras passé

dès que + futur antérieur for a future action completed first.

Exercise 3

J'___ dû te le dire plus tôt.

  • avais
  • aurais
  • aurai
  • ai

Hint: I should have…

Answer

aurais

Regret: j'aurais dû = I should have.

Exercise 4

Elle n'est pas encore là ? Elle ___ le train.

  • aura raté
  • rate
  • raterait
  • avait raté

Hint: A guess about the past

Answer

aura raté

The futur antérieur can express a probable explanation: she must have missed it.

Exercise 5

Which tense is « il eut fini »?

  • passé antérieur
  • plus-que-parfait
  • passé surcomposé
  • futur antérieur
Answer

passé antérieur

passé simple of avoir (eut) + participle = passé antérieur, a literary tense.

Exercise 6

D'ici 2030, nous ___ (finir) les travaux.

Hint: futur antérieur, nous

Answer

aurons fini

Deadline in the future → futur antérieur: nous aurons fini.

Exercise 7

Si tu étais venue, tu ___ (s'amuser).

Hint: conditionnel passé, être

Answer

te serais amusée / te serais amusé

Reflexive verb → être: tu te serais amusée.

Exercise 8

Il m'a rendu le livre que je lui ___ (prêter) l'an dernier.

Answer

avais prêté

Lending came before giving back → plus-que-parfait.

Exercise 9

Elles ___ (partir) quand le téléphone a sonné.

Hint: plus-que-parfait, être

Answer

étaient parties

partir takes être; feminine plural agreement: étaient parties.

Exercise 10

Pick the wrong word.

Quand j'ai fini ce livre demain, je te le prêterai.

Answer

Wrong word: j'ai.

Corrected: Quand j'aurai fini ce livre demain, je te le prêterai.

Future action finished first → futur antérieur: j'aurai fini.

Exercise 11

Pick the wrong word.

Elle avait arrivé avant nous.

Answer

Wrong word: avait.

Corrected: Elle était arrivée avant nous.

arriver takes être in every compound tense.

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

Le bus est déjà parti quand je suis arrivé.

Answer

Wrong word: est.

Corrected: Le bus était déjà parti quand je suis arrivé.

The earlier past action needs the plus-que-parfait: était parti.

Exercise 13

Match the tense to its meaning.

A B j'avais fait I would have done j'aurai fait I had done (literary) j'aurais fait I had done j'eus fait I will have done Answer

j'avais fait — I had done; j'aurai fait — I will have done; j'aurais fait — I would have done; j'eus fait — I had done (literary)

imparfait / futur / conditionnel / passé simple of avoir + participle.

Exercise 14

Match the regret phrase.

A B j'aurais dû I could have j'aurais pu we should have / it was necessary il aurait fallu I should have Answer

j'aurais dû — I should have; j'aurais pu — I could have; il aurait fallu — we should have / it was necessary

devoir, pouvoir and falloir in the conditionnel passé.

Exercise 15

Put the words in order: When you have finished, call me.

Words: auras / fini / appelle-moi / tu / Quand

Answer

Quand tu auras fini appelle-moi

quand + futur antérieur, then the imperative.

Exercise 16

Put the words in order: I should have listened to you.

Words: dû / J'aurais / t'écouter

Answer

J'aurais dû t'écouter

j'aurais dû + bare infinitive.

Exercise 17

Say it aloud.

Si j'avais su je serais venu

Answer

si + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel passé.

Exercise 18

Say it aloud.

Le film avait déjà commencé

Answer

plus-que-parfait: avait + commencé.

Next step

Tell the story of your worst journey in six sentences, using at least one plus-que-parfait and one conditionnel passé. Then continue with Passive & reported speech, where these tenses shift.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Adverbs
docs.text:
Les adverbes

An adjective describes a thing; an adverb describes an action or a quality: how, when, where, how much, how often. Most French adverbs end in -ment, like English “-ly”. The good news: adverbs never agree. The tricky part: where they go — often not where English puts them.

In one line

An adverb tells you how, when, where, how much or how often. It never changes its ending, and in a simple tense it comes right after the verb: Il parle bien.

docs.title: 15.1 What an adverb does
docs.text:
An adverb can describe a verb (she drives carefully), an adjective (very tired), another adverb (too slowly) or a whole sentence (luckily, it stopped raining). Hindi does the same job with words like dheere, bahut, kabhi-kabhi, or with se: dhyaan se = carefully.

  • Elle conduit prudemment. — She drives carefully. (describes the verb) [prew-da-MÃ]
  • Je suis très fatigué. — I am very tired. (describes the adjective) [treh fa-tee-GAY]
  • Tu parles trop vite. — You speak too fast. (trop describes vite) [troh VEET]
  • Heureusement, il ne pleut plus. — Luckily, it isn’t raining any more. (describes the whole sentence) [uh-ruhz-MÃ]

Adverbs never agree

Unlike adjectives, adverbs have one form only: il parle lentement, elles parlent lentement. No -e, no -s.

docs.title: 15.2 Making -ment adverbs
docs.text:
English adds -ly to an adjective: slow → slowly. French adds -ment — but to the feminine form of the adjective. Only three questions decide the spelling:

Figure 15.1. Three questions, three spellings. Then learn the handful of irregulars in section 3.

docs.title: The usual case: feminine + -ment
docs.text:
Masculine Feminine Adverb lent (slow) lente lentement heureux (happy) heureuse heureusement (luckily) doux (gentle) douce doucement sérieux sérieuse sérieusement complet complète complètement franc (frank) franche franchement actif · léger active · légère activement · légèrement facile · rapide facile · rapide facilement · rapidement
  • Parlez plus lentement, s’il vous plaît. — Speak more slowly, please. — the most useful adverb sentence for a learner! [lãt-MÃ]
  • Ferme la porte doucement, le bébé dort. — Close the door gently, the baby is sleeping. [doos-MÃ]
  • J’ai complètement oublié ! — I completely forgot! [kõ-plet-MÃ oo-blee-AY]
  • Franchement, ce film est nul. — Honestly, this film is rubbish. [frãsh-MÃ]

docs.title: Adjectives ending in a vowel: masculine + -ment
docs.text:
If the masculine already ends in a vowel (-ai, -i, -u, -é), just add -ment to it. No extra -e.

  • C’est vraiment délicieux. — It’s really delicious. (vrai → vraiment) [vreh-MÃ day-lee-SYUH]
  • Il a répondu poliment. — He answered politely. (poli → poliment) [po-lee-MÃ]

A few in -u take a circumflex: assidu → assidûment, continu → continûment. You will rarely need them.

docs.title: -ant → -amment, -ent → -emment
docs.text:
Adjectives ending in -ant or -ent drop the -nt and take -mment. The spelling differs (a or e), but the sound is the same: [a-MÃ]. So évidemment sounds like “ay-vee-da-MÃ”, never “ay-vee-duh-MÃ”.

-ant → -amment -ent → -emment constant → constamment évident → évidemment courant → couramment (fluently) récent → récemment suffisant → suffisamment patient → patiemment élégant → élégamment fréquent → fréquemment bruyant → bruyamment (noisily) prudent → prudemment
  • Elle parle couramment trois langues. — She speaks three languages fluently. [koo-ra-MÃ]
  • — Tu viens ce soir ? — Évidemment ! — Are you coming tonight? — Of course! [ay-vee-da-MÃ]
  • Mon voisin se plaint constamment. — My neighbour complains constantly. [kõs-ta-MÃ]

Three spellings

Feminine + -ment (lentement); vowel ending + -ment (vraiment); -ant/-ent → -amment/-emment (constamment, évidemment), both said [a-MÃ].

Careful with lent: it has only one syllable, so it follows the usual rule — lente → lentement, never “lemment”.

docs.title: 15.3 The irregulars, and adverbs that are not -ment
docs.text:
A short list does something unexpected. Learn them as vocabulary:

Adjective Adverb What happens gentil (kind) gentiment the l disappears bref (brief) brièvement new stem briè- précis précisément -é- instead of -e- énorme énormément -é- instead of -e- profond · intense profondément · intensément -é- instead of -e- bon · mauvais bien · mal completely different word
  • Il m’a aidé très gentiment. — He helped me very kindly. [zhã-tee-MÃ]
  • Expliquez brièvement votre projet. — Explain your project briefly. [bree-ev-MÃ]
  • C’est précisément le problème. — That is precisely the problem. [pray-see-zay-MÃ]
  • Ça m’a énormément plu. — I liked it enormously. (plaire → plu) [ay-nor-may-MÃ]

docs.title: Adjectives used as adverbs
docs.text:
In a few fixed pairs, French uses the plain masculine adjective as an adverb. It then never agrees — even with a feminine plural subject.

  • Ces chaussures coûtent cher. — These shoes cost a lot. (not “chères” — cher describes coûter) [koot SHEHR]
  • Les roses sentent bon. — Roses smell good. (also: sentir mauvais, travailler dur, chanter faux) [sãt BÕ]
  • Parle plus fort, je n’entends rien. — Speak louder, I can’t hear anything. (also: parler bas = speak quietly) [ploo FOR]

docs.title: 15.4 Bien or bon? Mal or mauvais? Mieux or meilleur?
docs.text:
This is the number-one adverb mistake. Ask one question: am I describing a thing (noun) or an action (verb)? A thing takes the adjective; an action takes the adverb. English has the same pair: good / well.

Describes a noun (adjective) Describes a verb (adverb) bon, bonne — good bien — well mauvais, mauvaise — bad mal — badly meilleur, meilleure — better mieux — better
  • C’est un bon cuisinier. Il cuisine bien. — He’s a good cook. He cooks well. [ɛ̃ BÕ kwee-zee-NYAY · eel kwee-ZEEN BYɛ̃]
  • J’ai une mauvaise nouvelle : j’ai mal dormi. — I have bad news: I slept badly. [mo-VEZ … MAL dor-MEE]
  • Ce gâteau est meilleur. Tu cuisines mieux que moi. — This cake is better. You cook better than me. [may-YUHR … MYUH]

Thing or action?

A thing is bon / mauvais / meilleur; an action is done bien / mal / mieux: un bon film, il chante bien.

docs.title: The exception: c’est bien
docs.text:
After être, bien can work like an adjective meaning “good, nice, right”: C’est bien ! (Well done! / That’s good.) Ce quartier est bien. (This area is nice.) C’est bon is about taste or “OK, that’s enough”: C’est bon, ce plat ! The full comparison system (plus vite, le mieux, le meilleur) is in Comparing.

  • Tu as fini tes devoirs ? C’est bien ! — You’ve finished your homework? Well done!
  • Mmm, c’est bon ! — Mmm, it’s tasty!

docs.title: 15.5 Where the adverb goes
docs.text:
English often puts an adverb before the verb: “I often eat out”. French never puts it between the subject and the verb. The adverb goes after the conjugated verb.

Figure 15.2. The dashed boxes are the adverb slots. Short adverbs squeeze in before the participle; long and time/place adverbs wait at the end.

docs.title: Simple tenses: right after the verb
docs.text:
• Je mange souvent au restaurant. — I often eat at restaurants. [zhuh mãzh soo-VÃ]
  • Nous aimons beaucoup ce quartier. — We like this neighbourhood a lot. [boh-KOO]
  • Elle ne sort pas souvent. — She doesn’t go out often. (adverb after the ne…pas sandwich)

docs.title: Compound tenses: short adverbs before the participle
docs.text:
In the passé composé, the conjugated verb is the helper (avoir/être). Short, common adverbs go between the helper and the participle: bien, mal, déjà, encore, toujours, souvent, beaucoup, trop, assez, peu, vite, presque. So do the common -ment words of degree and certainty: vraiment, complètement, probablement, certainement.

  • J’ai bien mangé. — I ate well. / I had a good meal. [zhay byɛ̃ mã-ZHAY]
  • J’ai déjà fini. — I have already finished. [zhay day-ZHA fee-NEE]
  • Il a probablement oublié. — He has probably forgotten.

docs.title: Long -ment adverbs of manner: after the participle
docs.text: • Il a parlé lentement. — He spoke slowly.

docs.title: Time and place: at the start or at the end
docs.text:
Words like hier, aujourd’hui, demain, ici, là-bas, partout never go between the helper and the participle.

  • Hier, je suis allé au cinéma. — Yesterday I went to the cinema. [ee-YEHR]
  • On a dîné ici hier soir. — We had dinner here last night. [ee-SEE ee-yehr SWAR]

docs.title: With an infinitive: before it
docs.text:
• Il faut bien réfléchir. — You have to think carefully.
  • Essaie de ne pas trop manger. — Try not to eat too much.

Position in three lines

After the conjugated verb (il parle bien); short adverbs before the participle (j’ai bien mangé); long manner adverbs and time/place words at the end (il a parlé lentement hier).

docs.title: 15.6 The everyday adverbs: time, place, quantity, frequency
Time and place
docs.text:
Time Place aujourd’hui, hier, demain — today, yesterday, tomorrow ici, là — here, there maintenant, bientôt — now, soon là-bas — over there tôt, tard — early, late partout, ailleurs — everywhere, elsewhere déjà, encore — already, still/again près, loin — near, far d’abord, ensuite, enfin — first, then, finally dedans, dehors — inside, outside tout de suite, longtemps — right away, (for) a long time dessus, dessous — on top, underneath
  • J’arrive tout de suite ! — I’m coming right away! [toot SWEET]
  • Il fait beau, on mange dehors ? — The weather’s nice — shall we eat outside? [duh-OR]
  • D’abord on visite le musée, ensuite on déjeune. — First we visit the museum, then we have lunch.

docs.title: Quantity and degree
docs.text:
très (very) goes with adjectives and adverbs; beaucoup (a lot) goes with verbs. With a noun, quantity adverbs take de: beaucoup de, trop de, assez de, peu de (see Articles).

Adverb Meaning Example très very très chaud, très bien beaucoup (de) a lot (of) Il lit beaucoup. · beaucoup de livres trop (de) too, too much trop cher · trop de sucre assez (de) enough, quite assez grand · assez de temps peu / un peu (de) little / a little Il mange peu. · un peu de lait tellement · si so (very) C’est tellement beau ! · Il est si gentil. presque almost J’ai presque fini.
  • C’est assez loin, mais c’est tellement joli ! — It’s quite far, but it’s so pretty! [a-SAY LWɛ̃ … tel-MÃ zho-LEE]

docs.title: Frequency: from always to never
docs.text:
French English Sound toujours always (also: still) [too-ZHOOR] souvent often [soo-VÃ] parfois · quelquefois sometimes [par-FWA · kel-kuh-FWA] de temps en temps from time to time [duh tã-zã-TÃ] rarement rarely [rar-MÃ] ne … jamais never [zha-MEH]
  • Je prends toujours le métro. — I always take the metro.
  • Il habite toujours à Lyon ? — Does he still live in Lyon? (toujours = still)
  • On va parfois à la plage, mais on ne va jamais à la montagne. — We sometimes go to the beach, but we never go to the mountains.

Jamais needs ne

jamais is a negative word: je ne mange jamais de viande. The full system of ne… jamais, ne… plus, ne… rien is in Saying no.

docs.title: 15.7 Tout as an adverb: “completely, very”
docs.text:
Before an adjective, tout means “quite, completely, very”: tout petit = tiny. It is an adverb, so normally it does not change. But French has one famous exception, for the ear: before a feminine adjective starting with a consonant (or an aspirated h), tout agrees.

Before a consonant Before a vowel / mute h masc. sing. il est tout petit il est tout heureux masc. pl. ils sont tout petits ils sont tout heureux fem. sing. elle est toute petite elle est tout heureuse fem. pl. elles sont toutes petites elles sont tout émues
  • Le chaton est tout petit. — The kitten is tiny. [too puh-TEE]
  • Sa fille est encore toute petite. — His/her daughter is still very small. [toot puh-TEET]
  • Elle est tout heureuse de te voir. — She is so happy to see you. (vowel sound → tout, with liaison [too-tuh-RUHZ])

Useful fixed phrases: tout de suite (right away), tout à fait (exactly, quite), tout à l’heure (in a moment / a moment ago), tout droit (straight on). Tout as “all, every” (tous les jours, toute la journée) is covered in Tout, chaque, quelqu’un….

docs.title: 15.8 Mistakes learners really make
docs.text:
Adverb traps

  • Wrong: Je souvent mange des fruits.
  • Right: Je mange souvent des fruits.

  • Why: English order (“I often eat”) does not work. The adverb follows the conjugated verb.

  • Wrong: Elle parle français très bon.

  • Right: Elle parle très bien français.

  • Why: parler is an action → bien. bon describes nouns: un bon livre.

  • Wrong: Je t’aime très.

  • Right: Je t’aime beaucoup.

  • Why: très needs an adjective or adverb after it. With a verb, use beaucoup. And never “très beaucoup”.

  • Wrong: J’ai mangé bien. / J’ai hier mangé.

  • Right: J’ai bien mangé. / J’ai mangé hier.

  • Why: Short adverbs go before the participle; time words go at the end (or the start).

  • Wrong: évidentement · constantment

  • Right: évidemment · constamment

  • Why: -ent → -emment, -ant → -amment. Both are pronounced [a-MÃ].

  • Wrong: vraiement · poliement

  • Right: vraiment · poliment

  • Why: After a vowel, no feminine -e: just add -ment to the masculine.

  • Wrong: Ces robes coûtent chères.

  • Right: Ces robes coûtent cher.
  • Why: cher here describes the verb coûter, so it is an adverb: no agreement. Compare: ces robes sont chères (adjective).

docs.title: 15.9 In real life — how was the weekend?
docs.text:
• — Alors, ce week-end à Paris, ça s’est bien passé ? — So, did the weekend in Paris go well?
  • — Très bien ! On a énormément marché et on a vraiment bien mangé. — Very well! We walked an enormous amount and we ate really well.
  • — Et ton français ? Tu as parlé facilement ? — And your French? Did you speak easily?
  • — Pas toujours. Les gens parlent tellement vite ! Mais ils répétaient patiemment. — Not always. People speak so fast! But they repeated patiently.
  • — Heureusement ! Tu y retournes bientôt ? — Luckily! Are you going back soon?
  • — Évidemment ! Probablement en mai. — Of course! Probably in May.

À retenir

  • An adverb tells you how, when, where, how much or how often. It never changes its ending, and in a simple tense it comes right after the verb: Il parle bien.
  • Unlike adjectives, adverbs have one form only: il parle lentement, elles parlent lentement. No -e, no -s.
  • Feminine + -ment (lentement); vowel ending + -ment (vraiment); -ant/-ent → -amment/-emment (constamment, évidemment), both said [a-MÃ].
  • A thing is bon / mauvais / meilleur; an action is done bien / mal / mieux: un bon film, il chante bien.
  • After the conjugated verb (il parle bien); short adverbs before the participle (j’ai bien mangé); long manner adverbs and time/place words at the end (il a parlé lentement hier).
  • jamais is a negative word: je ne mange jamais de viande. The full system of ne… jamais, ne… plus, ne… rien is in Saying no.

docs.title: 15.10 Practice — Adverbs
docs.text:
Exercise 1

lent → ___

  • lentement
  • lemment
  • lentment
  • lentamment
Answer

lentement

lent has one syllable: feminine lente + -ment.

Exercise 2

évident → ___

  • évidentement
  • évidemment
  • évidamment
  • évidentment
Answer

évidemment

-ent → -emment, pronounced [a-MÃ].

Exercise 3

Il chante très ___.

  • bon
  • bien
  • bonne
  • meilleur

Hint: chanter is an action

Answer

bien

An action is done bien; bon describes nouns.

Exercise 4

C'est un très ___ film.

  • bien
  • bon
  • mieux
  • bonnement
Answer

bon

film is a noun → the adjective bon.

Exercise 5

Elle est ___ petite.

  • tout
  • toute
  • tous
  • toutes

Hint: feminine + consonant

Answer

toute

Adverb tout agrees before a feminine adjective starting with a consonant.

Exercise 6

Ces chaussures coûtent ___.

  • cher
  • chères
  • chers
  • chèrement
Answer

cher

cher describes the verb coûter: it is an adverb, so no agreement.

Exercise 7

vrai → ___

Answer

vraiment

Vowel ending: just add -ment.

Exercise 8

constant → ___

Answer

constamment

-ant → -amment.

Exercise 9

heureux → ___

Hint: feminine first

Answer

heureusement

heureuse + -ment.

Exercise 10

Tu cuisines ___ que moi. (better)

Answer

mieux

Describes how you cook (a verb) → mieux, not meilleur.

Exercise 11

Pick the wrong word.

Je souvent mange au restaurant.

Answer

Wrong word: souvent.

Corrected: Je mange souvent au restaurant.

The adverb goes after the conjugated verb.

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

Je t'aime très.

Answer

Wrong word: très.

Corrected: Je t'aime beaucoup.

With a verb, use beaucoup; très needs an adjective or adverb.

Exercise 13

Put the words in order.

Words: J'ai / déjà / devoirs / fini / mes

Answer

J'ai déjà fini mes devoirs

Short adverb between the helper and the participle.

Exercise 14

Put the words in order.

Words: a / Il / parlé / lentement

Answer

Il a parlé lentement

A long -ment adverb of manner goes after the participle.

Exercise 15

Match the adjective to its adverb.

A B gentil précisément bref énormément précis gentiment énorme brièvement Answer

gentil — gentiment; bref — brièvement; précis — précisément; énorme — énormément

These four are irregular: learn them by heart.

Exercise 16

How often does the speaker go to the swimming pool?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Le week-end, je me lève toujours tard. Je vais parfois au cinéma, mais je ne vais jamais à la piscine.

  • never
  • sometimes
  • often
  • always
Answer

never

ne… jamais = never.

Exercise 17

What does the speaker always do at the weekend?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Le week-end, je me lève toujours tard. Je vais parfois au cinéma, mais je ne vais jamais à la piscine.

  • gets up late
  • goes to the cinema
  • gets up early
  • goes swimming
Answer

gets up late

je me lève toujours tard = I always get up late.

Exercise 18

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Elle parle couramment français et elle conduit prudemment.

couramment (-ant) and prudemment (-ent): same sound, different spelling.

Exercise 19

Say it aloud — the most useful request for a learner.

Parlez plus lentement, s'il vous plaît

Answer

lentement [lãt-MÃ]: the middle e is almost silent.

Next step

Now point at things: My, your, this, that covers mon/ma/mes and ce/cette/ces. Today, describe how you did five things yesterday — j’ai bien dormi, j’ai vite mangé… — checking where each adverb goes.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Alphabet & accents
docs.text:
L’alphabet et les accents

French uses the same 26 letters as English, but it names most of them differently — and it adds small marks called accents. An accent is not decoration: it can change the sound (e vs é) or the meaning (ou “or” vs où “where”). In this chapter you learn to say the letters, spell your name aloud, and read every accent.

Accents are part of the spelling

A word written without its accent is misspelled. Learn été as “é-t-é”, never as “ete”.

docs.title: 2.1 The 26 letters and their names
docs.text:
You need the letter names to spell words aloud — your name, your email, a street. Listen to each name and repeat it. The vowels are pure and short.

Letter French name Sounds like A a a [ah] B b bé [bay] C c cé [say] D d dé [day] E e e [uh] F f effe [ehf] G g gé [zhay] H h ache [ash] I i i [ee] J j ji [zhee] K k ka [kah] L l elle [ehl] M m emme [ehm] N n enne [ehn] O o o [oh] P p pé [pay] Q q qu [kew] R r erre [ehr] S s esse [ehss] T t té [tay] U u u [ew] V v vé [vay] W w double vé [doo-bluh-VAY] X x ixe [eeks] Y y i grec [ee-GREK] Z z zède [zehd]
  • A, B, C, D, E, F, G — The first seven letters in one breath.
  • W, X, Y, Z — The last four: double vé, ixe, i grec, zède.

docs.title: 2.2 The letters that trick English speakers
docs.text:
Most letter names are easy. A few are dangerous because they sound like a different English letter. These are the ones people get wrong when spelling an email on the phone.

Figure 2.1. Highlighted tiles are the traps. Above all: French G sounds like English “J” and French J like English “G” — they are swapped, with a soft “zh”.

The swapped pairs

G = gé [zhay], J = ji [zhee] — the reverse of English. And E = [uh], I = [ee]: French I sounds like English E.

Careful

  • Wrong: Spelling Gita as “jee, eye, tee, ay”.
  • Right: G-I-T-A = gé, i, té, a [zhay, ee, tay, ah].
  • Why: English letter names confuse French listeners: your “eye” means nothing to them, and your “jee” sounds to them like the letter J (ji).

Careful

  • Wrong: Saying “aitch” or “haitch” for H.
  • Right: H = ache [ash].
  • Why: And the letter itself is never pronounced in French words: hôtel = [o-TEL].

Careful

  • Wrong: Saying “why” for Y.
  • Right: Y = i grec [ee-GREK], “the Greek i”.
  • Why: Inside words, y usually sounds like [ee]: un stylo [stee-LO].
  • G, J — gé, ji — Say the swapped pair five times.
  • E, I — e, i — E is [uh], I is [ee].

docs.title: 2.3 Spelling words aloud
docs.text:
To spell is épeler [ay-puh-LAY]. These are the phrases you will hear at a hotel desk, on the phone, or when someone writes down your name.

  • Comment ça s’écrit ? — How do you spell that? (literally: how is that written?) [ko-mã sa say-KREE]
  • Vous pouvez épeler, s’il vous plaît ? — Can you spell it, please? [voo poo-vay ay-puh-LAY seel voo PLEH]
  • Mon prénom, c’est Priya. Ça s’écrit P, R, I, Y, A. — My first name is Priya. It is spelled P-R-I-Y-A.
  • Mon nom de famille, c’est Sharma : S, H, A, R, M, A. — My surname is Sharma: S-H-A-R-M-A.
  • Ça s’écrit avec deux L. — It is spelled with two Ls (double letters: deux L, “two L”).

docs.title: Words for spelling
docs.text:
You say Meaning e accent aigu é e accent grave è e accent circonflexe ê c cédille ç i tréma ï majuscule / minuscule capital / small letter arobase @ point . (dot) tiret / tiret bas - (hyphen) / _ (underscore)
  • priya.sharma@gmail.com — said: “priya point sharma arobase gmail point com”
  • Élodie : E accent aigu, L, O, D, I, E. — Spelling a French name with an accent.

docs.title: 2.4 The accents at a glance
docs.text:
French has five marks. Only e can take all three “roof” accents; the cedilla goes only under c.

Figure 2.2. Five marks, three jobs: change a sound (é, è, ç, ë), keep a history (ê), or tell two words apart (à, où). Mark Letters Main job accent aigu ´ é Sound: closed [ay] accent grave ` è, à, ù Sound on è: open [eh]. On à, ù: meaning only accent circonflexe ^ â, ê, î, ô, û History (lost s); ê = [eh], ô = closed [oh] tréma ¨ ë, ï, ü (ÿ in a few names) Say this vowel separately cédille ¸ ç c sounds [s] before a, o, u

docs.title: 2.5 é, è, ê — three e’s, two sounds
docs.text:
Plain e is usually a soft [uh] or silent. The accents fix its sound. Smile slightly for é; open your mouth a little more for è and ê.

  • l’été, le café, le bébé — summer, coffee, baby — é = [ay], short and pure, no “y” glide [lay-TAY, ka-FAY, bay-BAY]
  • la mère, le père, très — mother, father, very — è = [eh], like “e” in “bed” [MEHR, PEHR, TREH]
  • la fête, la tête, être — party, head, to be — ê = [eh] too [FET, TET, ETR]
  • un élève — a pupil — both sounds in one word: é then è [ɛ̃-nay-LEV]

é vs è/ê

é = [ay] (closed, smiling) · è = ê = [eh] (open, as in “bed”). Plain e with no accent is usually [uh] or silent.

docs.title: The circumflex: a missing s
docs.text:
Centuries ago many French words had an s after the vowel. The s disappeared, and the circumflex took its place. English often kept the s — so the circumflex is a free vocabulary key.

French English cousin la forêt forest l’hôpital hospital la fête feast (festival) l’île isle (island) le château castle la bête beast le coût cost

On î and û the circumflex changes nothing in sound. On ô it gives a closed [oh]: l’hôtel [lo-TEL]. On â some speakers make a deeper “ah” (pâte, pasta), but most people today say it like a normal a.

docs.title: 2.6 Accents that change the meaning
docs.text:
Some accents change nothing in the sound — they only tell two words apart in writing. You must write them, or your sentence means something else.

Without With Example a = has à = to, at Il a un billet pour aller à Paris. ou = or où = where Où est le thé ou le café ? la = the (f) là = there La clé est là. sur = on sûr = sure Tu es sûr ? C’est sur la table. du = some (m) dû = had to Il a dû acheter du pain. des = some (pl) dès = from (time) Dès demain, je vois des amis. mur = wall mûr = ripe Un fruit mûr près du mur.
  • Il a un billet pour aller à Paris. — He has a ticket to go to Paris. — a and à sound the same
  • Où est le thé ou le café ? — Where is the tea or the coffee? — ou and où sound the same [oo]
  • La clé est là. — The key is there.
  • Tu es sûr ? C’est sur la table. — Are you sure? It's on the table.

docs.title: When the accent changes the sound and the meaning
docs.text:
• je parle / j’ai parlé — I speak / I spoke — the é makes it past [PARL / zhay par-LAY]
  • jeune / le jeûne — young / fasting (like a vrat) — open vs closed eu [ZHÖN / luh ZHÖN]

Typical accent mistakes

  • Wrong: Je vais a Delhi.
  • Right: Je vais à Delhi.

  • Why: “to” = à with the grave accent. Plain a is the verb “has”.

  • Wrong: Ou habites-tu ?

  • Right: Où habites-tu ?

  • Why: The question word “where” always has the accent: où.

  • Wrong: Il fait chaud en ete.

  • Right: Il fait chaud en été.

  • Why: Without accents the word is unreadable: ete would be pronounced like [et].

  • Wrong: ECOLE (on a sign, accents dropped)

  • Right: ÉCOLE
  • Why: Capital letters keep their accents in careful French: À bientôt, État, Ça va.

docs.title: Hard and soft c and g
docs.text:
The letters c and g change sound depending on the next vowel — exactly like in English cat / city, gate / gem. The cedilla and a silent e or u let French choose the sound it wants.

Spelling Sound Examples c + a, o, u [k] le café, la côte, la culture c + e, i, y [s] le centre, la ville de Nice, le cycle ç + a, o, u [s] ça, le garçon, j’ai reçu g + a, o, u [g] la gare, le goût, aigu g + e, i, y [zh] le genou, la girafe, la gym ge + a, o [zh] nous mangeons, Georges gu + e, i [g] la guerre, la guitare
  • Ça va ? Le garçon est français. — How are you? The boy is French. [sa VA … luh gar-SÕ eh frã-SEH]
  • Nous commençons, nous mangeons. — We begin, we eat. — ç and ge keep the soft sound before o [noo ko-mã-SÕ, noo mã-ZHÕ]
  • la guitare, la guerre, la girafe — guitar, war, giraffe — gu = hard g, gi = soft zh [gee-TAR, GEHR, zhee-RAF]

Careful

  • Wrong: le garcon [gar-KÕ]
  • Right: le garçon [gar-SÕ]
  • Why: Before o, a plain c is [k]. The cedilla is what makes it [s].

docs.title: The tréma: say the vowels apart
docs.text:
Two vowels together usually make one sound (ai = [eh], oi = [wa]). The tréma (two dots) says: stop — pronounce this vowel on its own.

  • mais / le maïs — but / corn (maize) [MEH / ma-EESS]
  • Noël, naïf, égoïste — Christmas, naive, selfish [no-EL, na-EEF, ay-go-EEST]

The tréma on ü is rare. You will see it in aigüe (the 1990 spelling of aiguë, “sharp”, feminine).

docs.title: The joined letters œ and æ
docs.text:
œ (called e dans l’o, “e in the o”) is common and sounds like the [ö] of eu. æ is very rare.

  • le cœur, la sœur, un œuf — heart, sister, an egg [KÖR, SÖR, ɛ̃-NÖF]
  • une œuvre d’art, le bœuf — a work of art, beef [ew-NÖVR DAR, luh BÖF]
  • Ils sont ex æquo. — They are tied (equal score). — æ, from Latin [eel sõ eg-zay-KO]

Typing accents

On Windows, add the US-International keyboard: type ' then e for é, ` + e for è, ^ + e for ê, ' + c for ç.

docs.title: 2.8 Letter teams: a preview
docs.text:
French often uses two or three letters for one sound. Learn to see them as a single block. Each one is practised in detail in The sounds of French.

Letters Sound Example ou [oo] vous (you) oi [wa] moi (me) au, eau [oh] beau, l’eau (beautiful, water) ai, ei [eh] le lait, la neige (milk, snow) eu, œu [ö] deux, la sœur (two, sister) an, en [ã] l’enfant (child) on [õ] bonbon (sweet) in, ain, un [ɛ̃] le vin, le pain, un ch [sh] le chat (cat) gn [ny] la montagne (mountain) qu [k] qui, quatre (who, four) ill [y] la fille, la famille ph, th [f], [t] la photo, le thé

Two common exceptions

ill = [eel] in ville (town), mille (thousand) and tranquille (calm). And th is never the English “th”: le thé = [luh TAY].

  • La famille habite dans une ville tranquille. — The family lives in a quiet town. — famille [y], ville and tranquille [eel] [fa-MEEY … VEEL trã-KEEL]
  • Moi, je bois du thé au lait. — Me, I drink tea with milk. [MWA, zhuh bwa dew tay oh LEH]

À retenir

  • A word written without its accent is misspelled. Learn été as “é-t-é”, never as “ete”.
  • G = gé [zhay], J = ji [zhee] — the reverse of English. And E = [uh], I = [ee]: French I sounds like English E.
  • é = [ay] (closed, smiling) · è = ê = [eh] (open, as in “bed”). Plain e with no accent is usually [uh] or silent.
  • On Windows, add the US-International keyboard: type ' then e for é, ` + e for è, ^ + e for ê, ' + c for ç.
  • Spell your full name and your email aloud in French, three times. Then go on to The sounds of French, where every letter team from section 8 gets its own practice.

docs.title: 2.9 Practice — Alphabet & accents
docs.text:
Exercise 1

How do you say the letter G in French?

  • \[jee\]
  • [zhay] gé
  • \[gay\]
  • [zhee] ji
Answer

[zhay] gé

G = gé [zhay]. It is J that is called ji [zhee].

Exercise 2

The French letter J is called…

  • jay
  • ji [zhee]
  • gé [zhay]
  • ja
Answer

ji [zhee]

G and J are swapped compared with English: G = gé, J = ji.

Exercise 3

Which letter is called 'i grec'?

  • I
  • J
  • Y
  • X
Answer

Y

Y = i grec, 'the Greek i'.

Exercise 4

The French letter I sounds like…

  • English 'eye'
  • English 'ee'
  • English 'ay'
  • English 'uh'
Answer

English 'ee'

French I = [ee]; French E = [uh].

Exercise 5

Comment ça s'___ ? (How is it spelled?)

Hint: from écrire, to write

Answer

écrit / ecrit

Comment ça s'écrit ? = How do you spell that?

Exercise 6

Which letter always sounds [ay], as in café?

  • e
  • é
  • è
  • ê
Answer

é

é (accent aigu) is the closed [ay]. è and ê are open [eh].

Exercise 7

Which word means 'where'?

  • ou
  • où
  • au
  • eau
Answer

où

où = where; ou = or. Same sound, different meaning.

Exercise 8

Pick the word with the missing accent.

Il va a Paris demain.

Answer

Wrong word: a.

Corrected: Il va à Paris demain.

'to' = à. Plain a is the verb 'has'.

Exercise 9

Pick the wrong word.

Tu veux du thé où du café ?

Answer

Wrong word: où.

Corrected: Tu veux du thé ou du café ?

'or' = ou, without an accent. où means 'where'.

Exercise 10

The circumflex in 'forêt' often shows…

  • a lost s
  • a silent t
  • a plural
  • a question
Answer

a lost s

forêt = forest, hôpital = hospital, fête = feast: the s became ^.

Exercise 11

Match each mark to its name.

A B é accent circonflexe è cédille ê tréma ç accent aigu ï accent grave Answer

é — accent aigu; è — accent grave; ê — accent circonflexe; ç — cédille; ï — tréma

Five marks: aigu, grave, circonflexe, tréma, cédille.

Exercise 12

le gar___on (the boy) — c or ç?

Hint: before o, plain c sounds [k]

Answer

ç / c cédille

garçon needs ç to sound [s] before o.

Exercise 13

In 'Noël', the two dots on ë mean…

  • the e is silent
  • say o and e separately
  • the word is plural
  • say [ay]
Answer

say o and e separately

The tréma separates vowels: No-ël [no-EL].

Exercise 14

'le maïs' means…

  • but
  • corn
  • the month
  • my
Answer

corn

maïs [ma-EESS] = corn; mais [meh] = but.

Exercise 15

In an email address, '@' is said…

  • at
  • arobase
  • point
  • tiret
Answer

arobase

@ = arobase, . = point, - = tiret, _ = tiret bas.

Exercise 16

Put the words in order: 'How do you spell that?'

Words: ça / Comment / s'écrit

Answer

Comment ça s'écrit

Comment (how) + ça (that) + s'écrit (is written).

Exercise 17

Say it aloud.

Ça s'écrit avec un accent aigu

Answer

sa say-KREE a-vek ɛ̃-nak-SÃ-tay-GEW — notice the links between the words.

Exercise 18

Say it aloud.

Vous pouvez épeler s'il vous plaît

Answer

ay-puh-LAY: three short, even syllables.

Next step

Spell your full name and your email aloud in French, three times. Then go on to The sounds of French, where every letter team from section 8 gets its own practice.

docs.title: Chapter 40: Arguing & presenting
docs.text:
Argumenter et présenter

At B2 and above, people judge you less on grammar and more on how you build an argument. French culture loves a clear plan, announced in advance, with linked arguments, honest concessions and a firm conclusion. This chapter gives you that toolkit — and ends with a full model for the DELF B2 oral exam.

Announce, develop, conclude

Tell the audience what you will say (l’annonce du plan), say it in clearly signposted parts, then tell them what you said. French listeners expect the map before the journey.

docs.title: 40.1 The shape of a French presentation
docs.text:
A French exposé has a fixed skeleton. The introduction alone has three steps: a hook (l’accroche), the question you will answer (la problématique), and the plan (l’annonce du plan).

Figure 40.1. Introduction and conclusion are the shortest parts but the most important: examiners and audiences remember the beginning and the end. Step Signpost Hook Qui n’a jamais perdu une heure sur son téléphone sans s’en rendre compte ? Problem On peut donc se demander si… Plan Dans un premier temps, je montrerai…, puis, dans un second temps, j’examinerai… Part 1 Tout d’abord, … / En premier lieu, … Next point Ensuite, … / En second lieu, … Transition Passons maintenant à… / Venons-en à… Last point Enfin, … / Pour finir, … Conclusion Pour conclure, … / En définitive, …

Careful

  • Wrong: Finalement, je voudrais parler du coût. (meaning "lastly")
  • Right: Enfin, je voudrais parler du coût.
  • Why: Finalement means "in the end / after all" (a result). To introduce your last point, use enfin or pour finir.

docs.title: 40.2 Linking arguments
docs.text:
An argument without connectors is a list. Connectors show the logic: adding, giving a cause, drawing a consequence, illustrating, opposing. (The full family is in Linking words; here are the ones that work best out loud.)

Job Spoken connectors Add de plus · en outre · par ailleurs · qui plus est Cause car · puisque · étant donné que · en effet Consequence donc · par conséquent · c’est pourquoi · si bien que Example par exemple · notamment · prenons le cas de Contrast en revanche · pourtant · alors que · or
  • Le télétravail fait gagner du temps. En effet, il supprime les trajets quotidiens. — Remote work saves time. Indeed, it removes the daily commute. (en effet = "indeed, that’s because" — it confirms, it does not mean "in effect")
  • Les loyers ont beaucoup augmenté, si bien que les jeunes quittent le centre-ville. — Rents have risen a lot, so much so that young people are leaving the city centre.
  • Les villes investissent dans le vélo ; prenons le cas d’Amsterdam. — Cities are investing in cycling; take the case of Amsterdam.
Figure 40.2. Green = your arguments, dashed = examples, red = the other side. Naming the counter-argument yourself (with certes ) and answering it is what turns B1 opinion into B2 argument.

docs.title: 40.3 Nuance and hedging
docs.text:
Strong claims are easy to attack. Nuanced claims are hard to attack and sound more educated. French has a rich set of softeners — but watch which mood each one takes.

Hedge Meaning Il semblerait que les jeunes lisent moins. It would seem that young people read less. Il me semble que c’est une erreur. It seems to me that it’s a mistake. (+ indicative) Dans une certaine mesure, c’est vrai. To a certain extent, it’s true. Il se peut que la situation change. The situation may change. (+ subjunctive) C’est plutôt une bonne nouvelle. It’s rather good news. A priori, rien ne s’y oppose. On the face of it, nothing prevents it. Dans la plupart des cas, … In most cases, … Il est sans doute trop tôt pour juger. It’s probably too early to judge.

sans doute = probably

A classic false friend: sans doute means "probably", not "without doubt". For certainty, say sans aucun doute or certainement.

il semble que vs il me semble que

Il semble que (it seems) usually takes the subjunctive; il me semble que (it seems to me) takes the indicative. Adding me turns doubt into a personal opinion.

  • Il semble que le projet soit trop coûteux. — It seems that the project is too costly. (soit — subjunctive)
  • Il me semble que le projet est trop coûteux. — It seems to me that the project is too costly. (est — indicative)

docs.title: 40.4 Conceding — the "yes, but" of good arguers
docs.text:
To concede is to admit part of the other side before answering it. It shows fairness and makes your rebuttal stronger. Each frame has two halves: the concession, then the counter-point.

  • Certes, la voiture est pratique, mais elle pollue énormément. — Admittedly, the car is practical, but it pollutes enormously.
  • Il est vrai que les réseaux sociaux nous rapprochent ; néanmoins, ils favorisent la désinformation. — It’s true that social networks bring us closer; nevertheless, they encourage misinformation.
  • Bien que cette mesure soit impopulaire, elle est nécessaire. — Although this measure is unpopular, it is necessary. (bien que + subjunctive)
  • Même si c’est cher, c’est un investissement rentable. — Even if it’s expensive, it’s a worthwhile investment. (même si + indicative)
  • Je vous l’accorde, le risque existe. Il n’en reste pas moins que les avantages l’emportent. — I grant you, the risk exists. The fact remains that the advantages outweigh it.
  • On pourrait m’objecter que cela coûte cher. Pourtant, … — One could object that it’s expensive. And yet, … (you raise the objection yourself)

Mood traps in concession

  • Wrong: Bien que ce est difficile, …
  • Right: Bien que ce soit difficile, …

  • Why: Bien que and quoique always take the subjunctive. See The subjunctive.

  • Wrong: Même si ce soit difficile, …

  • Right: Même si c’est difficile, …

  • Why: Même si works like si: indicative, never subjunctive.

  • Wrong: Certes c’est vrai. (and nothing after)

  • Right: Certes, c’est vrai, mais…
  • Why: Certes announces a "but". Without the second half, you have simply agreed with the other side.

docs.title: 40.5 Persuading — making it land
docs.text:
Logic convinces; rhetoric persuades. A few classic devices make a French audience lean in. Use one or two per talk — not all of them.

  • Rhetorical question: Qui d’entre nous n’a jamais eu peur de parler en public ? — Which of us has never been afraid of speaking in public?
  • Imagine: Imaginez un instant une ville sans voitures. — Imagine for a moment a city without cars.
  • Urgency: Il est grand temps d’agir. — It is high time to act.
  • Necessity: Il est indispensable que chacun fasse un effort. — It is essential that everyone makes an effort. (+ subjunctive)
  • Rule of three: C’est plus simple, plus rapide et moins cher. — It’s simpler, faster and cheaper. (three items sound complete)
  • Include the audience: Vous l’avez sans doute remarqué vous-mêmes. — You have probably noticed it yourselves.
  • Personal story: Je me souviens de mon premier jour à Paris… — I remember my first day in Paris… (a short anecdote makes an idea concrete)

Facts beat adjectives

"C’est très, très important" persuades nobody. A precise example, a date, a source (selon un rapport de l’OCDE…) does. Only quote figures you are sure of — an examiner will ask.

docs.title: 40.6 Handling questions and objections
docs.text:
The hardest part of any talk is the questions. These lines buy you time, show respect, and let you answer on your terms.

Line Use it to… C’est une excellente question. buy two seconds Si je comprends bien, vous me demandez si… reformulate and check Vous soulevez un point important. acknowledge an objection Permettez-moi de nuancer. disagree politely Je n’avais pas envisagé les choses sous cet angle. accept a new idea gracefully Je n’ai pas les chiffres exacts en tête, mais… admit a gap honestly Si vous me permettez de terminer… stop an interruption Pour revenir à votre question, … return to the point

Careful

  • Wrong: Je ne sais pas. (silence)
  • Right: Je ne connais pas tous les détails, mais je dirais que…
  • Why: In an exam or a meeting, "I don’t know" ends the exchange. Admit the limit, then still give a reasoned view.

docs.title: 40.7 The DELF B2 oral — a full model
docs.text:
In the DELF B2 production orale, you draw a short document (an article or opinion piece) raising a debate. You have about 30 minutes to prepare, then about 20 minutes with the examiners: you present and defend your point of view, then you debate with them. It is marked out of 25. (Formats are updated from time to time — check the official France Éducation international site before your exam.)

Topic: Faut-il interdire le téléphone portable au lycée ? Should mobile phones be banned in secondary school?

Model monologue — introduction

  • Le document que j’ai choisi traite de la place du téléphone portable à l’école. — The document I chose deals with the place of mobile phones at school. (present the document)
  • Il pose une question simple, mais délicate : faut-il interdire le portable au lycée ? — It raises a simple but delicate question: should phones be banned at secondary school? (problématique)
  • Dans un premier temps, je montrerai les risques du portable en classe ; dans un second temps, j’expliquerai pourquoi une interdiction totale ne me semble pas la meilleure solution. — First I will show the risks of phones in class; then I will explain why a total ban doesn’t seem the best solution to me. (plan)

Model monologue — development and conclusion

  • Tout d’abord, il est évident que les notifications perturbent l’attention des élèves. — First of all, it is obvious that notifications disrupt pupils’ attention. (argument 1)
  • De plus, le portable peut favoriser le harcèlement, notamment sur les réseaux sociaux. — Moreover, phones can encourage bullying, especially on social media. (argument 2)
  • Certes, ces risques sont réels. Néanmoins, le téléphone est aussi un outil pédagogique : dictionnaires, applications, recherches. — Admittedly, these risks are real. Nevertheless, the phone is also a learning tool: dictionaries, apps, research. (concession + counter-point)
  • C’est pourquoi je suis favorable à un usage encadré plutôt qu’à une interdiction totale. — That is why I favour supervised use rather than a total ban. (your position)
  • Pour conclure, la question n’est pas d’interdire, mais d’apprendre aux jeunes à bien utiliser cet outil. — To conclude, the question is not whether to ban, but how to teach young people to use this tool well. (conclusion + opening)

The debate with the examiner

  • Examinateur : Mais un usage encadré, n’est-ce pas difficile à contrôler pour les enseignants ? — But isn’t supervised use hard for teachers to control?
  • Vous : Vous soulevez un point important. Je vous l’accorde, cela demande des règles claires. — You raise an important point. I grant you, it requires clear rules.
  • Vous : Par exemple, les téléphones pourraient rester dans un casier, sauf pendant certaines activités. — For example, phones could stay in a locker, except during certain activities.
  • Examinateur : Et dans votre pays, comment ça se passe ? — And in your country, how does it work?
  • Vous : En Inde, cela dépend des écoles ; il me semble que de plus en plus d’établissements limitent les portables. — In India it depends on the school; it seems to me that more and more schools restrict phones. (hedged — you are not sure of figures)

What B2 examiners reward

A clear position, an announced plan, at least two developed arguments with examples, a concession, varied connectors, and real interaction in the debate — reacting to what the examiner says, not reciting.

À retenir

  • Tell the audience what you will say (l’annonce du plan), say it in clearly signposted parts, then tell them what you said. French listeners expect the map before the journey.
  • Il semble que (it seems) usually takes the subjunctive; il me semble que (it seems to me) takes the indicative. Adding me turns doubt into a personal opinion.
  • "C’est très, très important" persuades nobody. A precise example, a date, a source (selon un rapport de l’OCDE…) does. Only quote figures you are sure of — an examiner will ask.
  • A clear position, an announced plan, at least two developed arguments with examples, a concession, varied connectors, and real interaction in the debate — reacting to what the examiner says, not reciting.
  • You have finished Parler. Record yourself giving the DELF model above, then make your own on a new topic. Next, build the words you argue with in the Vocabulaire part — starting with Core vocabulary by theme.

docs.title: 40.8 Practice — Arguing & presenting
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which phrase announces your plan?

  • Pour conclure,
  • Dans un premier temps…, dans un second temps…
  • Certes,
  • Il se peut que
Answer

Dans un premier temps…, dans un second temps…

L'annonce du plan uses ordinal signposts.

Exercise 2

'Il est sans doute trop tôt.' means…

  • It is without doubt too early.
  • It is probably too early.
  • It is never too early.
  • It is not too early.
Answer

It is probably too early.

sans doute = probably. For certainty: sans aucun doute.

Exercise 3

Bien que cette solution ___ chère, elle est efficace.

  • est
  • soit
  • sera
  • serait
Answer

soit

bien que + subjunctive.

Exercise 4

To introduce your LAST point, use…

  • Finalement
  • Enfin
  • En fait
  • Bref
Answer

Enfin

Finalement = in the end (a result). Enfin / pour finir = lastly.

Exercise 5

Même si c'___ difficile, il faut essayer.

Hint: même si + indicative

Answer

est

même si takes the indicative: même si c'est.

Exercise 6

Il me semble que c'___ une bonne idée.

Hint: il me semble que + ?

Answer

est

il me semble que takes the indicative.

Exercise 7

Pick the wrong word.

Bien que ce est cher, je l'achète.

Answer

Wrong word: est.

Corrected: Bien que ce soit cher, je l'achète.

bien que + subjunctive: soit.

Exercise 8

Pick the wrong word.

Même si ce soit difficile, nous continuerons.

Answer

Wrong word: soit.

Corrected: Même si c'est difficile, nous continuerons.

même si + indicative.

Exercise 9

Match the connector to its job.

A B en outre example par conséquent contrast notamment adding en revanche consequence Answer

en outre — adding; par conséquent — consequence; notamment — example; en revanche — contrast

Connectors show the logic between your ideas.

Exercise 10

Match the parts of the introduction.

A B l'accroche the outline la problématique summary and opening l'annonce du plan the hook la conclusion the question you will answer Answer

l'accroche — the hook; la problématique — the question you will answer; l'annonce du plan — the outline; la conclusion — summary and opening

The French introduction has three fixed steps.

Exercise 11

Put the words in order.

Words: voiture / la / Certes / elle / est / mais / pollue / pratique

Answer

Certes la voiture est pratique mais elle pollue

certes… mais = concession then counter-point.

Exercise 12

Put the words in order.

Words: à / encadré / pourquoi / un / usage / je / favorable / C'est / suis

Answer

C'est pourquoi je suis favorable à un usage encadré

c'est pourquoi introduces your conclusion or position.

Exercise 13

Concede a point.

Je vous l'accorde le risque existe

Answer

Je vous l'accorde = I grant you.

Exercise 14

Buy time when asked a question.

C'est une excellente question

Answer

Then reformulate: Si je comprends bien…

Exercise 15

Disagree politely with an examiner.

Permettez-moi de nuancer

Answer

A respectful way to disagree.

Exercise 16

Hedge your claim.

Dans une certaine mesure c'est vrai

Answer

dans une certaine mesure = to a certain extent.

Exercise 17

Create urgency.

Il est grand temps d'agir

Answer

il est grand temps de + infinitive = it is high time to.

Exercise 18

Conclude your presentation.

Pour conclure la question n'est pas d'interdire

Answer

Pour conclure + your final position.

Next step

You have finished Parler. Record yourself giving the DELF model above, then make your own on a new topic. Next, build the words you argue with in the Vocabulaire part — starting with Core vocabulary by theme.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Articles
docs.text:
Les articles

English often puts nothing in front of a noun: “I drink coffee”, “I love cats”. French almost never does. A French noun nearly always wears an article, and choosing the right one — le, un, du or just de — is one of the clearest signs of good French. This chapter gives you the system and a simple decision tree.

In one line

A French noun almost always needs an article: le/la/les (the, or things in general), un/une/des (a, some), du/de la (some of an uncountable thing).

  • J’aime le café. — I like coffee. (coffee in general) [zhem luh ka-FAY]
  • Je bois du café. — I drink (some) coffee. (an amount of it) [zhuh bwa dew ka-FAY]
  • Je voudrais un café. — I’d like a coffee. (one cup) [zhuh voo-DREH ɛ̃ ka-FAY]
  • Je ne bois pas de café. — I don’t drink coffee. (none at all) [zhuh nuh bwa pa duh ka-FAY]

Same noun, four different articles, four different meanings. Let’s take them one by one.

docs.title: 8.1 The three families at a glance
docs.text:
Masculine Feminine Plural Definite (the) le livre · l’arbre la table · l’eau les livres Indefinite (a, some) un livre une table des livres Partitive (some of) du pain · de l’argent de la soupe · de l’eau des épinards

Elision: le and la become l’ before a vowel or a silent h: l’ami, l’école, l’hôtel. Before an “aspirated” h there is no elision: le héros, la Hollande (see Silent letters & liaison).

  • l’hôtel, l’école, les‿hôtels — the hotel, the school, the hotels [lo-TEL, lay-KOL, lay-zo-TEL]
  • un homme, une heure — a man, an hour [ɛ̃-NOM, ew-NUHR]

docs.title: 8.2 The definite article: le, la, l’, les
docs.text:
French uses le / la / les in two situations. The first is the same as English “the”:

  • Ferme la porte, s’il te plaît. — Close the door, please. (a specific door) [ferm la PORT seel tuh PLEH]
  • Les clés sont sur la table. — The keys are on the table. [lay KLAY sõ sewr la TABL]

The second is where English uses nothing: when you talk about a thing in general — a whole category, a concept, a taste. This is the use English speakers forget most.

  • J’adore la musique indienne. — I love Indian music. [zha-DOR la mew-ZEEK ɛ̃-DYEN]
  • Les chats dorment beaucoup. — Cats sleep a lot. (cats in general) [lay SHA dorm boh-KOO]
  • La santé, c’est important. — Health is important. [la sã-TAY seh-tɛ̃-por-TÃ]
  • Je déteste les épinards. — I hate spinach. [zhuh day-TEST lay-zay-pee-NAR]

Likes take le / la / les

After aimer, adorer, préférer, détester, use the definite article: j’aime le café, je déteste les épinards.

docs.title: Other places French uses le / la / les
docs.text:
