  • Léa : Non, de Bretagne. Mais à mon avis, la cuisine indienne, c’est encore meilleur ! — No, from Brittany. But in my opinion, Indian food is even better!

Dialogue, part 2 — disagreeing nicely and closing

  • Arjun : Sans blague ! Mais je ne suis pas tout à fait d’accord : vos fromages sont imbattables. — No way! But I don’t quite agree: your cheeses are unbeatable.
  • Léa : Tu n’as pas tort ! Tu as déjà goûté le kouign-amann ? — You’re not wrong! Have you ever tried kouign-amann? (a Breton butter cake)
  • Arjun : Non, jamais. C’est quoi exactement ? — No, never. What is it exactly?
  • Léa : Un gâteau au beurre… Écoute, il faut que j’y aille, mais on reste en contact ? — A butter cake… Listen, I have to go, but shall we keep in touch?
  • Arjun : Avec plaisir ! Ça m’a fait plaisir de discuter avec toi. Bonne soirée ! — Gladly! It was nice talking to you. Have a good evening!

À retenir

  • Never give a one-word answer. Answer the question, add one detail, then ask something back. That single habit keeps any French conversation alive.
  • Tant mieux = "so much the better" (good news). Tant pis = "never mind / too bad" (bad news you accept). Mixing them up sounds sarcastic.
  • Missing a word? Describe it: C’est un truc pour… (a thing for…), C’est comme… (it’s like…), le contraire de… (the opposite of…). People will give you the word.
  • Real French conversations will not sound like this book — people drop words, squeeze sounds and sprinkle fillers. Real spoken French trains your ear for chais pas, du coup and friends.

docs.title: 37.9 Practice — Conversation & opinions
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Your friend says: 'Je n'aime pas le café.' You don't either. You say:

  • Moi aussi.
  • Moi non plus.
  • Moi si.
  • Tant mieux.
Answer

Moi non plus.

Agreeing with a negative = moi non plus (me neither).

Exercise 2

'Tu ne viens pas ?' — You ARE coming. You answer:

  • Oui, je viens.
  • Si, je viens !
  • Non, je viens.
  • Moi non plus.
Answer

Si, je viens !

Si contradicts a negative question.

Exercise 3

Your friend's train was cancelled but there's another in 10 minutes. Best reaction?

  • Tant pis !
  • Tant mieux !
  • Sans blague !
  • Félicitations !
Answer

Tant mieux !

Tant mieux = so much the better (relief, good news).

Exercise 4

Which is the softest way to disagree?

  • Pas du tout !
  • Au contraire !
  • Je vois ce que tu veux dire, mais…
  • Tu as tort.
Answer

Je vois ce que tu veux dire, mais…

Acknowledge first, then disagree — the polite French way.

Exercise 5

Je suis ___ avec toi. (in agreement)

Answer

d'accord / d’accord

être d'accord = to agree.

Exercise 6

Qu'est-ce que tu ___ penses ? (about it)

Hint: The pronoun for 'about it'.

Answer

en

penser quelque chose de… → en: Qu'est-ce que tu en penses ?

Exercise 7

Pick the wrong word.

J'ai d'accord avec ton idée.

Answer

Wrong word: J'ai.

Corrected: Je suis d'accord avec ton idée.

être d'accord, not avoir d'accord.

Exercise 8

Pick the wrong word.

Je ne pense pas que c'est vrai.

Answer

Wrong word: c'est.

Corrected: Je ne pense pas que ce soit vrai.

Negative opinion + que → subjunctive: ce soit.

Exercise 9

Match the reaction to the situation.

A B Félicitations ! Surprising news. Oh non, c'est dommage ! Bad news you accept. Sans blague ! She passed her exam. Tant pis. The concert is cancelled. Answer

Félicitations ! — She passed her exam.; Oh non, c'est dommage ! — The concert is cancelled.; Sans blague ! — Surprising news.; Tant pis. — Bad news you accept.

Matching the reaction to the news shows you are really listening.

Exercise 10

Match the opinion frames.

A B À mon avis As I see it Je trouve que Personally D'après moi In my opinion Personnellement I find that Answer

À mon avis — In my opinion; Je trouve que — I find that; D'après moi — As I see it; Personnellement — Personally

Rotate your frames so you don't repeat 'je pense que' every time.

Exercise 11

Put the words in order.

Words: la / vous / que / faites / dans / Qu'est-ce / vie

Answer

Qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie

= What do you do for a living?

Exercise 12

Put the words in order.

Words: discuter / de / plaisir / avec / Ça / m'a / fait / vous

Answer

Ça m'a fait plaisir de discuter avec vous

A warm way to end a conversation.

Exercise 13

Ask for their opinion.

Qu'est-ce que tu en penses

Answer

en = about it.

Exercise 14

React with surprise.

C'est vrai Sans blague

Answer

C'est vrai ? Sans blague ! — two classic surprise reactions.

Exercise 15

Disagree politely.

Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord

Answer

pas tout à fait = not quite — softer than a flat 'no'.

Exercise 16

Give your opinion.

À mon avis c'est une bonne idée

Answer

À mon avis + statement. No need to add je pense que.

Exercise 17

Leave politely.

Bon je vais vous laisser

Answer

The classic polite exit.

Exercise 18

Open a conversation at a party.

Tu connais Thomas comment

Answer

A shared-context opener: how do you know the host?

Next step

Real French conversations will not sound like this book — people drop words, squeeze sounds and sprinkle fillers. Real spoken French trains your ear for chais pas, du coup and friends.

docs.title: Chapter 41: Core vocabulary by theme
docs.text:
Le vocabulaire de base

These are the words you will use every single day: your family, your home, what you eat and wear, your body, the weather and the town around you. Every noun comes with its article and its colour — blue = masculine, pink = feminine, violet = plural — because in French a noun without its gender is only half learned.

Figure 41.1. Eight themes, about 150 words. Even the theme names are colour-coded: la famille, le corps, les couleurs.

docs.title: 41.1 Learn every noun with its article
docs.text:
Every French noun is either masculine or feminine — even a table, a shirt or the rain. The gender changes the article (le/la, un/une), the adjectives and the pronouns. If you learn only "maison", you will have to guess later. If you learn "la maison", the gender comes for free.

The golden rule

Never learn a bare noun. Learn la chaise, le lit — the article is part of the word.

When the article hides the gender

Before a vowel, le and la both become l’. So learn those words with un/une: un appartement, une école.

Hindi speakers: Hindi also has two genders, which is a real advantage — you already think in "masculine/feminine". But never copy the Hindi gender across. Kitaab is feminine in Hindi, but le livre is masculine; paani is masculine, but l’eau is feminine; chai is feminine, but le thé is masculine.

Some endings help: words in -tion, -té, -ette are mostly feminine; words in -ment, -age, -eau are mostly masculine. The full list is in Nouns, gender & plurals.

  • La table est dans la cuisine. — The table is in the kitchen. [la TABL ay dã la kwee-ZEEN]
  • Le problème, c’est le prix. — The problem is the price. [luh pro-BLEM say luh PREE]

Careful

  • Wrong: La problème est simple.
  • Right: Le problème est simple.
  • Why: Words in -ème from Greek are masculine, even though they end in -e: le problème, le système, le thème.

Three habits that work

Say each word aloud with its article · stick labels on things at home (la porte, le frigo) · learn ten words a day and review them the next morning.

docs.title: 41.2 La famille — the family
docs.text:
French English Sound le père father [luh PEHR] la mère mother [la MEHR] les parents parents [lay pa-RÃ] le frère brother [luh FREHR] la sœur sister [la SUHR] le fils son [luh FEESS] la fille daughter; girl [la FEEY] le mari husband [luh ma-REE] la femme wife; woman [la FAM] le grand-père grandfather [luh grã-PEHR] la grand-mère grandmother [la grã-MEHR] l’oncle (m) uncle [LÕKL] la tante aunt [la TÃT] le cousin / la cousine cousin [koo-Zɛ̃ / koo-ZEEN] les enfants children [lay-zã-FÃ]

Two words do double duty: la femme is both "woman" and "wife", and la fille is both "girl" and "daughter". Context tells you which. Hindi has separate words for every uncle (chacha, mama, tau, mausa…); French has just l’oncle. To be precise, say l’oncle du côté de mon père (my father’s side).

  • J’ai deux frères et une sœur. — I have two brothers and a sister. [zhay duh FREHR ay ewn SUHR]
  • Ma mère s’appelle Priya. — My mother is called Priya.
  • Mon oncle habite à Lyon avec sa femme. — My uncle lives in Lyon with his wife.
  • Nous sommes cinq dans ma famille. — There are five of us in my family.

Careful

  • Wrong: Mon mère est professeur.
  • Right: Ma mère est professeur.
  • Why: "My" agrees with the noun (mère is feminine), not with the person speaking. A man also says ma mère. See My, your, this, that.

docs.title: 41.3 La maison — home and rooms
docs.text:
Figure 41.2. A French house, colour-coded. Upstairs is le premier étage ; the ground floor is le rez-de-chaussée . French English Sound la maison house, home [la may-ZÕ] un appartement flat, apartment [ɛ̃-na-par-tuh-MÃ] la chambre bedroom [la SHÃBR] la cuisine kitchen; cooking [la kwee-ZEEN] le salon living room [luh sa-LÕ] la salle de bains bathroom [la sal duh Bɛ̃] les toilettes (f) toilet [lay twa-LET] la salle à manger dining room [la sal a mã-ZHAY] le jardin garden [luh zhar-Dɛ̃] la porte · la fenêtre door · window [PORT · fuh-NETR] le lit · la chaise bed · chair [LEE · SHEZ] le canapé · une armoire sofa · wardrobe [ka-na-PAY · ar-MWAR] le frigo · la clé fridge · key [free-GO · KLAY]

Which floor?

French counts floors like British English: le rez-de-chaussée = ground floor, le premier étage = the floor above it (an American "second floor").

  • J’habite dans un appartement au troisième étage. — I live in a flat on the third floor.
  • Il y a trois chambres dans la maison. — There are three bedrooms in the house. [eel-ya trwa SHÃBR]
  • La cuisine est petite, mais le salon est grand. — The kitchen is small, but the living room is big.

Careful

  • Wrong: Ce soir, je vais à ma maison.
  • Right: Ce soir, je rentre à la maison / chez moi.
  • Why: "Home" = à la maison or chez moi — never "à ma maison". See Prepositions & places for chez.

docs.title: 41.4 Manger et boire — food and drink
docs.text: French English Sound le pain bread [luh Pɛ̃] le beurre · le fromage butter · cheese [BUHR · fro-MAZH] la viande meat [la VYÃD] le poulet · le poisson chicken · fish [poo-LAY · pwa-SÕ] un œuf → des œufs an egg → eggs [ɛ̃-NUHF → day-ZUH] le riz · les légumes (m) rice · vegetables [REE · lay-GEWM] les fruits (m) · la pomme fruit · apple [FRWEE · POM] la pomme de terre potato ("earth apple") [la pom duh TEHR] l’eau (f) water [LO] le lait · le thé · le café milk · tea · coffee [LAY · TAY · ka-FAY] le jus d’orange · le vin orange juice · wine [zhew do-RÃZH · Vɛ̃] le sucre · le sel sugar · salt [SEWKR · SEL]

docs.title: The three meals
docs.text:
France English Québec le petit-déjeuner breakfast le déjeuner le déjeuner lunch le dîner le dîner dinner le souper

When you eat or drink some of something, French uses du, de la, de l’ — the partitive. The details are in Articles; here, just copy the pattern.

  • Le matin, je bois du thé avec du lait. — In the morning I drink tea with milk.
  • Je voudrais un café et un croissant, s’il vous plaît. — I would like a coffee and a croissant, please.
  • Je ne mange pas de viande : je suis végétarien. — I don’t eat meat: I’m vegetarian. (A woman says végétarienne.) [vay-zhay-ta-RYɛ̃]

Poisson or poison?

le poisson [pwa-SÕ] with a hard s = fish. le poison [pwa-ZÕ] with a z sound = poison. Order carefully!

docs.title: 41.5 Le corps — the body
docs.text:
French English Sound la tête head [la TET] les cheveux (m) hair (on the head) [lay shuh-VUH] un œil → les yeux an eye → the eyes [ɛ̃-NUHY → lay-ZYUH] le nez · la bouche nose · mouth [NAY · BOOSH] une oreille · les dents (f) ear · teeth [o-RAY · DÃ] le cou · le dos neck · back [KOO · DO] le bras · la main arm · hand [BRA · Mɛ̃] le doigt · le ventre finger · stomach [DWA · VÃTR] la jambe · le genou leg · knee [ZHÃB · zhuh-NOO] le pied foot [luh PYAY]

It hurts: avoir mal à

Pain = avoir mal à + the body part: j’ai mal à la tête, au dos, à l’oreille, aux dents.

  • J’ai mal à la tête. — I have a headache. (literally: I have pain at the head) [zhay MAL a la TET]
  • Mon père a mal au dos. — My father has backache.
  • Elle a les yeux marron et les cheveux longs. — She has brown eyes and long hair.
  • Je me lave les mains. — I wash my hands.

Notice: with body parts, French usually says the hand, not my hand — the owner is already clear (je me lave). See Reflexive verbs.

Careful

  • Wrong: J’ai mal à ma tête.
  • Right: J’ai mal à la tête.
  • Why: With avoir mal à, use the article, not "my". The "j’" already says whose head it is.

docs.title: 41.6 Les vêtements et les couleurs — clothes and colours
docs.text:
French English Sound le pantalon trousers (one pair) [luh pã-ta-LÕ] le jean · le short jeans · shorts [DJEEN · SHORT] la chemise shirt [la shuh-MEEZ] le tee-shirt · le pull T-shirt · sweater [tee-SHUHRT · PEWL] la robe · la jupe dress · skirt [ROB · ZHEWP] la veste · le manteau jacket · coat [VEST · mã-TO] les chaussures (f) shoes [lay sho-SEWR] les chaussettes (f) socks [lay sho-SET] le chapeau · une écharpe hat · scarf [sha-PO · ay-SHARP]

Two key verbs: porter = to wear (state), mettre = to put on (action).

  • Aujourd’hui, je porte un jean et un pull bleu. — Today I’m wearing jeans and a blue sweater.
  • Mets ton manteau, il fait froid ! — Put your coat on, it’s cold!

Careful

  • Wrong: J’ai acheté des pantalons noirs. (meaning one pair)
  • Right: J’ai acheté un pantalon noir.
  • Why: English says "trousers, jeans, shorts" (plural); French counts one pair as one thing: un pantalon, un jean, un short.

docs.title: Colours — and how they agree
docs.text:
Masculine Feminine English noir noire black blanc blanche white vert verte green bleu bleue blue (same sound) gris grise grey violet violette purple rouge · jaune · rose · beige same red · yellow · pink · beige marron · orange never change brown · orange

Colours come after the noun and agree

un pull vert · une jupe verte · des chaussures vertes — but marron and orange never change. More in Adjectives.

  • Elle porte une robe rouge et des chaussures noires. — She is wearing a red dress and black shoes.
  • J’aime ta chemise blanche. — I like your white shirt. [ta shuh-meez BLÃSH]

docs.title: 41.7 Le temps et les saisons — weather and seasons
docs.text:
French describes weather with il fait (literally "it makes"), with a few special verbs like il pleut, or with il y a (there is). The word le temps means both "weather" and "time".

  • Quel temps fait-il ? — What’s the weather like? [kel tã feh-TEEL]
  • Il fait beau. Il fait chaud. — The weather is nice. It’s hot. [eel feh BO · eel feh SHO]
  • Il fait froid. Il fait mauvais. — It’s cold. The weather is bad. [feh FRWA · feh mo-VEH]
  • Il pleut. Il neige. — It’s raining. It’s snowing. [eel PLUH · eel NEZH]
  • Il y a du vent et des nuages. — It’s windy and cloudy. (there is wind and clouds)
  • Il fait trente degrés à Delhi. — It’s thirty degrees in Delhi.
Season In … English le printemps au printemps spring l’été (m) en été summer l’automne (m) en automne autumn l’hiver (m) en hiver winter la mousson pendant la mousson monsoon
  • En Inde, la mousson commence en juin. — In India, the monsoon starts in June.

Careful

  • Wrong: Il est froid aujourd’hui.
  • Right: Il fait froid aujourd’hui.
  • Why: Weather uses il fait. "Il est froid" means "he (or it, a thing) is cold" — like a cold plate or an unfriendly man.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je suis froid.
  • Right: J’ai froid.
  • Why: A person has cold or heat: j’ai froid, j’ai chaud. "Je suis froid" means "I am a cold, unfriendly person". See Être & avoir.

Three weather owners

The weather: il fait froid. A thing: c’est froid. A person: j’ai froid.

docs.title: 41.8 La ville — the city
docs.text:
French English Sound la ville · la rue town, city · street [VEEL · REW] la place · le parc square · park [PLASS · PARK] le magasin · le marché shop · market [ma-ga-Zɛ̃ · mar-SHAY] la boulangerie bakery [la boo-lã-zhuh-REE] la pharmacie · la banque chemist · bank [far-ma-SEE · BÃK] la gare train station [la GAR] un arrêt de bus bus stop [a-reh duh BEWS] un hôpital · une école hospital · school [o-pee-TAL · ay-KOL] le musée museum [luh mew-ZAY] le cinéma · le restaurant cinema · restaurant [see-nay-MA · res-to-RÃ] la voiture · le vélo car · bicycle [vwa-TEWR · vay-LO] le bus · le métro · le train bus · underground · train [BEWS · may-TRO · TRɛ̃]

How you travel

Inside a vehicle: en voiture, en bus, en train. On top of it or on your feet: à vélo, à pied.

  • La gare est près de la banque. — The station is near the bank.
  • Je vais au marché à pied. — I walk to the market. (I go to the market on foot)
  • Il y a une pharmacie dans cette rue ? — Is there a chemist’s in this street?
  • On va au cinéma ce soir ? — Shall we go to the cinema tonight?

Careful

  • Wrong: Je visite la musée du Louvre.
  • Right: Je visite le musée du Louvre.
  • Why: Most words in -ée are feminine (la journée), but le musée and le lycée are masculine. Learn them with their article.

Asking the way, buying bread and taking the metro are practised as full dialogues in Everyday French.

docs.title: 41.9 In real life — a postcard from Lyon
docs.text:
Ananya is staying with her aunt in France. Almost every theme of this chapter is in her card.

  • Salut Rohan ! Je suis à Lyon chez ma tante. — Hi Rohan! I’m in Lyon at my aunt’s.
  • Elle habite dans une grande maison avec un joli jardin. — She lives in a big house with a pretty garden.
  • Ma chambre est au premier étage, à côté de la salle de bains. — My room is on the first floor, next to the bathroom.
  • Ici, il fait froid et il pleut souvent, alors je porte mon gros manteau. — Here it’s cold and it often rains, so I wear my thick coat.
  • Le matin, on mange du pain avec du beurre et de la confiture. — In the morning we eat bread with butter and jam.
  • Demain, on va au marché et au musée. Bises, Ananya — Tomorrow we’re going to the market and the museum. Love, Ananya

À retenir

  • Never learn a bare noun. Learn la chaise, le lit — the article is part of the word.
  • Before a vowel, le and la both become l’. So learn those words with un/une: un appartement, une école.
  • Say each word aloud with its article · stick labels on things at home (la porte, le frigo) · learn ten words a day and review them the next morning.
  • Pain = avoir mal à + the body part: j’ai mal à la tête, au dos, à l’oreille, aux dents.
  • un pull vert · une jupe verte · des chaussures vertes — but marron and orange never change. More in Adjectives.
  • The weather: il fait froid. A thing: c’est froid. A person: j’ai froid.

docs.title: 41.10 Practice — Core vocabulary
docs.text:
Exercise 1

___ problème (the problem)

  • le
  • la
  • les
  • l'

Hint: -ème words from Greek

Answer

le

problème is masculine: le problème, le système.

Exercise 2

How do you say "It's cold" (the weather)?

  • Il est froid
  • Il fait froid
  • J'ai froid
  • Je suis froid
Answer

Il fait froid

Weather uses il fait.

Exercise 3

How do you say "I'm cold" (I feel cold)?

  • Je suis froid
  • Il fait froid
  • J'ai froid
  • Je fais froid
Answer

J'ai froid

A person has cold: avoir froid.

Exercise 4

___ mère s'appelle Anita. (My)

Hint: mère is feminine

Answer

Ma

ma + feminine noun: ma mère.

Exercise 5

J'ai mal ___ dos. (I have backache)

Hint: à + le

Answer

au

à + le dos = au dos.

Exercise 6

À Mumbai, il ___ beaucoup en juillet. (pleuvoir)

Hint: it rains

Answer

pleut

pleuvoir → il pleut.

Exercise 7

Pick the wrong word.

Elle porte une robe vert.

Answer

Wrong word: vert.

Corrected: Elle porte une robe verte.

robe is feminine, so the colour takes -e: verte.

Exercise 8

Pick the wrong word.

Mon mère habite à Delhi.

Answer

Wrong word: Mon.

Corrected: Ma mère habite à Delhi.

The possessive agrees with mère (feminine): ma.

Exercise 9

Pick the wrong word.

Ce matin, je suis froid.

Answer

Wrong word: suis.

Corrected: Ce matin, j'ai froid.

Feeling cold = avoir froid.

Exercise 10

Match the family words.

A B le frère uncle la sœur daughter l'oncle brother la fille sister Answer

le frère — brother; la sœur — sister; l'oncle — uncle; la fille — daughter

la fille also means girl.

Exercise 11

Match the rooms.

A B la cuisine living room la chambre bathroom le salon kitchen la salle de bains bedroom Answer

la cuisine — kitchen; la chambre — bedroom; le salon — living room; la salle de bains — bathroom

la chambre is a bedroom, not any room.

Exercise 12

Match the weather.

A B Il pleut It's windy Il neige The weather is nice Il y a du vent It's raining Il fait beau It's snowing Answer

Il pleut — It's raining; Il neige — It's snowing; Il y a du vent — It's windy; Il fait beau — The weather is nice

il fait, il pleut, il y a — three weather patterns.

Exercise 13

I bought ___ (one pair of trousers).

  • un pantalon
  • une pantalon
  • des pantalons
  • un pantalons
Answer

un pantalon

One pair of trousers is one masculine noun: un pantalon.

Exercise 14

___ printemps (in spring)

  • en
  • au
  • à
  • dans
Answer

au

au printemps, but en été, en automne, en hiver.

Exercise 15

Put the words in order.

Words: y / trois / la / chambres / Il / dans / maison / a

Answer

Il y a trois chambres dans la maison

il y a = there is / there are.

Exercise 16

Put the words in order.

Words: yeux / Elle / les / a / bleus

Answer

Elle a les yeux bleus

French uses avoir + les + body part + colour.

Exercise 17

Say it aloud.

J'ai deux frères et une sœur

Answer

sœur sounds like [SUHR].

Exercise 18

Say it aloud.

Quel temps fait-il aujourd'hui

Answer

fait-il links as [feh-TEEL].

Next step

Nouns name the world; verbs make it move. Go on to The 100 essential verbs to learn the verbs you will use with all these words.

docs.title: Chapter 57: Culture & the francophone world
docs.text:
Culture et francophonie

Perfect grammar is only half of speaking French. The other half is knowing what people expect: the bonjour at the bakery, the vous at the office, two kisses — or four. And French is not only France: more than 320 million people speak it on five continents, from Montréal to Dakar, and even in a corner of India.

In one line

Greet before you ask (Bonjour, madame), use vous until you are invited to switch, and remember that French sounds different — and uses different words — in Paris, Montréal, Brussels, Dakar and Pondichéry.

  • Bonjour, madame. Une baguette, s’il vous plaît. — Hello (madam). A baguette, please.
  • On peut se tutoyer ? — Shall we say “tu” to each other?
  • Au Québec, on dîne à midi. — In Québec, people have “dîner” (lunch) at noon.

docs.title: 57.1 Bonjour first — la politesse
docs.text:
In France, bonjour is not just “hello”. It is a small ritual that says “I see you as a person”. You say it when you walk into a small shop, a pharmacy, a doctor’s waiting room, a lift, and when you get on a bus and pass the driver. Asking a question without it feels rude — even if your French is perfect.

The shop rule

Enter: Bonjour, madame / monsieur. Leave: Merci, au revoir, bonne journée ! No name needed — madame or monsieur alone is polite.

  • Bonjour, monsieur. Je voudrais deux croissants, s’il vous plaît. — Hello. I’d like two croissants, please.
  • Excusez-moi de vous déranger, vous savez où est la poste ? — Sorry to bother you, do you know where the post office is?
  • Merci, au revoir ! Bonne journée ! — Thanks, goodbye! Have a nice day!
Situation Say Meaning Arriving (day / after about 6 p.m.) Bonjour / Bonsoir Hello / Good evening Asking for something S’il vous plaît Please Answering “merci” (formal / casual) Je vous en prie / De rien You’re welcome Leaving Au revoir, bonne journée Goodbye, have a good day

Careful

  • Wrong: (walking in) Une baguette, s’il vous plaît.
  • Right: Bonjour, madame ! Une baguette, s’il vous plaît.
  • Why: Skipping bonjour sounds cold and demanding. Many French people will reply with a pointed “Bonjour…” first.

docs.title: 57.2 Tu or vous? — le vouvoiement
docs.text:
French has two ways to say “you”. Vous is polite and keeps a respectful distance; tu is close and friendly. Indian readers already know the idea: vous ≈ Hindi aap, tu ≈ tum. French simply has no third, very intimate level like Hindi tu. The verbs are vouvoyer (to say vous) and tutoyer (to say tu). Vous is also always the plural “you”, even among friends.

Vous — by default Tu — normally Strangers, shop and office staff Family, friends, partners Older people you don’t know well Children and teenagers Your boss, clients, teachers (from lycée on) Classmates, people your age at a party Your partner’s parents — until they invite you Animals — and God, in prayers

Who decides to switch? Usually the older or more senior person offers. Young people and many start-ups use tu almost at once; banks, law firms and the civil service keep vous much longer. In Québec, tu is far more common, even with strangers.

  • On peut se tutoyer, si vous voulez. — We can say “tu”, if you like. (said in vous — the switch hasn’t happened yet)
  • Vous êtes prêts, les enfants ? — Are you ready, kids? (plural vous — not formal at all)

Careful

  • Wrong: (to a stranger in the street) Tu sais où est la gare ?
  • Right: Excusez-moi, vous savez où est la gare ?
  • Why: “Do you know where the station is?” With an adult stranger, tu sounds rude or oddly familiar. When in doubt, use vous — nobody is offended by it.

Once tu, always tu

After you switch to tu, going back to vous sounds like a cold message: “we are no longer close”.

docs.title: 57.3 La bise — how many kisses?
docs.text:
Friends and family in France greet with la bise: you touch cheeks lightly and make a small kiss sound in the air. Lips do not really touch the skin. Women greet women and men this way; men give each other the bise mostly in the family or among close friends (more often in the south). At work, a handshake — une poignée de main — is safer.

The famous question is how many. The answer depends on the region, the town, the family and the age group. The map below is a rough sketch, not a rule.

Figure 57.1. A schematic sketch of la bise in France. Borders are fuzzy: two neighbouring towns, or two families, may do it differently.
  • On se fait la bise ? — Shall we do the bise? (a perfectly normal question today)
  • Chez toi, c’est combien de bises ? — Where you’re from, how many kisses is it? (a classic small-talk topic)

Careful

  • Wrong: En France, on fait toujours deux bises.
  • Right: En France, on fait souvent deux bises, mais ça dépend de la région.
  • Why: “In France people often do two kisses, but it depends on the region.” Anything from one to four is normal. Pulling away after two in Montpellier leaves the other person hanging.

docs.title: 57.4 At the table — à table !
docs.text:
Meals are a big part of French life — long, social and fairly regular. Lunch (le déjeuner) is usually between noon and 2 p.m., and many restaurant kitchens close after that. Dinner (le dîner) is around 7.30–9 p.m., later in the south. Children have le goûter, an afternoon snack, around 4.30. Before dinner with friends comes l’apéro: a drink and nibbles, sometimes so big it replaces dinner (un apéro dînatoire).

Table manners in four lines

Bread goes on the table beside your plate, and you tear it by hand. Keep both hands visible on the table (wrists on the edge), not on your lap. Let the host pour the wine. Wait for « Bon appétit ! » before you start.

  • Bon appétit ! — Merci, à vous aussi. — Enjoy your meal! — Thanks, you too.
  • On prend l’apéro ? — Shall we have a pre-dinner drink?
  • C’était délicieux. Je reprendrais bien un peu de fromage ! — That was delicious. I’d gladly have a little more cheese!

The bill: traditionally, one person invites and pays — « C’est moi qui invite. » Splitting a restaurant bill item by item used to be frowned upon, and some places still dislike it; today friends often split it evenly or pay each other back by app. Service is included in French prices (service compris), so a tip is small and optional.

  • Non, non, c’est moi qui invite ! — No, no, it’s my treat!

Careful

  • Wrong: Je suis plein, merci.
  • Right: Merci, je n’ai plus faim. C’était délicieux.
  • Why: For “I’m full”, say “I’m not hungry any more”. In France je suis plein sounds odd or jokey (plein can mean drunk; pleine is used for pregnant animals). In Québec, je suis plein is fine.

The bon appétit nuance

Everyday French says « Bon appétit ! » all the time — at home, at work, even to strangers eating lunch. Only in very formal, old-school etiquette is it seen as unrefined. As a learner, say it: it is warm and expected.

docs.title: In real life — invited to dinner
docs.text:
Arrive about ten to fifteen minutes after the time given — never early. Bring flowers, chocolates or a bottle of wine (but never chrysanthemums: they are for graves).

  • Bonsoir ! Entrez, entrez ! — Good evening! Come in, come in!
  • Merci de m’avoir invitée. Je vous ai apporté des fleurs. — Thank you for inviting me. I’ve brought you some flowers. (a woman speaking: invitée; a man says invité)

docs.title: 57.5 The French year — fêtes et rythmes
docs.text:
Holidays, food traditions, a long summer break, a big restart in September: knowing the French year helps you follow small talk and the news.

Date Fête What happens 6 January (or 1st Sunday) l’Épiphanie la galette des rois: whoever finds the fève (charm) is king or queen and wears the paper crown 2 February la Chandeleur crêpes for everyone 1 April le poisson d’avril jokes; children stick paper fish on people’s backs 1 May la fête du Travail holiday, marches; people offer du muguet (lily of the valley) for luck 14 July la fête nationale military parade on the Champs-Élysées, fireworks, bals 1 November la Toussaint families put chrysanthemums on graves 11 November l’Armistice remembrance of 1918, ceremonies at war memorials 24–25 December Noël le réveillon (big Christmas Eve meal), la bûche de Noël
  • Poisson d’avril ! — April fool!

docs.title: Three words for the French rhythm
docs.text:
Faire le pont — “to make the bridge”: when a holiday falls on a Thursday, many people also take Friday off. May, with several holidays, is full of ponts. Les grandes vacances — the long summer holidays (July–August); Paris empties in August. La rentrée — early September, when school, work, politics and even new novels (la rentrée littéraire) start again.

  • Cette année, le 1er mai tombe un jeudi : on fait le pont ! — This year, 1 May falls on a Thursday: we’re taking the Friday off too!
  • Tu pars où pendant les grandes vacances ? — Where are you going for the summer holidays?

docs.title: 57.6 The Republic — symboles et institutions
docs.text:
France calls itself la République, and its symbols are everywhere. The motto Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité is carved on town halls (mairies) and schools. Marianne, a woman in a red Phrygian cap, stands for the Republic: her bust is in every mairie, and her face is on stamps and French euro coins. Add the drapeau tricolore (blue, white, red), the anthem La Marseillaise and the cockerel (le coq) of sports teams.

Word What it is Why it comes up l’Assemblée nationale the lower house: 577 députés votes laws, with the Sénat l’Académie française 40 writers and scholars, founded in 1635 gives (advisory!) opinions on “good French” la Sécu la Sécurité sociale, public health insurance you show your carte Vitale at the doctor’s le bac the end-of-school exam, around age 18 job ads say bac +3, bac +5 = years of study after it les grandes écoles very selective schools: Polytechnique, ENS, HEC… entered after two years of prépa — a bit like the IIT/IIM race

docs.title: La laïcité
docs.text:
La laïcité is French secularism, based on a 1905 law separating the Churches and the State. The State favours no religion, and since 2004 pupils in state schools may not wear conspicuous religious signs. Indian secularism is closer to “equal respect for all religions”; laïcité means “religion stays out of public institutions”. It is a sensitive topic.

  • La France est une république laïque. — France is a secular republic.
  • Elle a un bac +5 en informatique. — She has a master’s-level degree (five years after the bac) in computer science.

docs.title: 57.7 La francophonie — French on five continents
docs.text:
About 321 million people speak French (estimate of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, OIF, 2022), which makes it one of the most spoken languages in the world. The OIF brings together nearly 90 states and governments, and 20 March is the Journée internationale de la Francophonie. The surprise for many learners: most people who use French every day live in Africa, not in Europe.

Figure 57.2. French speakers by region — rounded orders of magnitude, not exact census figures.

docs.title: West and Central Africa
docs.text:
In Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire, Mali, Cameroon or the DR Congo, French is the language of school, government and media, next to local languages (Wolof, Bambara, Lingala…). Kinshasa is often called the largest French-speaking city in the world. Abidjan’s street slang, nouchi, has spread far beyond Côte d’Ivoire.

  • Ne t’inquiète pas, ça va aller. — Don’t worry, it’s going to be OK. (heard everywhere in West Africa)
  • Ce soir, on va s’enjailler au maquis avec ma go. — Tonight we’re going to have fun at the open-air restaurant with my girlfriend. (nouchi: s’enjailler from English “enjoy”, une go = a girl / girlfriend)

docs.title: The Maghreb
docs.text:
Everyday speech switches freely between Arabic (often local darija), Tamazight and French — sometimes inside one sentence. Some of these words have entered French slang in France.

  • Wesh, ça va ? Yalla, on y va ! — Hey, how’s it going? Come on, let’s go! (wesh and yalla come from Arabic)

docs.title: The Caribbean and overseas France
docs.text:
Martinique, Guadeloupe, French Guiana (la Guyane), La Réunion and Mayotte are full French départements: part of France and of the EU, with the euro. Many people there also speak a creole — a full language whose vocabulary comes mostly from French but whose grammar is its own. La Réunion, in the Indian Ocean, has a large community of Tamil origin, with Hindu temples and festivals. Haiti, independent since 1804, has two official languages: French and Haitian Creole.

  • Sak pase ? — N ap boule ! — Haitian Creole: What’s up? — Doing fine! (the French voice will read it imperfectly)

Careful

  • Wrong: Le créole, c’est du français mal parlé.
  • Right: Le créole est une langue à part entière.
  • Why: “Creole is a language in its own right.” A French speaker cannot simply understand it: it has its own grammar, sounds and literature.

docs.title: 57.8 Québec, Belgium, Switzerland — same language, other words
docs.text:
About eight million people speak French in Québec, around four and a half million in Belgium (Wallonia and Brussels) and around two million in western Switzerland (la Suisse romande). Grammar is the same; accents, numbers and some everyday words differ. All three call the meals déjeuner – dîner – souper (breakfast – lunch – dinner), the older French system.

English France Québec Belgium / Switzerland breakfast le petit-déjeuner le déjeuner le déjeuner lunch le déjeuner le dîner le dîner dinner le dîner le souper le souper 70 / 90 soixante-dix / quatre-vingt-dix soixante-dix / quatre-vingt-dix septante / nonante 80 quatre-vingts quatre-vingts quatre-vingts (BE); huitante (Vaud, Valais, Fribourg) mobile phone un portable un cellulaire, un cell un GSM (BE); un natel (CH) email un mail, un e-mail un courriel un mail, un e-mail weekend le week-end la fin de semaine le week-end to go shopping faire du shopping magasiner faire du shopping car une voiture un char (informal), une auto une voiture

docs.title: Québec
docs.text:
Québec protects French by law (the Charte de la langue française, 1977) and prefers French-made words to English ones: courriel, magasiner, fin de semaine. The accent is distinctive, and tu is used much more.

  • Je vais magasiner en fin de semaine avec ma blonde. — I’m going shopping this weekend with my girlfriend. (mon chum = my boyfriend, or my buddy)
  • Il fait frette, mets ta tuque ! — It’s freezing, put your wool hat on! (frette = very cold, Québec)
  • Mon char est encore au garage, c’est plate ! — My car is still at the garage, what a drag! (c’est plate = it’s boring / too bad)
  • Merci ! — Bienvenue ! — Thanks! — You’re welcome! (Québec; in France: de rien)

Québec swear words — recognise, don’t use

Québec’s strongest swear words (les sacres) come from Catholic church vocabulary: tabarnak (from tabernacle), câlisse, hostie. They are far more offensive than they look to a learner. Understand them in films; leave them out of your own French.

Careful

  • Wrong: (in Montréal) « Viens dîner samedi » = come on Saturday evening.
  • Right: Au Québec, le dîner = lunch ; le souper = the evening meal.
  • Why: An invitation à dîner in Québec, Belgium or Switzerland is usually for lunch. Turn up at 8 p.m. and you are seven hours late.

docs.title: Belgium and Switzerland
docs.text:
Belgians and Swiss count in tens: septante (70), nonante (90) — much simpler than soixante-dix. Belgium keeps quatre-vingts for 80; the Swiss cantons of Vaud, Valais and Fribourg say huitante. Everyone in France understands them — they just mark where you are from.

  • Ça fait septante-cinq euros. — That’s 75 euros. (Belgium, Switzerland)
  • Votre café, s’il vous plaît ! — Here’s your coffee! (Belgium: s’il vous plaît when handing something over = France’s voilà)
  • Viens une fois ici ! — Come here a sec! (Brussels: une fois softens a request — and is a favourite joke about Belgians)
  • Je t’envoie un message sur ton natel, ça joue ? — I’ll text your mobile, is that OK? (Swiss: natel = mobile, ça joue ? = does that work?)

docs.title: 57.9 Pondichéry — France’s link with India
docs.text:
From the 17th century, the French East India Company held a few trading posts (comptoirs) in India: Pondichéry, Karikal and Yanaon on the east coast, Mahé on the Malabar coast, and Chandernagor near Kolkata. Chandernagor joined India first (in the early 1950s). The other four were handed over in practice in 1954, and the transfer became legally complete (de jure) in 1962. Today they form the Union Territory of Puducherry (Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahé, Yanam).

Pondichéry in one line

A French comptoir until 1954 (legally until 1962), Pondichéry still has a French quarter, French schools and institutes, and a Tamil–French community.

In the old town, the Ville Blanche (the former French quarter) by the sea is separated by a canal from the Ville tamoule. Streets keep French names (rue Suffren, rue Romain-Rolland, rue Dumas) and police officers wear red képis. The Lycée français international, the Alliance française and the Institut français de Pondichéry keep French alive, and a French consulate serves several thousand French citizens, many from Tamil families. On 14 July a ceremony is held at the seafront war memorial.

  • Pondichéry était un comptoir français jusqu’en 1954. — Pondicherry was a French trading post until 1954.
  • Certains habitants de Pondichéry ont la nationalité française. — Some residents of Pondicherry have French nationality.

For learners in India

The Alliance française network (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Pondichéry and many more cities) runs courses and the official DELF and DALF exams — see DELF, DALF & your level.

À retenir

  • Greet before you ask (Bonjour, madame), use vous until you are invited to switch, and remember that French sounds different — and uses different words — in Paris, Montréal, Brussels, Dakar and Pondichéry.
  • Enter: Bonjour, madame / monsieur. Leave: Merci, au revoir, bonne journée ! No name needed — madame or monsieur alone is polite.
  • After you switch to tu, going back to vous sounds like a cold message: “we are no longer close”.
  • Bread goes on the table beside your plate, and you tear it by hand. Keep both hands visible on the table (wrists on the edge), not on your lap. Let the host pour the wine. Wait for « Bon appétit ! » before you start.
  • Everyday French says « Bon appétit ! » all the time — at home, at work, even to strangers eating lunch. Only in very formal, old-school etiquette is it seen as unrefined. As a learner, say it: it is warm and expected.
  • A French comptoir until 1954 (legally until 1962), Pondichéry still has a French quarter, French schools and institutes, and a Tamil–French community.

docs.title: 57.10 Practice — culture and francophonie
docs.text:
Exercise 1

You walk into a small bakery in Lyon. What do you say first?

  • Bonjour, madame !
  • Salut !
  • Une baguette !
  • Coucou !

Hint: The shop rule

Answer

Bonjour, madame !

Always greet first: Bonjour + madame / monsieur.

Exercise 2

In Québec, « le dîner » is…

  • breakfast
  • lunch
  • the evening meal
  • an afternoon snack
Answer

lunch

Québec, Belgium and Switzerland: déjeuner (breakfast), dîner (lunch), souper (dinner).

Exercise 3

How do people in Belgium usually say 90?

  • quatre-vingt-dix
  • nonante
  • huitante
  • septante
Answer

nonante

Belgium and Switzerland say septante (70) and nonante (90).

Exercise 4

On peut se ___ ? (= shall we say tu to each other?)

Hint: the verb for saying tu

Answer

tutoyer

tutoyer = to say tu; vouvoyer = to say vous.

Exercise 5

Le 1er mai, on offre du ___ pour porter bonheur.

Hint: lily of the valley

Answer

muguet

On 1 May people give sprigs of muguet (lily of the valley) for luck.

Exercise 6

Le 14 juillet tombe un jeudi : beaucoup de gens font le ___.

Hint: a 'bridge' to the weekend

Answer

pont

faire le pont = take the extra day off between a holiday and the weekend.

Exercise 7

Pick the word that sounds odd at a French dinner table.

Merci, je suis plein.

Answer

Wrong word: plein.

Corrected: Merci, je n'ai plus faim.

In France say je n'ai plus faim; je suis plein sounds odd (plein can mean drunk). It is fine in Québec.

Exercise 8

Pick the wrong word (you are talking to a shopkeeper).

Bonjour, une baguette, s'il te plaît.

Answer

Wrong word: te.

Corrected: Bonjour, une baguette, s'il vous plaît.

With staff and strangers use vous: s'il vous plaît.

Exercise 9

Pick the wrong number word.

Dans le canton de Vaud, 80 se dit souvent septante.

Answer

Wrong word: septante.

Corrected: Dans le canton de Vaud, 80 se dit souvent huitante.

septante = 70. In Vaud, Valais and Fribourg, 80 is huitante.

Exercise 10

Match the Québec word to its meaning.

A B un char my girlfriend une tuque to go shopping ma blonde a car magasiner a wool hat Answer

un char — a car; une tuque — a wool hat; ma blonde — my girlfriend; magasiner — to go shopping

Québec French: char, tuque, blonde, magasiner.

Exercise 11

Match the fête to its tradition.

A B l'Épiphanie le muguet la Chandeleur chrysanthemums on graves le 1er mai la galette des rois la Toussaint les crêpes Answer

l'Épiphanie — la galette des rois; la Chandeleur — les crêpes; le 1er mai — le muguet; la Toussaint — chrysanthemums on graves

Each fête has its food or flower.

Exercise 12

French « laïcité » means that…

  • the State is neutral and stays out of religion
  • everyone must belong to a religion
  • the State funds all religions equally
  • religion is banned in private life
Answer

the State is neutral and stays out of religion

Law of 1905: separation of the Churches and the State; private belief is free.

Exercise 13

Pondichéry was handed to India in practice in 1954. When did the transfer become legally complete?

  • 1947
  • 1954
  • 1962
  • 1975
Answer

1962

De facto transfer 1954, de jure 1962.

Exercise 14

A French job ad asks for « bac +5 ». It means…

  • five years of study after the bac
  • a grade of 5 out of 20
  • five years of work experience
  • five foreign languages
Answer

five years of study after the bac

bac +3 ≈ bachelor's level, bac +5 ≈ master's level.

Exercise 15

Put the words in order: 'It's my treat.'

Words: invite / qui / C'est / moi

Answer

C'est moi qui invite

C'est moi qui + verb agreeing with moi: invite.

Exercise 16

Put the words in order: 'Thank you for inviting me.'

Words: de / m'avoir / invité / Merci

Answer

Merci de m'avoir invité

merci de + past infinitive: avoir invité (invitée for a woman).

Exercise 17

Say it aloud, as you walk into the bakery.

Bonjour madame, une baguette, s'il vous plaît

Answer

Greeting first, then the order, then s'il vous plaît.

Exercise 18

Say it aloud: suggest switching to tu.

On peut se tutoyer

Answer

A friendly, common way to offer tu.

Next step

Culture lives in the details. Next, clean up the errors that most often give a learner away in The 50 most common mistakes — and practise your greetings out loud with Everyday French.

docs.title: Chapter 59: DELF, DALF & your level
docs.text:
DELF, DALF et autoévaluation

"What is my level?" is the question every learner asks. This chapter answers it in three ways: what each CEFR level (A1 to C2) lets you do, how the official exams — DELF, DALF, TCF and TEF — test it paper by paper, and which chapters of this book carry you from one level to the next. At the end you get a checklist for each level, so you can test yourself honestly before you pay for an exam.

In one line

A level is not a number of words you know — it is a list of things you can do in French: order a coffee (A1), tell a story (B1), defend an opinion (B2), summarise a report (C1).

docs.title: 59.1 The six levels in one picture
docs.text:
The CEFR (Common European Framework of Reference — in French le CECRL) divides language ability into six levels. A = basic user, B = independent user, C = proficient user. Every serious French exam, school and employer in the world uses these six labels.

Figure 59.1. The official French names of the levels, with rough cumulative hours of guided study (classes or a structured book like this one). Each step is taller than the last: B2 → C1 takes longer than A1 → A2.

The hours are estimates commonly given by French teaching centres such as the Alliance française. They assume regular homework on top. Your real number depends on your other languages: English already gives you thousands of French-looking words (see Cognates & false friends), and Hindi speakers already know grammatical gender and the polite/familiar split of aap / tum — which is exactly vous / tu.

The rule of thumb

Twenty minutes a day, out loud, every day, beats three hours on Sunday. At about one hour a day, most English speakers reach a solid B1 in one year and B2 in about two.

docs.title: 59.2 What you can do at each level
docs.text:
Here are the levels described as real abilities (a simplified version of the official CEFR descriptions), each with one sentence that is typical of that level.

Level You can… Typical exam A1 Introduce yourself, ask and answer very simple personal questions, understand slow, clear speech about basic needs. DELF A1 A2 Handle routine tasks (shopping, transport, simple work), describe your family, your past weekend and your plans in simple sentences. DELF A2 B1 Follow the main points of clear speech on familiar topics, cope with most travel situations, tell a story and give short reasons for an opinion. DELF B1 B2 Understand the main ideas of complex texts, talk with native speakers without strain on both sides, argue for and against a point of view. DELF B2 C1 Understand long, demanding texts and implicit meaning, speak fluently without searching for words, write well-structured texts on complex subjects. DALF C1 C2 Understand virtually everything, summarise sources and rebuild their arguments, express fine shades of meaning precisely and naturally. DALF C2

docs.title: One sentence per level
docs.text:
• A1 — Je m’appelle Priya et j’habite à Pune. — My name is Priya and I live in Pune.
  • A2 — Le week-end dernier, je suis allée au marché avec ma sœur. — Last weekend I went to the market with my sister.
  • B1 — Si j’avais plus de temps, je ferais du sport tous les jours. — If I had more time, I would do sport every day.
  • B2 — Bien que le télétravail soit pratique, il peut isoler les salariés. — Although working from home is convenient, it can isolate employees.
  • C1 — Force est de constater que les mesures prises n’ont pas suffi. — One has to admit that the measures taken were not enough.
  • C2 — Loin d’être anodine, cette réforme risque de bouleverser l’équilibre du système. — Far from being harmless, this reform could upset the balance of the whole system.

Levels are per skill

You can be B2 in reading and A2 in speaking. Exams test four skills separately: listening, reading, writing, speaking. Your weakest skill decides whether you pass.

docs.title: 59.3 DELF and DALF — the diplomas
docs.text:
The DELF (Diplôme d’études en langue française) covers A1 to B2; the DALF (Diplôme approfondi de langue française) covers C1 and C2. They are official diplomas of the French Ministry of Education, run by France Éducation international and taken at Alliances françaises and French institutes around the world — in India, at the Alliances françaises of Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Pondichéry, Bangalore and many other cities.

How DELF/DALF are scored

Four papers, each out of 25, total out of 100. You pass with 50/100 and at least 5/25 in every paper. The diploma is valid for life.

Figure 59.2. An example result. Weak writing (10/25) is fine because the total is 60 and no paper is under 5. A 4/25 in any one paper would fail the whole exam, even with 80/100.

The four papers have French abbreviations you will see on every exam document:

Code French English CO compréhension de l’oral listening CE compréhension des écrits reading PE production écrite writing PO production orale (and interaction) speaking, face to face with two examiners

Check before you register

Formats are revised from time to time (recent versions added new task types to B1 and B2). The tables below give the standard structure; always check the current sample papers on the France Éducation international website or with your exam centre.

docs.title: 59.4 Paper by paper: DELF A1 → DALF C2
docs.text: The listening, reading and writing papers are taken together in one sitting ("collective" papers). The speaking paper is a separate appointment, often the same day.

docs.title: DELF A1 and A2
docs.text: Paper A1 A2 CO ~20 min · short recordings: announcements, messages, numbers, times ~25 min · announcements, short dialogues, radio snippets CE 30 min · signs, notices, a simple email, a timetable 30 min · ads, instructions, short articles PE 30 min · fill in a form + a short message or postcard 45 min · two short texts (~60 words each): tell, describe, invite, reply PO 5–7 min, 10 min prep · answer about yourself, ask questions, a role-play (buying something) 6–8 min, 10 min prep · about yourself, a short monologue, a role-play

docs.title: DELF B1 and B2
docs.text: Paper B1 B2 CO ~25 min · interviews, radio, conversations ~30 min · longer interviews, reports, lectures CE 45 min · articles, letters, finding useful information 1 h · argued articles, opinion pieces PE 45 min · essay, letter or forum post, 160 words minimum, giving your opinion 1 h · argued text (letter, article, essay), 250 words minimum PO ~15 min · talk about yourself, a role-play, then give your view on a short text ~20 min, 30 min prep · present a short document and defend a point of view, then debate with the examiner

docs.title: DALF C1 and C2
docs.text:
Paper C1 C2 Listening + reading CO ~40 min (a long interview + short documents); CE 50 min (a long text) Two combined papers, each /50: oral (listen, then present and debate — 30 min, 1 h prep); written (a 3 h 30 paper: read a file of documents and write a structured text of about 700 words) Writing 2 h 30 · a synthèse of two documents (~220 words) + an argued essay (~250 words) Speaking 30 min, 1 h prep · an exposé built from a file of documents, then a discussion Pass: 50/100 with at least 10/50 per paper

At C1 and C2 you choose a domain: lettres et sciences humaines (humanities) or sciences. The synthèse — summarising two or more documents with no personal opinion — surprises many learners; it is taught step by step in Essays & structured writing.

docs.title: 59.5 TCF and TEF — the tests
docs.text:
A test is different from a diploma: you cannot fail it. You get a score that is converted into a CEFR level, and the result is usually valid for two years. Tests are what governments and universities ask for.

Test Run by Format Used for TCF Tout public France Éducation international 3 compulsory MCQ papers (listening, language structures, reading; about 1 h 30); optional writing and speaking job applications, personal record TCF Canada France Éducation international listening, reading (MCQ), writing (1 h, 3 tasks), speaking (about 12 min) Canadian immigration TCF IRN / TCF DAP France Éducation international adapted versions French residence and citizenship / admission to a French university TEF (TEF Canada, TEFAQ, TEF IRN…) CCI Paris Île-de-France reading, listening, writing, speaking Canada, Québec, French residence and citizenship
  • Pour l’immigration au Canada, on peut passer le TEF Canada ou le TCF Canada. — For immigration to Canada, you can take the TEF Canada or the TCF Canada.
  • Les résultats du TCF sont valables deux ans. — TCF results are valid for two years.
  • Le DELF et le DALF sont valables à vie. — The DELF and DALF are valid for life.

Which one should I take?

For a permanent qualification and your CV: DELF/DALF. For a visa, citizenship or Canadian points: the TCF or TEF version that the authority names. Requirements change (France has recently raised the levels needed for residence and citizenship), so read the official page before booking.

docs.title: 59.6 How long it takes — and a 12-week exam plan
docs.text:
Use the staircase in section 1 to estimate. If you are A2 today and want B1, you need roughly 200 more guided hours — about six months at an hour a day. Plan backwards from your exam date.

Weeks Focus Every day (≈ 1 h) 1–2 Diagnosis Do one full sample paper under exam conditions; list your three weakest points. 3–6 Repair grammar and vocabulary One chapter of this book linked to your level (section 9); its quiz twice, one day apart. 7–9 Skills, one per day Mon listening · Tue reading · Wed writing · Thu speaking · Fri your weakest · weekend a podcast or film. 10–11 Timed papers A full paper every other day; correct your writing with the official grading grid. 12 Rest and rehearse Light review, your prepared opening phrases, sleep. No new grammar.

Train with the grid

Writing and speaking are marked with a public grille d’évaluation (task, coherence, vocabulary, grammar). Mark your own work with it — you will see exactly where your points go.

docs.title: 59.7 Exam French: instructions and lifesaving phrases
docs.text:
Exam instructions (les consignes) are always in French, even at A1. Learn them now so they never cost you time on the day.

Consigne Meaning Cochez la bonne réponse. Tick the right answer. Entourez / Soulignez… Circle / Underline… Justifiez votre réponse. Give evidence (quote the text) for your answer. Vrai ou faux ? On ne sait pas. True or false? Not stated. Rédigez un texte de 250 mots minimum. Write a text of at least 250 words. Vous dégagerez le thème du document. Identify the main theme of the document.

docs.title: In the speaking room
docs.text:
• Pourriez-vous répéter la question, s’il vous plaît ? — Could you repeat the question, please?
  • Excusez-moi, je n’ai pas bien compris le mot « … ». — Sorry, I didn’t quite understand the word "…".
  • Si j’ai bien compris, vous voulez savoir pourquoi… — If I have understood correctly, you want to know why…
  • Je vais vous présenter le document, puis je donnerai mon avis. — I am going to present the document to you, then I will give my opinion.
  • Ce document traite de la place du numérique à l’école. — This document deals with the role of digital technology at school.
  • C’est une bonne question. Laissez-moi réfléchir un instant. — That’s a good question. Let me think for a moment.
  • Je comprends votre point de vue, mais je ne le partage pas entièrement. — I understand your point of view, but I don’t fully share it.
  • Pour conclure, je dirais que les avantages l’emportent sur les inconvénients. — To conclude, I would say that the advantages outweigh the drawbacks.

docs.title: At the desk — what candidates say before and after
docs.text:
• Je voudrais m’inscrire au DELF B2 de juin. — I would like to register for the June DELF B2.
  • Je passe le DALF C1 la semaine prochaine. — I am taking the DALF C1 next week.
  • J’ai réussi mon DELF B1 avec 78 sur 100 ! — I passed my DELF B1 with 78 out of 100!
  • Il a raté l’oral de deux points, il le repassera en décembre. — He failed the oral by two points; he will retake it in December.

Exam-day mistakes

  • Wrong: (meaning "I passed") J’ai passé le DELF B2 !
  • Right: J’ai réussi le DELF B2 ! / J’ai eu mon DELF B2 !

  • Why: passer un examen = to take it. To pass = réussir; to fail = rater or échouer à.

  • Wrong: Je ne comprends pas. (then silence)

  • Right: Excusez-moi, pourriez-vous reformuler la question ?

  • Why: Asking politely is part of interaction — it earns points. Silence earns nothing.

  • Wrong: Je ne partage pas ton avis.

  • Right: Je ne partage pas votre avis.

  • Why: The examiner is a stranger: vous from the first word to the last, unless the task is a role-play with a friend.

  • Wrong: Je suis prêt pour passer le DELF.

  • Right: Je suis prêt à passer le DELF.

  • Why: prêt à + infinitive; prêt pour + noun: prêt pour l’examen.

  • Wrong: Dans le document, il dit que…

  • Right: Dans cet article, l’auteur affirme que…

  • Why: Name your source (l’auteur, la journaliste, le sondage) and use a precise verb: affirmer, souligner, dénoncer.

  • Wrong: Je suis B2.

  • Right: J’ai le niveau B2. / J’ai un niveau B2 en français.
  • Why: You have a level in French — the same logic as j’ai 20 ans (see Être & avoir).

docs.title: 59.8 Self-assessment checklists
docs.text: Read each list aloud. If you can honestly tick every line of a level — out loud, without notes — you are ready to sit that exam. If two or more lines are shaky, work on the chapters in section 9 first.

docs.title: A1 — Je peux…
docs.text:
• ☐ me présenter — introduce myself (name, age, city, job).
  • ☐ dire les nombres, la date et l’heure — say numbers, the date and the time.
  • ☐ commander dans un café — order in a café, politely, with vous.
  • ☐ poser des questions simples — ask where, when, how much.

docs.title: A2 — Je peux…
docs.text:
• ☐ raconter mon week-end au passé composé — tell my weekend in the past.
  • ☐ décrire ma famille, ma maison, ma ville — describe my family, home and town.
  • ☐ acheter un billet, demander mon chemin — buy a ticket, ask the way.
  • ☐ écrire un court message pour inviter ou m’excuser — write a short invitation or apology.

docs.title: B1 — Je peux…
docs.text:
• ☐ raconter une histoire avec l’imparfait et le passé composé — tell a story with both past tenses.
  • ☐ donner mon avis et le justifier — give and justify an opinion.
  • ☐ comprendre l’essentiel d’un podcast sur un sujet familier — follow the main points of a podcast.
  • ☐ écrire 160 mots clairs sur mon expérience — write 160 clear words about an experience.

docs.title: B2 — Je peux…
docs.text:
• ☐ défendre un point de vue pendant dix minutes — defend a view for ten minutes.
  • ☐ utiliser le subjonctif et le conditionnel sans y penser — use the subjunctive and conditional naturally.
  • ☐ suivre un débat à la radio — follow a radio debate.
  • ☐ écrire un texte argumenté de 250 mots — write a 250-word argued text.

docs.title: C1 — Je peux…
docs.text:
• ☐ synthétiser deux documents sans donner mon avis — synthesise two documents neutrally.
  • ☐ comprendre l’implicite et l’ironie — understand implied meaning and irony.
  • ☐ changer de registre selon la situation — switch register to suit the situation.
  • ☐ lire un roman contemporain avec plaisir — read a contemporary novel for pleasure.

docs.title: C2 — Je peux…
docs.text:
• ☐ reformuler finement une idée complexe — rephrase a complex idea with precision.
  • ☐ comprendre l’humour, les jeux de mots et les accents régionaux — get humour, puns and regional accents.
  • ☐ rédiger 700 mots structurés à partir d’un dossier — write 700 structured words from a file of documents.

docs.title: 59.9 Your route through this book, level by level
docs.text:
Every chapter of the book belongs to a step. Finish all the chapters of a level (and their quizzes) before you book that level’s exam.

Level Chapters to master Exam A1 How to use this book · Alphabet & accents · The sounds of French · Silent letters & liaison · Hello, please, thank you · Numbers, dates & time · Nouns, gender & plurals · Articles · Être & avoir · Present tense: -er verbs · Saying no · Asking questions · Core vocabulary by theme DELF A1 A2 Present tense: the rest · Adjectives · My, your, this, that · Prepositions & places · Object pronouns · Reflexive verbs · The past: passé composé · The future · Giving instructions · Everyday French · The 100 essential verbs · Spelling & punctuation DELF A2 B1 Y, en & pronoun order · Imparfait vs passé composé · Comparing · Relative pronouns · Conditional & si clauses · Pronunciation clinic · Travel & emergencies · Conversation & opinions · Cognates & false friends · Linking words · Messages, letters & emails DELF B1 B2 The subjunctive · Advanced compound tenses · Passive & reported speech · Gérondif & participles · Real spoken French · Work, phone & interviews · Idioms & expressions · Registers & slang · Essays & structured writing · Culture & the francophone world · The 50 most common mistakes DELF B2 C1 Literary & formal French · Arguing & presenting · Word building & advanced words · DELF, DALF & your level (this chapter) DALF C1 C2 The whole book again, faster, plus real books, films and newspapers every day — then the Final test as a check-up. DALF C2

Not sure where you are?

Take the Final test. Its "reopen this chapter" table sends each wrong answer back to the right page, and its score bands map onto the levels above.

À retenir

  • A level is not a number of words you know — it is a list of things you can do in French: order a coffee (A1), tell a story (B1), defend an opinion (B2), summarise a report (C1).
  • Twenty minutes a day, out loud, every day, beats three hours on Sunday. At about one hour a day, most English speakers reach a solid B1 in one year and B2 in about two.
  • You can be B2 in reading and A2 in speaking. Exams test four skills separately: listening, reading, writing, speaking. Your weakest skill decides whether you pass.
  • Four papers, each out of 25, total out of 100. You pass with 50/100 and at least 5/25 in every paper. The diploma is valid for life.
  • For a permanent qualification and your CV: DELF/DALF. For a visa, citizenship or Canadian points: the TCF or TEF version that the authority names. Requirements change (France has recently raised the levels needed for…
  • Writing and speaking are marked with a public grille d’évaluation (task, coherence, vocabulary, grammar). Mark your own work with it — you will see exactly where your points go.

docs.title: 59.10 Practice — DELF, DALF & your level
docs.text:
Exercise 1

To pass a DELF or DALF C1 exam you need…

  • 50/100 and at least 5/25 in each paper
  • 60/100 overall
  • 50/100, even with 0 in one paper
  • full marks in speaking

Hint: Two conditions

Answer

50/100 and at least 5/25 in each paper

The pass mark is 50/100, and any paper under 5/25 is eliminatory.

Exercise 2

Which of these is valid for life?

  • DELF / DALF
  • TCF
  • TEF
  • TCF Canada
Answer

DELF / DALF

DELF and DALF are diplomas, valid for life. TCF and TEF results are usually valid for two years.

Exercise 3

Match each level to its official French name.

A B A1 autonome B1 maîtrise C1 découverte C2 seuil Answer

A1 — découverte; B1 — seuil; C1 — autonome; C2 — maîtrise

A1 découverte, A2 survie, B1 seuil, B2 avancé, C1 autonome, C2 maîtrise.

Exercise 4

The DALF C1 writing paper asks for…

  • a synthèse of documents and an argued essay
  • a postcard
  • a form to fill in
  • a 700-word text only
Answer

a synthèse of documents and an argued essay

C1: synthèse (~220 words, no opinion) + essai argumenté (~250 words). The 700-word text is C2.

Exercise 5

Minimum length of the DELF B2 written text?

  • 60 words
  • 160 words
  • 250 words
  • 700 words
Answer

250 words

B1 asks for 160 words, B2 for 250 words.

Exercise 6

Pourriez-vous ___ la question, s'il vous plaît ? (repeat)

Hint: répéter = to repeat

Answer

répéter / repeter

Pourriez-vous répéter… ? is the polite way to ask an examiner to repeat.

Exercise 7

Pick the word that is wrong when speaking to an examiner.

Je ne partage pas ton avis, Madame.

Answer

Wrong word: ton.

Corrected: Je ne partage pas votre avis, Madame.

An examiner is a stranger: use vous, so votre avis.

Exercise 8

« J'ai passé l'examen hier » means…

  • I took the exam yesterday
  • I passed the exam yesterday
  • I skipped the exam yesterday
  • I failed the exam yesterday

Hint: A famous false friend

Answer

I took the exam yesterday

passer un examen = to take it. To pass = réussir un examen.

Exercise 9

Put the words in order.

Words: B2 / voudrais / Je / DELF / au / m'inscrire

Answer

Je voudrais m'inscrire au DELF B2

Je voudrais + infinitive: polite request. s'inscrire à = to register for.

Exercise 10

You need a French test for Canadian immigration. Which one?

  • TEF Canada or TCF Canada
  • DELF A1
  • the French bac
  • any diploma at all
Answer

TEF Canada or TCF Canada

Canada asks for the TEF Canada or TCF Canada.

Exercise 11

Roughly how many guided hours (cumulative) does it take to reach B2?

  • about 50
  • about 600
  • about 3,000
  • about 10
Answer

about 600

Common estimates: ~550–650 guided hours for B2, plus homework.

Exercise 12

Match each exam instruction to its meaning.

A B Cochez write Justifiez circle Rédigez tick Entourez give evidence Answer

Cochez — tick; Justifiez — give evidence; Rédigez — write; Entourez — circle

Exam instructions are always in French — learn them before the day.

Exercise 13

Force est de ___ que les mesures n'ont pas suffi. (to note)

Hint: A C1 phrase: one has to admit…

Answer

constater

Force est de constater que… = one has to admit that… — a classic C1 phrase.

Exercise 14

In the DELF B2 speaking paper you…

  • present a short document and defend a point of view
  • spell your name
  • read a poem aloud
  • fill in a form
Answer

present a short document and defend a point of view

B2 oral: 30 min preparation, then an exposé and a debate with the examiner.

Exercise 15

Pick the wrong word.

Je suis prêt pour passer le DELF.

Answer

Wrong word: pour.

Corrected: Je suis prêt à passer le DELF.

prêt à + infinitive; prêt pour + noun.

Exercise 16

Say it aloud — your lifeline in the oral exam.

Si j'ai bien compris, vous voulez savoir pourquoi

Answer

Reformulating the question buys you time and shows interaction skills.

Exercise 17

Say your goal aloud.

Je souhaiterais passer le DALF C1 l'année prochaine

Answer

souhaiterais = would like (polite conditional); passer = to take an exam.

Next step

Pick a target level and a date, write both on paper, and book the exam — a date makes you study. Then check where you stand with the Final test.

docs.title: Chapter 53: Essays & structured writing
docs.text:
Rédiger un texte argumenté

French schools train every pupil in one way of arguing on paper: a clear question, a plan announced in advance, paragraphs that each prove one point, and a conclusion that opens a new door. DELF and DALF examiners mark exactly this. Learn the architecture once and you can write about any subject — phones at school, remote work, tourism.

The French essay in one line

Introduction (ends with a question and the plan) → 2 or 3 parts linked by transitions → conclusion (answer + ouverture).

docs.title: 53.1 What the exams ask you to write
docs.text:
From B1 upwards, the written test is an argumentative text: you take a position on a general question and defend it. The format changes with the level. Details on scoring and timing are in DELF, DALF & your level; here is the writing side.

Exam Typical task Length DELF B1 essay, article, letter or forum post giving your opinion 160 words minimum DELF B2 texte argumenté: formal letter, article, forum contribution, essay 250 words minimum DALF C1 ① synthèse of two documents ② essai argumenté about 220 words; 250 words minimum DALF C2 a structured text (article, editorial, speech…) built from a file of documents about 700 words

docs.title: The genres and their frames
docs.text:
Genre Frame Key feature l’essai title + intro / parts / conclusion the purest form of the French plan la lettre au courrier des lecteurs formal letter frame you react to an article in a newspaper l’article title + short chapeau (standfirst) written for readers; can use subheadings la contribution à un forum pseudonym, lighter tone still structured; still argued
  • J’ai lu avec intérêt votre article du 3 mars et je souhaiterais réagir. — I read your article of 3 March with interest and I would like to respond. — the classic first line of a reader’s letter. The letter frame itself is in Messages, letters & emails.

Word counts are rules

Below the minimum you lose marks, and in a DALF synthèse you must stay close to the target. Write the total at the end: Nombre de mots : 262.

docs.title: 53.2 The shape of a French essay
docs.text:
Picture the essay as two funnels with a solid body between them. The introduction goes from the general to the precise question. The development proves your answer step by step. The conclusion goes back from the precise answer to a wider horizon.

Figure 53.1. Two funnels and a body. The question (pink) closes the introduction; the answer (pink) opens the conclusion.

docs.title: 53.3 Choose your plan
docs.text:
Before writing a single sentence, spend five to ten minutes on the plan. The type of question tells you which plan to use.

Figure 53.2. Let the question choose the plan. Plan The parts Example subject dialectique I. thèse (yes, because…) II. antithèse (but…) III. synthèse (a higher answer) Faut-il interdire les voitures en ville ? problème – causes – solutions I. the facts II. causes and consequences III. solutions Comment lutter contre le gaspillage alimentaire ? thématique one part per aspect: economic, social, cultural… Quels sont les effets du tourisme de masse ?

The synthèse part of a dialectical plan is not a summary of I and II: it goes beyond them, often with a condition or a compromise (“yes, but only if…”). At DELF B2, two parts (for / against) and a conclusion that settles the debate are perfectly acceptable.

Plan first, sentences second

Jot down the question, two or three part titles and one example per paragraph before you write. A good plan saves more marks than good vocabulary.

docs.title: 53.4 The introduction in four moves
docs.text:
A French introduction is one paragraph of four short moves. Here they are on the subject Le télétravail est-il un progrès ? (Is remote work progress?).

  • Amorce : Depuis 2020, des millions de salariés travaillent régulièrement depuis chez eux. — Hook: Since 2020, millions of employees have regularly worked from home. — a fact, a figure or a recent event.
  • Sujet : Le télétravail, longtemps réservé à quelques professions, est devenu une pratique courante. — Subject: Remote work, long limited to a few professions, has become common practice.
  • Problématique : Mais représente-t-il vraiment un progrès pour les salariés ? — Central question: But is it really progress for employees? — always a real question.
  • Annonce du plan : Nous examinerons d’abord ses avantages, puis ses limites. — Plan: We will first examine its advantages, then its limits.

docs.title: Ready-made frames
docs.text:
Move French English problématique Dans quelle mesure… ? To what extent…? problématique Peut-on affirmer que… ? Can we claim that…? annonce Nous verrons dans un premier temps…, puis dans un second temps… We will first see…, then… annonce Après avoir montré que…, nous nous demanderons si… Having shown that…, we will ask whether…

Avoid the tired hooks

Depuis la nuit des temps… (since the dawn of time) and a bare De nos jours… (nowadays) make examiners sigh. Start with something precise.

Careful

  • Wrong: Dans cette essai, je vais parler des téléphones.
  • Right: Nous nous demanderons s’il faut interdire les téléphones à l’école.
  • Why: Two problems. Un essai is masculine, so it is cet essai (cet before a vowel). And “I am going to talk about…” is a topic, not a question: the introduction must end on a problématique. We will ask whether phones should be banned at school.

docs.title: 53.5 Paragraphs and an impersonal voice
docs.text:
Each paragraph of the development proves one idea in four steps. Start a new paragraph (with an indent or a blank line) for every new idea — examiners check this.

  • Idée : Tout d’abord, le télétravail améliore la qualité de vie des salariés. — Idea: First of all, remote work improves employees’ quality of life.
  • Argument : En effet, il supprime les longs trajets et laisse plus de temps pour la famille. — Argument: Indeed, it removes long commutes and leaves more time for family.
  • Exemple : Ainsi, un salarié de la banlieue parisienne peut gagner jusqu’à deux heures par jour. — Example: For instance, an employee in the Paris suburbs can save up to two hours a day.
  • Mini-conclusion : Sur ce point, le télétravail apparaît donc comme un net progrès. — Mini-conclusion: On this point, remote work therefore looks like clear progress. — it links back to the question.

One paragraph, one idea

Idée → argument → exemple → mini-conclusion. The connectors inside the paragraph (en effet, ainsi, donc) are listed in Linking words.

docs.title: Giving an opinion without “je”
docs.text:
In a DELF essay you may say je — you are asked for your opinion. But a repeated je pense que sounds childish, and a real French dissertation prefers on, nous or an impersonal phrase. Watch the mood after each one (see The subjunctive).

  • Il semble que cette mesure soit efficace. — It seems that this measure is effective. — + subjunctive.
  • On peut considérer que l’école a un rôle à jouer. — One may consider that schools have a role to play. — + indicative.
  • Force est de constater que les écrans ont envahi notre quotidien. — One has to admit that screens have invaded our daily lives. — + indicative; very C1.
  • Il est indéniable que le numérique transforme l’école. — It is undeniable that digital technology is transforming schools.
  • Il convient de nuancer ce point de vue. — This point of view should be qualified. — + infinitive.
  • Il serait souhaitable que chaque établissement fixe ses propres règles. — It would be desirable for each school to set its own rules. — + subjunctive.
  • Nombreux sont ceux qui dénoncent cette réforme. — Many people criticise this reform.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je pense que c’est utile. Je pense aussi que c’est dangereux. Je pense que…
  • Right: Il est indéniable que c’est utile. Force est de constater cependant que c’est risqué.
  • Why: Vary the frames and keep the personal je for one clear moment, usually the conclusion. It is undeniable that it is useful. One must admit, however, that it is risky.

Careful

  • Wrong: Il y a beaucoup de gens qui pensent que le télétravail isole.
  • Right: Nombreux sont ceux qui estiment que le télétravail isole. / On considère souvent que…
  • Why: Il y a beaucoup de gens qui… is spoken French. Written argument uses a tighter, impersonal frame. Many people believe that remote work isolates.

Careful

  • Wrong: Il semble que cette mesure est efficace.
  • Right: Il semble que cette mesure soit efficace.
  • Why: Il semble que normally takes the subjunctive. (With a pronoun, il me semble que, the indicative is used: il me semble que c’est efficace.)

docs.title: 53.6 Transitions and the conclusion
docs.text:
Between two parts you need a transition: one or two sentences that close the previous part and open the next. Connectors inside paragraphs are in Linking words; these are only the bridges between parts.

  • Nous avons vu que le télétravail libère du temps. Il convient à présent d’en examiner les limites. — We have seen that remote work frees up time. We should now examine its limits.
  • Après avoir examiné ses avantages, intéressons-nous à ses inconvénients. — Having examined its advantages, let us turn to its drawbacks.
  • Si le télétravail offre une réelle liberté, il n’en comporte pas moins des risques. — Although remote work offers real freedom, it nonetheless carries risks. — si here means “although”.
  • Dès lors, comment concilier liberté et protection des salariés ? — So how can freedom and employee protection be reconciled? — a question that opens part III.

Careful

  • Wrong: Premièrement, … Deuxièmement, … Troisièmement, …
  • Right: Tout d’abord, … Nous avons vu que… Voyons à présent… … Dès lors, …
  • Why: A numbered list is not an argument. Each part must lead logically into the next, so the reader feels the reasoning move forward.

docs.title: The conclusion: bilan, réponse, ouverture
docs.text:
• Bilan : Au terme de cette réflexion, il apparaît que le télétravail présente autant d’atouts que de risques. — Summary: At the end of this discussion, remote work appears to have as many strengths as risks.
  • Réponse : Il constitue donc un progrès, à condition qu’il reste choisi et encadré. — Answer: It is therefore progress, provided it remains a choice and is regulated. — à condition que + subjunctive.
  • Ouverture : Reste à savoir si nos villes sauront s’adapter à ce nouveau mode de vie. — Opening: It remains to be seen whether our cities will adapt to this new way of life.

Careful

  • Wrong: En conclusion, il faut aussi ajouter que le télétravail coûte cher aux entreprises.
  • Right: En conclusion, le télétravail constitue un progrès, à condition qu’il reste encadré.
  • Why: The conclusion never brings a new argument. If the idea matters, move it into the development. The conclusion sums up, answers, and opens.

docs.title: 53.7 Model essay, annotated
docs.text:
A B2-level essay of about 290 words, dialectical plan in two parts with a nuanced answer. Read each block, then its note.

Faut-il interdire les téléphones portables à l’école ? Should mobile phones be banned at school?

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• Aujourd’hui, la plupart des adolescents possèdent un smartphone et le consultent des dizaines de fois par jour. En France, depuis 2018, la loi interdit d’ailleurs son utilisation à l’école et au collège. — Today most teenagers own a smartphone and check it dozens of times a day. In France, since 2018, the law has in fact banned its use in primary and lower secondary schools. — amorce + sujet: a fact, then the precise topic. La plupart des takes a plural verb.
  • Cette mesure divise pourtant parents et enseignants. Faut-il vraiment bannir le téléphone des établissements scolaires ? — Yet this measure divides parents and teachers. Should phones really be banished from schools? — the debate, then the problématique, reworded rather than copied from the title.
