Nous voilà enfin débarrassés de ces minutes vides où il ne se passait rien… sinon, peut-être, une pensée. Car c’est bien là le problème : la disparition de l’ennui n’est pas sans conséquences. Les psychologues le répètent : c’est dans le désœuvrement que naissent bien des idées, et c’est à force de regarder par la fenêtre que l’enfant finit par inventer des histoires.

Loin de moi l’idée de jouer les donneurs de leçons : je suis le premier à dégainer mon téléphone dès que l’ascenseur tarde. Mais il faudrait que nous réapprenions à supporter l’attente, avant que la moindre seconde d’inactivité ne nous devienne insupportable. Qu’on le veuille ou non, le refus de l’ennui est aussi un refus de la lenteur, et donc de la réflexion. Alors, la prochaine fois que vous attendrez le bus, laissez votre téléphone dans votre poche. Vous risquez de vous ennuyer. C’est précisément le but.

English translation

It seems we no longer know how to be bored. In the queue, on the metro, even at a red light, out comes the phone at the slightest lull. What progress! At last we are rid of those empty minutes when nothing happened… except, perhaps, a thought. Because that is exactly the problem: the disappearance of boredom is not without consequences. Psychologists keep saying it: many ideas are born of idleness, and it is by staring out of the window that a child ends up inventing stories.

Far be it from me to lecture anyone: I am the first to whip out my phone as soon as the lift is slow. But we ought to relearn how to bear waiting, before the slightest second of inactivity becomes unbearable to us. Whether we like it or not, refusing boredom also means refusing slowness — and therefore thought. So next time you wait for the bus, leave your phone in your pocket. You might get bored. That is precisely the point.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Quel progrès ! Nous voilà enfin débarrassés… — Antiphrasis: the columnist means the opposite. The clue is the next line: “except, perhaps, a thought”.
  • La disparition de l’ennui n’est pas sans conséquences. — Nominalisation (la disparition) + litotes (pas sans = it has serious consequences).
  • … avant que la moindre seconde d’inactivité ne nous devienne insupportable. — avant que + subjunctive, with the elegant “expletive” ne — it is not a negative.

The expletive ne

After avant que, à moins que, de peur que and in comparisons (plus difficile qu’on ne le pense), formal French adds a ne with no pas. It does not mean “not”. Mishearing it as a negative reverses the meaning.

docs.title: 56.6 Le texte littéraire — le passé simple à l’oreille
docs.text:
Audiobooks and literature programmes use the passé simple, the tense of written narration. You don’t need to use it, but you must recognise it instantly. Here is an original passage in classic 19th-century style, then two famous public-domain opening lines to recognise. See Literary & formal French for the full forms.

You hear Infinitive Meaning elle atteignit atteindre she reached elle s’arrêta s’arrêter she stopped elle hésita hésiter she hesitated la porte céda céder the door gave way elle comprit comprendre she understood il fut · il eut · il vint être · avoir · venir he was · had · came
  • ▶ Le retour (original passage) — Sort the verbs as you listen: actions in the passé simple, background in the imparfait.
Transcript

Le soir tombait lorsque Mathilde atteignit enfin le village. La pluie avait cessé, mais une brume épaisse montait de la rivière et noyait les toits dans une lumière grise. Elle s’arrêta devant la maison de son enfance. Les volets étaient clos ; le jardin, autrefois si soigné, n’était plus qu’un fouillis d’herbes folles. Elle hésita longtemps, la main sur la grille froide. Puis elle poussa la porte, qui céda avec un gémissement. Une odeur de poussière et de cire la saisit. Rien n’avait changé : la pendule, sur la cheminée, marquait toujours cinq heures. Mathilde comprit alors que le temps, dans cette maison, s’était arrêté le jour de son départ.

English translation

Evening was falling when Mathilde at last reached the village. The rain had stopped, but a thick mist was rising from the river, drowning the roofs in a grey light. She stopped in front of her childhood home. The shutters were closed; the garden, once so well kept, was now nothing but a tangle of weeds. She hesitated for a long time, her hand on the cold gate. Then she pushed the door, which gave way with a groan. A smell of dust and wax seized her. Nothing had changed: the clock on the mantelpiece still said five o’clock. Mathilde understood then that time, in this house, had stopped on the day she left.

docs.title: Two famous lines to recognise
docs.text:
• « Demain, dès l’aube, à l’heure où blanchit la campagne, / Je partirai. » — Victor Hugo, Les Contemplations (1856). “Tomorrow, at dawn, when the countryside turns white, I will set off.” Note the inversion où blanchit la campagne — verb before subject, a poetic and formal habit.
  • « Longtemps, je me suis couché de bonne heure. » — Marcel Proust, Du côté de chez Swann (1913). “For a long time, I went to bed early.” Famous precisely because it opens a novel with the passé composé, not the passé simple.

Careful

  • Wrong: Puis elle poussait la porte, qui céda.
  • Right: Puis elle poussa la porte, qui céda.
  • Why: Puis introduces a new event in the chain: passé simple. The imparfait is for the scenery (le soir tombait).

Careful

  • Wrong: Il venit le lendemain.
  • Right: Il vint le lendemain.
  • Why: venir, tenir and their family have a passé simple in -in-: il vint, ils vinrent; il tint, ils tinrent.

docs.title: 56.7 La conversation rapide — entre potes
docs.text:
Now the opposite end: two friends chatting about a film, fast and relaxed. Everything from Real spoken French is here — no ne, t’as, y a, fillers like bah, quoi, bref, du coup — plus humour you must catch from the context.

You hear Standard / meaning t’as vu ? tu as vu ? — did you see? j’ai pas trop accroché I didn’t really get into it je dis pas I’ll grant you that c’est n’importe quoi it’s nonsense un mec a guy kiffer (j’ai trop kiffé) to love (I loved it) t’es dur you’re harsh c’est pas faux fair point (often humorous)
  • ▶ La conversation (fast) — Who liked the film? Why can’t one of them really judge it?
Transcript

— Alors, t’as vu le dernier film de Lucas ? — Ouais, hier soir. Franchement, j’ai pas trop accroché. — Ah bon ? Pourtant, tout le monde dit que c’est génial ! — Bah, les images sont belles, je dis pas. Mais l’histoire, c’est n’importe quoi. Y a un mec qui disparaît au milieu, on sait jamais pourquoi… Bref, deux heures et demie, quoi. — T’es dur, là. Moi, j’ai trop kiffé la fin. — Ouais, enfin, la fin, je l’ai un peu ratée : je m’étais endormi. — Non ! T’es sérieux ? Bon, ben du coup, t’as pas le droit de donner ton avis ! — C’est pas faux.

English translation

— So, have you seen Lucas’s latest film? — Yeah, last night. Honestly, I didn’t really get into it. — Really? Everyone says it’s brilliant, though! — Well, the visuals are beautiful, I’ll give you that. But the story is nonsense. There’s a guy who disappears halfway through, you never find out why… Anyway — two and a half hours, you know. — You’re being harsh. I loved the ending. — Yeah, well, the ending — I sort of missed it: I’d fallen asleep. — No! Seriously? Well then, you’re not allowed to give your opinion! — Fair point.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Bref, deux heures et demie, quoi. — Implicit: “far too long”. The judgement is never said — bref… quoi and the tone do the work.
  • La fin, je l’ai un peu ratée : je m’étais endormi. — Dislocation (la fin, je l’ai…) puts the topic first — typical of speech. ratée agrees with l’ = la fin.
  • C’est pas faux. — A comic concession: he admits he has no real argument. Understatement again.

Careful

  • Wrong: (oral exam) Bah, j’ai pas trop accroché à cette thèse, quoi.
  • Right: Je ne suis pas entièrement convaincu par cette thèse.
  • Why: Understand the familiar register; switch back to standard French in an exam, an interview or a presentation.

À retenir

  • At this level, the questions are “What does the speaker think?” and “What do they mean?” — not “What did they say?”. Tone, register and connectors carry the answer.
  • Turn what you hear into nouns: « la pollution recule » → ↓ pollution; « on a fermé la rue » → fermeture rue. This is nominalisation — see Nominalisation & formal style.
  • A speaker who suddenly switches register is telling you something: going up (je l’ignore) adds distance or coldness; going down (ça me saoule) shows emotion or complicity. See Registers & slang.
  • Make this a habit: one debate or column a week, notes with the template, then a one-sentence synthesis. For the exam side, DELF, DALF & your level explains the C1–C2 listening papers — and the Final test is waiting.

docs.title: 56.8 Practice — Expert listening
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is Claire Morel's position?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Claire Morel, vous êtes favorable à une interdiction totale ? Totale, non, mais progressive, oui. Il est temps que nous cessions de considérer la rue comme un parking.

  • For a gradual ban
  • For a total, immediate ban
  • Against any restriction
  • Undecided
Answer

For a gradual ban

Totale, non, mais progressive, oui.

Exercise 2

What is Patrick Garnier's main argument? (inference)

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Qu'on ne vienne pas nous dire que tout le monde peut se passer de sa voiture ! Allez expliquer ça à une infirmière qui habite à trente kilomètres et qui finit son service à minuit.

  • A ban penalises people with no real alternative
  • Nurses cause traffic jams
  • Pollution is not a real problem
  • Public transport is too expensive
Answer

A ban penalises people with no real alternative

The nurse is an example of someone who cannot do without a car.

Exercise 3

What does Garnier really mean here? (attitude)

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Alors, la ville apaisée, je veux bien, à condition que ce ne soit pas une ville réservée à ceux qui peuvent se le permettre.

  • He accepts the idea in principle but fears it will favour the wealthy
  • He fully supports the project
  • He wants cities to be reserved for residents
  • He refuses any discussion
Answer

He accepts the idea in principle but fears it will favour the wealthy

je veux bien = reluctant yes; à condition que… = the real objection.

Exercise 4

What is the structure of the lecture?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Dans un premier temps, nous verrons d'où elle vient ; dans un second temps, nous nous demanderons à quoi elle sert aujourd'hui.

  • Origins, then its role today
  • Its members, then its dictionary
  • Its role today, then the future
  • A list of famous members
Answer

Origins, then its role today

d'où elle vient / à quoi elle sert aujourd'hui.

Exercise 5

What is the tone of this opening? (attitude)

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Je voudrais vous parler d'une institution que le monde entier nous envie, ou dont il se moque, selon les cas : l'Académie française.

  • Gently ironic, self-mocking
  • Angry and hostile
  • Purely admiring
  • Sad
Answer

Gently ironic, self-mocking

envie… ou dont il se moque: the lecturer laughs a little at French pride.

Exercise 6

What is the lecturer's conclusion?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Autrement dit, ce n'est pas l'Académie qui fait la langue, ce sont ceux qui la parlent. Son rôle est donc aujourd'hui plus symbolique que normatif, ce qui, après tout, n'est pas rien.

  • Its role is mainly symbolic, but that still matters
  • It should be abolished
  • It controls how French people speak
  • It has never had any influence
Answer

Its role is mainly symbolic, but that still matters

plus symbolique que normatif + n'est pas rien (litotes = it matters).

Exercise 7

'Quel progrès !' — what does the columnist mean? (irony)

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Le téléphone surgit au moindre temps mort. Quel progrès ! Nous voilà enfin débarrassés de ces minutes vides où il ne se passait rien, sinon, peut-être, une pensée.

  • The opposite: this is not real progress
  • Phones are a great invention
  • We should buy better phones
  • Waiting has become shorter
Answer

The opposite: this is not real progress

Antiphrasis. 'sinon, peut-être, une pensée' reveals what we lost.

Exercise 8

According to the columnist, what is boredom good for?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

La disparition de l'ennui n'est pas sans conséquences. C'est dans le désœuvrement que naissent bien des idées, et c'est à force de regarder par la fenêtre que l'enfant finit par inventer des histoires.

  • Creativity and new ideas
  • Sleeping better
  • Saving time
  • Learning languages
Answer

Creativity and new ideas

naissent bien des idées / inventer des histoires.

Exercise 9

How does the columnist avoid sounding preachy?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Loin de moi l'idée de jouer les donneurs de leçons : je suis le premier à dégainer mon téléphone dès que l'ascenseur tarde.

  • He admits he does the same
  • He quotes an expert
  • He blames young people
  • He changes the subject
Answer

He admits he does the same

je suis le premier à dégainer mon téléphone = self-criticism.

Exercise 10

What is the mood of this passage?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Elle s'arrêta devant la maison de son enfance. Les volets étaient clos ; le jardin, autrefois si soigné, n'était plus qu'un fouillis d'herbes folles. Elle hésita longtemps, la main sur la grille froide.

  • Melancholic, nostalgic
  • Joyful, festive
  • Comic
  • Angry
Answer

Melancholic, nostalgic

closed shutters, a neglected garden, hesitation, cold: loss and memory.

Exercise 11

What does Mathilde understand? (inference)

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Rien n'avait changé : la pendule, sur la cheminée, marquait toujours cinq heures. Mathilde comprit alors que le temps, dans cette maison, s'était arrêté le jour de son départ.

  • The house has stayed as it was since she left
  • The clock needs a new battery
  • She is late
  • Someone is waiting for her
Answer

The house has stayed as it was since she left

The stopped clock symbolises a house left untouched since her departure.

Exercise 12

Which work opens with this line?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Longtemps, je me suis couché de bonne heure.

  • Proust, Du côté de chez Swann
  • Hugo, Les Contemplations
  • Flaubert, Madame Bovary
  • Maupassant, Bel-Ami
Answer

Proust, Du côté de chez Swann

The famous first sentence of À la recherche du temps perdu (1913).

Exercise 13

Did the second speaker like the film?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Alors, t'as vu le dernier film de Lucas ? Ouais, hier soir. Franchement, j'ai pas trop accroché. Les images sont belles, je dis pas. Mais l'histoire, c'est n'importe quoi.

  • Not really — nice images, poor story
  • Yes, very much
  • He hasn't seen it
  • Only the ending
Answer

Not really — nice images, poor story

j'ai pas trop accroché; je dis pas = concession about the images only.

Exercise 14

Why does his friend say he can't give his opinion? (inference)

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Moi, j'ai trop kiffé la fin. Ouais, enfin, la fin, je l'ai un peu ratée : je m'étais endormi. Non ! T'es sérieux ? Bon, ben du coup, t'as pas le droit de donner ton avis !

  • He fell asleep before the end
  • He arrived late
  • He watched it on his phone
  • He didn't pay for the ticket
Answer

He fell asleep before the end

je m'étais endormi = I had fallen asleep.

Exercise 15

'Selon nos informations, le ministre aurait démissionné.' The journalist…

  • reports unconfirmed information
  • says the minister will resign
  • says the minister should resign
  • denies the resignation
Answer

reports unconfirmed information

The journalistic conditional = reportedly, not confirmed.

Exercise 16

Match the expression to what it really means.

A B Ce n'est pas rien That's all we needed Je ne vous le fais pas dire Fair point Il ne manquait plus que ça It's significant C'est pas faux You said it Answer

Ce n'est pas rien — It's significant; Je ne vous le fais pas dire — You said it; Il ne manquait plus que ça — That's all we needed; C'est pas faux — Fair point

Understatement and irony: the literal meaning is not the real one.

Exercise 17

Dictée — debate (subjunctive).

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Il est temps que nous cessions de considérer la rue comme un parking.

cessions = subjunctive of cesser after il est temps que.

Exercise 18

Dictée — lecture.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Bien que ses avis n'aient aucune valeur contraignante, l'Académie conserve un rôle symbolique.

bien que + subjunctive: n'aient; contraignante agrees with valeur (f).

Exercise 19

Dictée — column (expletive ne).

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Il faudrait que nous réapprenions à supporter l'attente, avant que la moindre seconde d'inactivité ne nous devienne insupportable.

réapprenions (subjunctive), avant que + ne explétif + devienne.

Exercise 20

Agree strongly with someone, in elegant French.

Je ne vous le fais pas dire

Answer

= You said it — I couldn't agree more.

Next step

Make this a habit: one debate or column a week, notes with the template, then a one-sentence synthesis. For the exam side, DELF, DALF & your level explains the C1–C2 listening papers — and the Final test is waiting.

docs.title: Chapter 60: Final test
docs.text:
L’examen final

Forty questions, one for (almost) every chapter, in the order of the book: sounds first, then the foundations, the big grammar machine, speaking, vocabulary, writing and culture. It is not an official exam — it is a map of your gaps. Every wrong answer points to exactly one or two chapters to reopen.

How to use this test

Do it in one sitting, without looking back at the chapters. Write down the number of every question you miss — then use the table in section 6 to see which chapter to reopen.

docs.title: 60.1 How the test works
docs.text:
The test mixes all six question types you have met in the book: multiple choice, fill the gap, spot the mistake, put the words in order, match the pairs, and say it aloud.

  • Time: about 45 minutes. Do not stop to look things up.
  • Paper: keep a notebook open and write the numbers of the questions you miss.
  • Voice: read every French sentence in your head with its sounds — liaison, nasals, silent letters.
  • Retake: do it again in a week. The second score is the one that counts.

Read the hint only after you try

Answer first, then check the hint. A guess you correct teaches you more than an answer you copy.

docs.title: 60.2 What the test covers
docs.text:
The questions follow the seven Parts of the book. Part 3 (Construire) has the most, because it is where most marks are lost in real exams: pronouns, past tenses, the subjunctive.

Figure 60.1. Each bar is one Part of the book. Several questions test two chapters at once (for example Q23 tests both the subjunctive and linking words), so every chapter is covered.

The weighting

More than half the test (22 of 40) is grammar from Parts 2 and 3 — the skeleton of every sentence you will ever say.

docs.title: 60.3 Warm-up — say these aloud first
docs.text:
Ten sentences from across the book. Listen, repeat each one twice, then start the test. If any of them feels strange, note the chapter in brackets.

  • Les‿enfants sont‿au jardin. — The children are in the garden. (Silent letters & liaison)
  • Il a quatre-vingt-dix-sept ans. — He is ninety-seven. (Numbers, dates & time · Être & avoir)
  • Je n’ai pas de voiture, mais j’ai un vélo. — I don’t have a car, but I have a bike. (Articles · Saying no)
  • Tu en veux ? — Oui, j’en veux deux. — Do you want some? — Yes, I want two. (Y, en & pronoun order)
  • Quand j’étais petit, j’habitais à Chennai. — When I was little, I lived in Chennai. (Imparfait vs passé composé)
  • Il faut que tu viennes avec nous. — You have to come with us. (The subjunctive)
  • Si j’avais su, je serais venu plus tôt. — If I had known, I would have come earlier. (Advanced compound tenses)
  • Bah, du coup, on y va ou quoi ? — Well, so, are we going or what? (Real spoken French)
  • J’ai la flemme de sortir, il pleut des cordes. — I can’t be bothered to go out, it’s pouring. (Idioms & expressions)
  • Je vous prie d’agréer, Madame, l’expression de mes salutations distinguées. — Yours faithfully. (Messages, letters & emails)
  • Néanmoins, cette démarche suscite de nombreuses questions. — Nevertheless, this approach raises many questions. (Word building & advanced words)
  • À Pondichéry, on voit encore des noms de rue en français. — In Pondicherry you still see street names in French. (Culture & the francophone world)

docs.title: 60.4 Four traps to avoid on the way
docs.text:
These are not in the test — but they are the slips that most often make a learner change a right answer into a wrong one. Read them once, then start.

Classic traps

  • Wrong: Je suis fini.
  • Right: J’ai fini.

  • Why: Je suis fini means "I am done for". Finishing something takes avoir.

  • Wrong: J’attends pour le bus.

  • Right: J’attends le bus.

  • Why: attendre, chercher, écouter, regarder take a direct object — no "for", "at" or "to".

  • Wrong: Si j’aurais su…

  • Right: Si j’avais su…

  • Why: Never the conditional right after si (= if). Si + imparfait / plus-que-parfait.

  • Wrong: Il pleut des chats et des chiens.

  • Right: Il pleut des cordes.
  • Why: Idioms do not travel word for word. French rain falls in "ropes".

docs.title: 60.5 Your score — what it means
docs.text:
Count one point per question. The bands below are a rough guide to which level you are building on — only an official exam gives you a certified level (see DELF, DALF & your level).

Score What it suggests What to do next 36–40 A solid B2 foundation Work on C1 material: Literary & formal French, Arguing & presenting, Word building & advanced words; try DELF B2 / DALF C1 sample papers. 28–35 Around B1, heading to B2 Reopen only the chapters of the questions you missed (section 6), then retake the test in a week. 18–27 Around A2, heading to B1 Redo Part 3 Construire in order, with each chapter’s quiz twice. 0–17 A1–A2 No problem — start again from How to use this book and go through Part 2 Les bases slowly, out loud.

Speaking counts double in real life

If you missed the three spoken questions (Q2, Q4, Q20), give them extra time: reopen Pronunciation clinic before anything else.

docs.title: 60.6 Where did you go wrong? Reopen this chapter
docs.text: Find each question you missed. The chapter named on the right is where the answer is taught.

docs.title: 60.7 After the test — a one-week repair plan
docs.text:
Do not reread the whole book. Reopen only what the table told you, and use the chapter quizzes, which are short enough to do every day.

Day What to do 1 List the chapters from section 6. Read the first one and do its quiz. 2–4 One or two chapters a day; redo yesterday’s quiz before starting a new one. 5 Say every say example of your weakest chapter aloud — twice. 6 Write five sentences using what you repaired; check them against the chapters. 7 Retake this final test. Compare the two scores.

À retenir

  • Do it in one sitting, without looking back at the chapters. Write down the number of every question you miss — then use the table in section 6 to see which chapter to reopen.
  • Answer first, then check the hint. A guess you correct teaches you more than an answer you copy.
  • More than half the test (22 of 40) is grammar from Parts 2 and 3 — the skeleton of every sentence you will ever say.
  • If you missed the three spoken questions (Q2, Q4, Q20), give them extra time: reopen Pronunciation clinic before anything else.
  • Write your score and the date in your notebook. Fix the chapters from section 6 this week, then retake the test — and when you score 36 or more twice, book your next exam (see DELF, DALF & your level). Bravo et bonne…

docs.title: 60.8 Final test — the whole book
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Q1 · Match each accent to its sound.

A B é s, as in garçon è oh, as in hôtel ç ay, as in café ô eh, as in mère Answer

é — ay, as in café; è — eh, as in mère; ç — s, as in garçon; ô — oh, as in hôtel

é is closed [e], è is open [ɛ], ç is always [s], ô is a closed [o]. See Alphabet & accents.

Exercise 2

Q2 · Say it aloud: u and ou in one line.

Toute la rue a vu le loup

Answer

toute, loup = ou [u]; rue, vu = u [y]: say ee with rounded lips. See The sounds of French.

Exercise 3

Q3 · How do you pronounce « les amis »?

  • lay-ah-MEE
  • lay-zah-MEE
  • less-ah-MEE
  • lay-sah-MEE

Hint: liaison

Answer

lay-zah-MEE

The silent s of les is pronounced z before a vowel: les‿amis. See Silent letters & liaison.

Exercise 4

Q4 · At the bakery — say it politely.

Bonjour Madame, je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît

Answer

Bonjour first, then je voudrais (not je veux), then s'il vous plaît. See Hello, please, thank you.

Exercise 5

Q5 · 99 = quatre-vingt-___

Hint: 4 × 20 + 19

Answer

dix-neuf / dix neuf

quatre-vingt-dix-neuf = 80 + 19. See Numbers, dates & time.

Exercise 6

Q6 · C'est ___ problème difficile.

  • un
  • une
  • la
  • des

Hint: Words in -ème from Greek

Answer

un

le problème, le système, le thème are masculine despite the final -e. See Nouns, gender & plurals.

Exercise 7

Q7 · Le matin, je mange ___ pain. (some bread)

Answer

du

An unspecified amount of a masculine noun: du pain. See Articles.

Exercise 8

Q8 · Tap the wrong word.

Mon frère est vingt-cinq ans.

Answer

Wrong word: est.

Corrected: Mon frère a vingt-cinq ans.

French has its age: avoir 25 ans. See Être & avoir.

Exercise 9

Q9 · Nous ___ (manger) au restaurant ce soir.

Hint: Keep the g soft

Answer

mangeons

-ger verbs keep an e before -ons: nous mangeons. See Present tense: -er verbs.

Exercise 10

Q10 · Ils ___ au cinéma ce soir. (aller)

  • vont
  • allent
  • vas
  • allons
Answer

vont

aller: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont. See Present tense: the rest.

Exercise 11

Q11 · Put the words in order: I never eat meat.

Words: mange / viande / Je / de / jamais / ne

Answer

Je ne mange jamais de viande

ne + verb + jamais, and de (not de la) after a negation. See Saying no.

Exercise 12

Q12 · ___ apprends-tu le français ? — Parce que je veux vivre à Montréal.

  • Pourquoi
  • Comment
  • Quand
  • Où
Answer

Pourquoi

The answer parce que (because) matches pourquoi (why). See Asking questions.

Exercise 13

Q13 · Cette pizza est ___ que l'autre.

  • meilleure
  • plus bonne
  • meilleur
  • mieux

Hint: bon → ?

Answer

meilleure

bon becomes meilleur, and agrees with pizza (feminine): meilleure. mieux is the adverb. See Adjectives and Comparing.

Exercise 14

Q14 · Tap the wrong word.

Ma amie Sophie arrive demain.

Answer

Wrong word: Ma.

Corrected: Mon amie Sophie arrive demain.

Before a vowel sound, ma becomes mon, even for a feminine noun: mon amie. See My, your, this, that.

Exercise 15

Q15 · Tap the wrong word.

Cet été, je vais en Japon.

Answer

Wrong word: en.

Corrected: Cet été, je vais au Japon.

Masculine countries take au (au Japon, au Canada); feminine ones take en (en France, en Inde). See Prepositions & places.

Exercise 16

Q16 · Je donne le livre à Paul → replace both with pronouns.

Words: le / lui / donne / Je

Answer

Je le lui donne

Order: le / la / les before lui / leur. See Object pronouns and Y, en & pronoun order.

Exercise 17

Q17 · Ce matin, elle s'est ___ (lever) à six heures.

Hint: être + agreement

Answer

levée / levee

Reflexive verbs take être, and the participle agrees: elle s'est levée. See Reflexive verbs and The past: passé composé.

Exercise 18

Q18 · Je ___ la télé quand le téléphone a sonné.

  • regardais
  • ai regardé
  • regarde
  • regarderai
Answer

regardais

The action in progress (the scene) is in the imparfait; the interruption (the event) in the passé composé. See Imparfait vs passé composé.

Exercise 19

Q19 · Demain, nous ___ (partir) à huit heures. (futur simple)

Answer

partirons

Futur simple = infinitive + -ons: partirons. See The future.

Exercise 20

Q20 · Tell a friend not to worry.

Ne t'inquiète pas, tout va bien

Answer

Negative imperative of a reflexive verb: the pronoun stays in front — ne t'inquiète pas. See Giving instructions.

Exercise 21

Q21 · C'est le livre ___ je t'ai parlé.

  • dont
  • que
  • qui
  • où

Hint: parler de…

Answer

dont

parler de quelque chose → dont replaces de + noun. See Relative pronouns.

Exercise 22

Q22 · Si j'avais le temps, je ___ (voyager) plus souvent.

Answer

voyagerais

si + imparfait → conditionnel présent: je voyagerais. See Conditional & si clauses.

Exercise 23

Q23 · Bien qu'il ___ fatigué, il continue à travailler.

  • soit
  • est
  • sera
  • était
Answer

soit

bien que always takes the subjunctive: qu'il soit. See The subjunctive and Linking words.

Exercise 24

Q24 · Quand je suis arrivé, le film ___ déjà commencé.

  • avait
  • a
  • aura
  • aurait
Answer

avait

An action before another past action: plus-que-parfait, il avait commencé. See Advanced compound tenses.

Exercise 25

Q25 · Il a dit : « Je viendrai demain. » → Il a dit qu'il ___ le lendemain.

Hint: future in the past

Answer

viendrait

After a past reporting verb, the future becomes the conditional: viendrait; demain becomes le lendemain. See Passive & reported speech.

Exercise 26

Q26 · Il s'est blessé ___ du vélo. (while riding)

  • en faisant
  • en fait
  • pour faire
  • faisant en
Answer

en faisant

Gérondif = en + present participle: en faisant = while doing. See Gérondif & participles.

Exercise 27

Q27 · Match the passé simple (novels) to the passé composé (speech).

A B il fut ils ont fait elle alla nous avons eu ils firent il a été nous eûmes elle est allée Answer

il fut — il a été; elle alla — elle est allée; ils firent — ils ont fait; nous eûmes — nous avons eu

You must recognise the passé simple to read novels. See Literary & formal French.

Exercise 28

Q28 · Emergency numbers in France.

A B 15 pompiers (fire brigade) 17 European emergency number 18 SAMU (medical emergency) 112 police Answer

15 — SAMU (medical emergency); 17 — police; 18 — pompiers (fire brigade); 112 — European emergency number

15 doctor, 17 police, 18 fire, 112 anywhere in Europe. See Travel & emergencies.

Exercise 29

Q29 · À mon ___, c'est une excellente idée. (opinion)

Answer

avis

À mon avis = in my opinion (never « dans mon opinion »). See Conversation & opinions.

Exercise 30

Q30 · Match spoken or slang French to standard French.

A B chais pas travail bagnole femme boulot je ne sais pas meuf voiture Answer

chais pas — je ne sais pas; bagnole — voiture; boulot — travail; meuf — femme

chais pas is fast speech; bagnole and boulot are familier; meuf is verlan for femme. See Real spoken French and Registers & slang.

Exercise 31

Q31 · On the phone, « Ne quittez pas » means…

  • Hold the line
  • Don't leave the building
  • Don't quit your job
  • Stay seated
Answer

Hold the line

Ne quittez pas = please hold. See Work, phone & interviews.

Exercise 32

Q32 · Match the French to the English.

A B le genou coat la cuisine summer le manteau knee l'été kitchen Answer

le genou — knee; la cuisine — kitchen; le manteau — coat; l'été — summer

Body, home, clothes and seasons. See Core vocabulary by theme.

Exercise 33

Q33 · How do you say « I miss you »?

  • Tu me manques
  • Je te manque
  • Je manque toi
  • Je te rate
Answer

Tu me manques

With manquer, the person who is missed is the subject: tu me manques = you are missing to me. See The 100 essential verbs.

Exercise 34

Q34 · Tap the word that is a false friend here.

Je vais à la librairie pour emprunter des livres.

Answer

Wrong word: librairie.

Corrected: Je vais à la bibliothèque pour emprunter des livres.

une librairie is a bookshop; a library is une bibliothèque. See Cognates & false friends.

Exercise 35

Q35 · « Il m'a posé un lapin » means…

  • He stood me up
  • He gave me a rabbit
  • He played a trick on me
  • He made me laugh
Answer

He stood me up

poser un lapin à quelqu'un = to not turn up to a date. See Idioms & expressions.

Exercise 36

Q36 · changer (to change) → le ___ (a change)

Hint: a common noun suffix

Answer

changement

verb stem + -ment makes many masculine nouns: changement, développement. See Word building & advanced words.

Exercise 37

Q37 · Tap the spelling mistake.

Hier, elle est allée a Lyon.

Answer

Wrong word: a.

Corrected: Hier, elle est allée à Lyon.

Can you say « avait » instead? No → it is the preposition à. See Spelling & punctuation.

Exercise 38

Q38 · The best ending for a formal letter:

  • Veuillez agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
  • Gros bisous et à bientôt !
  • Merci, à plus !
  • Salut et bonne journée !
Answer

Veuillez agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.

The formule de politesse repeats the opening (Madame, Monsieur). See Messages, letters & emails.

Exercise 39

Q39 · Match each part of a French essay to its job.

A B l'amorce tells the reader the parts la problématique widens the topic at the very end l'annonce du plan catches the reader's attention l'ouverture the question the essay answers Answer

l'amorce — catches the reader's attention; la problématique — the question the essay answers; l'annonce du plan — tells the reader the parts; l'ouverture — widens the topic at the very end

Introduction: amorce, problématique, annonce du plan; conclusion: bilan, ouverture. See Essays & structured writing.

Exercise 40

Q40 · In France 70 is soixante-dix. In Belgium and Switzerland people say…

  • septante
  • soixante-dix
  • huitante
  • septante-dix
Answer

septante

Belgium and Switzerland: septante (70) and nonante (90); some Swiss cantons also say huitante (80). See Culture & the francophone world.

Next step

Write your score and the date in your notebook. Fix the chapters from section 6 this week, then retake the test — and when you score 36 or more twice, book your next exam (see DELF, DALF & your level). Bravo et bonne continuation !

docs.title: Chapter 54: First stories
docs.text:
Premières histoires

Six short stories, read slowly, about real everyday moments: buying bread, a first day at work, a rainy weekend, a family, a phone call from mum and a trip to the market. You listen first, without the text. Then you check the key words, open the transcript, and finally write a classic French dictée. This is how your ear learns French — one small story at a time.

Listen first, read last

Play each story twice before you open the transcript. Your brain only learns to decode sounds when it has to try. Reading first turns listening into reading.

docs.title: 54.1 How to use these stories
docs.text:
Every story follows the same five steps. One story takes about ten minutes. Do one a day rather than all six in one evening — your ear improves with repetition, not with long sessions.

Figure 54.1. The listening cycle. Steps 1–2 train your ear; steps 3–5 fix the words in your memory.

You don’t need every word

At A1–A2, understanding 60–70% of a story is a success. Catch the names, numbers, places and times first — they carry most of the meaning.

In the key-word tables, the colours show gender, as everywhere in this book: masculine, feminine, plural.

  • Pardon, vous pouvez répéter ? — Sorry, can you repeat? — the most useful listening sentence in French. [par-DÕ, voo poo-VAY ray-pay-TAY]
  • Plus lentement, s’il vous plaît. — More slowly, please. [plew lãt-MÃ, seel voo PLAY]

docs.title: 54.2 Histoire 1 — Léa à la boulangerie
docs.text:
It is Saturday morning. Léa goes to buy bread, like many French people do every day. Listen for: what does she buy, and how much does it cost?

Français English Sound la boulangerie bakery [la boo-lãzh-REE] la boulangère the (woman) baker [la boo-lã-ZHEHR] une baguette a baguette [ewn ba-GET] un croissant a croissant [ɛ̃ krwa-SÃ] Ça fait combien ? How much is it? [sa fay kõ-BYɛ̃] payer (elle paie) to pay (she pays) [pay-YAY, el PAY] le petit-déjeuner breakfast [luh puh-tee day-zhuh-NAY] encore still / again [ã-KOR]
  • ▶ Toute l’histoire (slow) — Listen twice. Then answer in your head: what? how much? who is still asleep?
Transcript

Le samedi matin, Léa va à la boulangerie. Elle entre et dit : « Bonjour, madame ! » La boulangère sourit : « Bonjour, Léa ! Qu’est-ce que je vous sers ? » Léa veut une baguette et deux croissants. « Ça fait combien ? » demande-t-elle. « Trois euros quarante, s’il vous plaît. » Léa paie, dit merci et rentre à la maison. Son petit frère dort encore. Elle prépare le petit-déjeuner pour toute la famille.

English translation

On Saturday mornings, Léa goes to the bakery. She goes in and says: “Hello, madam!” The baker smiles: “Hello, Léa! What can I get you?” Léa wants a baguette and two croissants. “How much is it?” she asks. “Three euros forty, please.” Léa pays, says thank you and goes back home. Her little brother is still asleep. She makes breakfast for the whole family.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Qu’est-ce que je vous sers ? — What can I get you? (literally “What do I serve you?”) — you hear it in every shop and café. [kess-kuh zhuh voo SEHR]
  • Trois euros quarante. — €3.40 — prices are said “euros” first, then the cents, with no “and”. [trwa-zuh-ROH ka-RÃT]
  • Son petit frère dort encore. — Her little brother is still sleeping — French uses the simple present for “is sleeping”. [sõ puh-tee FREHR dor ã-KOR]

le samedi = every Saturday

Samedi, je vais au marché = this Saturday. Le samedi, je vais au marché = every Saturday. One little le turns a day into a habit.

docs.title: 54.3 Histoire 2 — Le premier jour de Raj à Lyon
docs.text:
Raj comes from Pune. He has just moved to Lyon for a job in IT. The story is in the passé composé (the past). Listen for: what time did he arrive, and what did he eat for the first time?

Français English Sound une entreprise a company [ewn ã-truh-PREEZ] l’informatique IT, computing [lɛ̃-for-ma-TEEK] le bureau office, desk [luh bew-ROH] les collègues colleagues [lay ko-LEG] la cantine staff canteen [la kã-TEEN] goûter (il a goûté) to taste (he tasted) [goo-TAY] depuis une semaine for a week (and still) [duh-PWEE ewn suh-MEN] fatigué / content tired / happy [fa-tee-GAY / kõ-TÃ]
  • ▶ Toute l’histoire (slow) — Listen twice. Count the times you hear a past verb (il a…, il est…).
Transcript

Raj est indien. Il habite à Lyon depuis une semaine. Lundi, il a commencé son nouveau travail dans une entreprise d’informatique. Il s’est levé à six heures et il a pris le métro. Il est arrivé au bureau à huit heures et demie. Ses collègues ont été très gentils. À midi, ils ont mangé ensemble à la cantine et Raj a goûté une quiche lorraine pour la première fois. Le soir, il a téléphoné à sa mère, à Pune : « Maman, je suis fatigué, mais je suis content ! »

English translation

Raj is Indian. He has been living in Lyon for a week. On Monday, he started his new job in an IT company. He got up at six o’clock and took the metro. He arrived at the office at half past eight. His colleagues were very kind. At noon, they ate together in the canteen and Raj tasted a quiche lorraine for the first time. In the evening, he phoned his mother in Pune: “Mum, I’m tired, but I’m happy!”

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Il habite à Lyon depuis une semaine. — He has been living in Lyon for a week. French uses the present with depuis — exactly like Hindi: “woh ek hafte se Lyon mein rehta hai”.
  • Il a pris le métro. — He took the metro. prendre → pris (the s is silent). [ee-la PREE luh may-TROH]
  • Il est arrivé au bureau. — He arrived at the office. arriver uses être in the past. [ee-lay-ta-ree-VAY oh bew-ROH]

How to hear the past

Listen for a little helper before the verb: j’ai, il a, ils ont or je suis, il est + a verb ending in the sound “ay” (mangé, arrivé). je mange = now; j’ai mangé = past.

Careful

  • Wrong: Il a arrivé à huit heures.
  • Right: Il est arrivé à huit heures.
  • Why: Verbs of movement like arriver, aller, partir, rentrer take être (see The past: passé composé).

docs.title: 54.4 Histoire 3 — Un week-end à la mer
docs.text:
Paul and Camille spend a weekend in Brittany, in the north-west of France. The weather changes a lot there! Listen for: what was the weather like each day, and what did they do?

Français English Sound la mer the sea [la MEHR] la plage the beach [la PLAZH] nager (ils ont nagé) to swim (they swam) [na-ZHAY] il a fait beau the weather was nice [ee-la fay BOH] il a plu it rained [ee-la PLEW] un musée a museum [ɛ̃ mew-ZAY] des cartes postales postcards [day kart pos-TAL] heureux happy [uh-RUH]
  • ▶ Toute l’histoire (slow) — Listen twice. Draw two little weather icons: Saturday and Sunday.
Transcript

Le week-end dernier, Paul et Camille sont allés à la mer, en Bretagne. Ils sont partis vendredi soir en train. Samedi, il a fait très beau. Ils ont nagé, ils ont joué au volley sur la plage et, le soir, ils ont mangé des crêpes. Dimanche, il a plu toute la journée ! Alors, ils ont visité un petit musée et ils ont acheté des cartes postales. Ils sont rentrés à Paris dimanche soir, fatigués mais heureux.

English translation

Last weekend, Paul and Camille went to the seaside, in Brittany. They left on Friday evening by train. On Saturday, the weather was lovely. They swam, they played volleyball on the beach and, in the evening, they ate crêpes. On Sunday, it rained all day! So they visited a small museum and bought postcards. They came back to Paris on Sunday evening, tired but happy.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Ils ont nagé. — They swam. Hear the z: ils‿ont = [eel-ZÕ]. [eel-zõ na-ZHAY]
  • Ils sont partis. — They left. Hear the s: ils sont = [eel SÕ]. [eel sõ par-TEE]
  • Il a plu toute la journée. — It rained all day. pleuvoir → il a plu. (Don’t confuse with plus, “more”.) [ee-la PLEW toot la zhoor-NAY]
  • fatigués mais heureux — tired but happy — the -s of fatigués is silent; you only see the plural on paper.

ils ont [z] or ils sont [s]?

A buzzing z = ils‿ont (they have). A hissing s = ils sont (they are). It is the only difference — train your ear on it.

docs.title: 54.5 Histoire 4 — La famille de Sophie
docs.text:
Sophie introduces her family. This is a classic first-conversation topic, so you will hear these sentences again and again. Listen for: the ages of the children and where her brother lives.

Français English Sound le mari husband [luh ma-REE] les enfants children [lay-zã-FÃ] le fils son [luh FEESS] la fille daughter [la FEE-y] la campagne the countryside [la kã-PAN-yuh] à la retraite retired [a la ruh-TRET] célibataire single [say-lee-ba-TEHR] une fois par an once a year [ewn fwa pa-RÃ]
  • ▶ Toute l’histoire (slow) — Listen twice. Note every number you hear: 32, 2, 7, 4…
Transcript

Je m’appelle Sophie. J’ai trente-deux ans et j’habite à Bordeaux avec mon mari, Thomas, et nos deux enfants. Notre fils, Hugo, a sept ans. Il adore le football. Notre fille, Inès, a quatre ans. Elle aime dessiner et chanter. Mes parents habitent à la campagne, près de Toulouse. Ma mère est professeure de musique et mon père est à la retraite. J’ai aussi un frère, Julien. Il est célibataire et il travaille à Montréal. Nous le voyons une fois par an, à Noël.

English translation

My name is Sophie. I’m thirty-two and I live in Bordeaux with my husband, Thomas, and our two children. Our son, Hugo, is seven. He loves football. Our daughter, Inès, is four. She likes drawing and singing. My parents live in the countryside, near Toulouse. My mother is a music teacher and my father is retired. I also have a brother, Julien. He is single and he works in Montreal. We see him once a year, at Christmas.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Notre fils a sept ans. — Our son is seven. Age uses avoir: he “has” seven years. [no-truh FEESS a set-TÃ]
  • Ma mère est professeure de musique. — My mother is a music teacher — no une before a job after être.
  • Nous le voyons une fois par an. — We see him once a year. le = him, placed before the verb. [noo luh vwa-YÕ ewn fwa pa-RÃ]

Careful

  • Wrong: Ma mère est une professeure.
  • Right: Ma mère est professeure.
  • Why: After être, a job or nationality has no article: il est ingénieur, elle est indienne.

Careful

  • Wrong: Notre fils est sept ans.
  • Right: Notre fils a sept ans.
  • Why: Age = avoir + number + ans. Listen for the liaison: sept‿ans [set-TÃ].

docs.title: 54.6 Histoire 5 — Un appel de maman
docs.text:
A short phone call between a mother and her daughter. There are two voices but one reader, so follow the questions and answers. Listen for: the day, the time, and what the daughter forgot.

Français English Sound Allô ? Hello? (phone only) [a-LOH] ma chérie darling, sweetheart [ma shay-REE] déjeuner to have lunch [day-zhuh-NAY] apporter to bring [a-por-TAY] l’anniversaire birthday [la-nee-vehr-SEHR] la grand-mère grandmother [la grã-MEHR] des fleurs flowers [day FLUHR] Bisous ! Kisses! (bye, informal) [bee-ZOO]
  • ▶ Toute l’histoire (slow) — Listen twice. Who invites whom? Who is cooking?
Transcript

— Allô, maman ? — Bonjour, ma chérie ! Tu vas bien ? — Oui, ça va, et toi ? — Très bien. Dis, tu viens déjeuner dimanche ? Ton père fait un couscous. — Avec plaisir ! À quelle heure ? — Vers midi et demi. Tu peux apporter du pain ? — Bien sûr. Je viens avec Marc, d’accord ? — Oui, bien sûr ! Ah, et n’oublie pas : dimanche, c’est l’anniversaire de ta grand-mère. — Oh là là, j’ai complètement oublié ! Je vais acheter des fleurs. — Parfait. À dimanche, ma chérie. Bisous ! — Bisous, maman !

English translation

— Hello, Mum? — Hello, sweetheart! Are you well? — Yes, fine, and you? — Very well. Say, are you coming for lunch on Sunday? Your dad is making couscous. — With pleasure! What time? — Around half past twelve. Can you bring some bread? — Of course. I’m coming with Marc, OK? — Yes, of course! Oh, and don’t forget: on Sunday it’s your grandmother’s birthday. — Oh dear, I completely forgot! I’ll buy some flowers. — Perfect. See you Sunday, sweetheart. Kisses! — Kisses, Mum!

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Tu viens déjeuner dimanche ? — Are you coming for lunch on Sunday? venir + infinitive, no word for “for”. A question only by rising voice.
  • N’oublie pas ! — Don’t forget! (the tu imperative) [noo-BLEE PA]
  • À dimanche ! — See you on Sunday! à + day/time = see you then: à demain, à ce soir, à lundi.

déjeuner or dîner?

In France, le déjeuner = lunch (around 12–2 pm) and le dîner = dinner (evening). In Belgium, Switzerland and Québec, dîner often means lunch! And ma chérie is the kind of word an Indian parent would say as “beta”.

docs.title: 54.7 Histoire 6 — Au marché
docs.text:
Karim goes to an open-air market to buy food for a dinner with friends. Listen for: what he buys, from whom, and the total price.

Français English Sound le marché market [luh mar-SHAY] un kilo de tomates a kilo of tomatoes [ɛ̃ kee-LOH duh to-MAT] le marchand stallholder, seller [luh mar-SHÃ] une fraise a strawberry [ewn FREZ] une barquette a punnet, small tray [ewn bar-KET] le fromager cheese seller [luh fro-ma-ZHAY] un morceau a piece [ɛ̃ mor-SOH] délicieux / délicieuse delicious (m / f) [day-lee-SYUH / -SYUHZ]
  • ▶ Toute l’histoire (slow) — Listen twice. Make a shopping list in English as you listen.
Transcript

Ce matin, Karim est allé au marché avec sa liste. Il a acheté un kilo de tomates, des pommes et un melon. Le marchand de fruits lui a dit : « Goûtez cette fraise, elle est délicieuse ! » Karim a goûté et il a pris une barquette de fraises. Ensuite, il est passé chez le fromager. Il a choisi un morceau de comté et un camembert. Au total, il a payé vingt-deux euros. Ce soir, il invite des amis : il va préparer une grande salade et une tarte aux fraises.

English translation

This morning, Karim went to the market with his list. He bought a kilo of tomatoes, some apples and a melon. The fruit seller said to him: “Taste this strawberry, it’s delicious!” Karim tasted it and took a punnet of strawberries. Then he stopped at the cheese seller’s. He chose a piece of Comté and a Camembert. In total, he paid twenty-two euros. Tonight he is having friends over: he is going to make a big salad and a strawberry tart.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Goûtez cette fraise ! — Taste this strawberry! (vous imperative — sellers love to offer a taste) [goo-TAY set FREZ]
  • un kilo de tomates, une barquette de fraises — After a quantity, just de — never “de les”.
  • Il va préparer une tarte. — He is going to make a tart. aller + infinitive = the near future.

Careful

  • Wrong: un kilo des tomates
  • Right: un kilo de tomates
  • Why: Quantity words (un kilo, une barquette, beaucoup, un peu) are followed by plain de.

docs.title: 54.8 La dictée — from sound to spelling
docs.text:
French children do a dictée at school every week: the teacher reads, they write. It is the best test of listening and spelling, because French writes many letters that you never hear. Here is the method:

  • 1. Listen to the whole sentence once. Don’t write. — Understand the meaning first — meaning tells you the spelling.
  • 2. Listen again and write it, group of words by group of words. — Use 🐢 slow mode as many times as you need.
  • 3. Check: verbs, plurals, accents, être + participle. — Most mistakes are silent letters, not wrong words.
Figure 54.2. …five spellings. In a dictée, the grammar around the word tells you which one to write.

-é or -er? The vendre trick

Replace the verb with vendre. If vendu fits, write -é (il a mangé → il a vendu). If vendre fits, write -er (je vais manger → je vais vendre).

  • Il a mangé. Il va manger. — He ate. He is going to eat. — same sound at the end, two spellings.
  • Léa est à la boulangerie et elle a faim. — Léa is at the bakery and she is hungry. est (is) / et (and) · a (has) / à (at).
  • Ils parlent avec leurs amis. — They talk with their friends. parlent sounds exactly like parle: -ent is silent.
  • Elles sont parties à huit heures. — They (women) left at eight. You hear “par-tee”; you write -ies.

Careful

  • Wrong: Il a manger une crêpe.
  • Right: Il a mangé une crêpe.
  • Why: After a, the vendre test gives “il a vendu” → write the participle -é.

Careful

  • Wrong: Léa et à la plage.
  • Right: Léa est à la plage.
  • Why: Same sound. If you can say “était” (was), write est; if you can say “et puis” (and then), write et.

Careful

  • Wrong: Ils parle français.
  • Right: Ils parlent français.
  • Why: ils/elles → always -ent in the present, even though you don’t hear it.

Accents are not decoration

a (has) ≠ à (at, to) · ou (or) ≠ où (where) · du (some) ≠ dû (had to). In a dictée, a missing accent is a mistake. More in Spelling & punctuation.

À retenir

  • Play each story twice before you open the transcript. Your brain only learns to decode sounds when it has to try. Reading first turns listening into reading.
  • At A1–A2, understanding 60–70% of a story is a success. Catch the names, numbers, places and times first — they carry most of the meaning.
  • Samedi, je vais au marché = this Saturday. Le samedi, je vais au marché = every Saturday. One little le turns a day into a habit.
  • Listen for a little helper before the verb: j’ai, il a, ils ont or je suis, il est + a verb ending in the sound “ay” (mangé, arrivé). je mange = now; j’ai mangé = past.
  • A buzzing z = ils‿ont (they have). A hissing s = ils sont (they are). It is the only difference — train your ear on it.
  • Replace the verb with vendre. If vendu fits, write -é (il a mangé → il a vendu). If vendre fits, write -er (je vais manger → je vais vendre).

docs.title: 54.9 Practice — First stories
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What does Léa buy?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Le samedi matin, Léa va à la boulangerie. Elle achète une baguette et deux croissants.

  • a baguette and two croissants
  • two baguettes and a croissant
  • a cake and a baguette
  • bread and milk
Answer

a baguette and two croissants

une baguette et deux croissants.

Exercise 2

How much does she pay?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Léa demande : ça fait combien ? La boulangère répond : trois euros quarante, s'il vous plaît.

  • €3.40
  • €2.40
  • €3.14
  • €13.40
Answer

€3.40

trois euros quarante = €3.40.

Exercise 3

What time did Raj arrive at the office?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Raj s'est levé à six heures. Il a pris le métro et il est arrivé au bureau à huit heures et demie.

  • 8:30
  • 6:00
  • 8:15
  • 9:30
Answer

8:30

huit heures et demie = half past eight. Six heures is when he got up.

Exercise 4

What was new for Raj?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

À midi, Raj et ses collègues ont mangé ensemble à la cantine. Raj a goûté une quiche lorraine pour la première fois.

  • tasting quiche lorraine
  • eating in a restaurant
  • taking the metro
  • meeting his boss
Answer

tasting quiche lorraine

pour la première fois = for the first time.

Exercise 5

What was the weather like on Sunday?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Samedi, il a fait beau. Ils ont nagé et ils ont joué au volley sur la plage. Dimanche, il a plu toute la journée.

  • It rained all day
  • It was sunny
  • It was windy
  • It snowed
Answer

It rained all day

il a plu = it rained (pleuvoir).

Exercise 6

What did they do because of the rain?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Dimanche, il a plu. Alors, ils ont visité un petit musée et ils ont acheté des cartes postales.

  • They visited a museum
  • They went swimming
  • They ate crêpes
  • They went home on Saturday
Answer

They visited a museum

alors = so: ils ont visité un petit musée.

Exercise 7

How old is Inès?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Notre fils, Hugo, a sept ans. Il adore le football. Notre fille, Inès, a quatre ans. Elle aime dessiner et chanter.

  • 4
  • 7
  • 14
  • 2
Answer

4

Inès a quatre ans. Hugo is the one who is seven.

Exercise 8

How often does Sophie see her brother?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

J'ai aussi un frère, Julien. Il est célibataire et il travaille à Montréal. Nous le voyons une fois par an, à Noël.

  • once a year
  • twice a year
  • once a month
  • every weekend
Answer

once a year

une fois par an = once a year, at Christmas.

Exercise 9

What is the mother's invitation?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Dis, tu viens déjeuner dimanche ? Ton père fait un couscous. On mange vers midi et demi.

  • Sunday lunch at 12:30
  • Sunday dinner at 7:30
  • Saturday lunch at noon
  • a party on Monday
Answer

Sunday lunch at 12:30

déjeuner dimanche, vers midi et demi.

Exercise 10

What had the daughter forgotten?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Et n'oublie pas : dimanche, c'est l'anniversaire de ta grand-mère. Oh là là, j'ai complètement oublié ! Je vais acheter des fleurs.

  • her grandmother's birthday
  • the bread
  • the time of lunch
  • her father's couscous
Answer

her grandmother's birthday

l'anniversaire de ta grand-mère.

Exercise 11

Which fruit did Karim NOT buy?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Karim a acheté un kilo de tomates, des pommes et un melon. Ensuite, il a pris une barquette de fraises.

  • bananas
  • apples
  • a melon
  • strawberries
Answer

bananas

He bought pommes, un melon and fraises — no bananes.

Exercise 12

Why is Karim doing his shopping?

Read this aloud or have someone read it to you:

Au total, Karim a payé vingt-deux euros. Ce soir, il invite des amis : il va préparer une grande salade.

  • He has friends coming tonight
  • His fridge is empty
  • It is his birthday
  • He sells vegetables
Answer

He has friends coming tonight

Ce soir, il invite des amis.

Exercise 13

You hear a buzzing z sound: [eel-ZÕ]. What was said?

  • ils ont
  • ils sont
  • ils font
  • il a
Answer

ils ont

The liaison z = ils‿ont (they have). ils sont starts with a hissing s.

Exercise 14

Match the key words.

A B la boulangerie cheese seller la plage retired le fromager birthday à la retraite bakery l'anniversaire beach Answer

la boulangerie — bakery; la plage — beach; le fromager — cheese seller; à la retraite — retired; l'anniversaire — birthday

All from the six stories.

Exercise 15

Dictée 1 — write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Léa achète une baguette et deux croissants.

achète has a grave accent; croissants ends in a silent -s.

Exercise 16

Dictée 2 — write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Raj est arrivé au bureau à huit heures.

est arrivé (être + -é); à with an accent = at.

Exercise 17

Dictée 3 — write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Nous sommes allés à la mer en train.

allés takes -s: it agrees with nous (être verb).

Exercise 18

Dictée 4 — write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Ma mère est professeure et mon père est à la retraite.

est (is) vs et (and) — you need both here.

Exercise 19

Dictée 5 — write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Answer

Ils ont acheté des fraises au marché.

ils‿ont (z sound) + acheté; fraises has a silent plural -s.

Exercise 20

Ask for a baguette politely.

Je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît

Answer

Je voudrais = I would like — the polite way to order.

Next step

Replay one story a day this week, then try shadowing: play a sentence and speak with the voice. When the six stories feel easy, move on to Everyday listening — voicemails, announcements and dialogues at normal speed.

docs.title: Chapter 32: Gérondif & participles
docs.text:
Gérondif, participe, infinitif

This chapter is about compressing sentences. Instead of pendant que je marchais, j’écoutais de la musique, say j’écoutais de la musique en marchant. Instead of quand j’ai fini, je suis sorti, say *après avoir fini, je suis sorti. These structures make your French sound fluent and precise — and they finish with two power tools: the causative faire faire and emphasis with c’est… qui*.

Forming the -ant form

Take the nous form of the present, drop -ons, add -ant: nous parlons → parlant, nous finissons → finissant. Only three exceptions: étant (être), ayant (avoir), sachant (savoir).

Infinitive nous… -ant form marcher marchons marchant manger mangeons mangeant commencer commençons commençant choisir choisissons choisissant prendre prenons prenant faire faisons faisant être · avoir · savoir — étant · ayant · sachant

docs.title: 32.1 The gérondif: en + -ant
docs.text:
The gérondif is en + the -ant form. It never changes (no agreement) and its subject is always the subject of the main verb. It answers four questions: when? how? on what condition? why?

Meaning Example = simultaneity (while) Il chante en prenant sa douche. pendant qu’il prend manner, means (by) Elle a appris en regardant des séries. grâce au fait de regarder condition (if) En partant maintenant, tu seras à l’heure. si tu pars cause (because) Il s’est blessé en tombant. parce qu’il est tombé
  • Je fais mes devoirs en écoutant de la musique. — I do my homework while listening to music.
  • J’ai rencontré Paul en sortant du métro. — I met Paul as I was coming out of the metro.
  • Elle a perdu cinq kilos en faisant du vélo tous les jours. — She lost five kilos by cycling every day.
  • En travaillant un peu plus, tu réussirais. — If you worked a little harder, you would succeed.
  • C’est en forgeant qu’on devient forgeron. — Practice makes perfect. (proverb: it is by forging that one becomes a blacksmith)

Hindi does something very close with -te hue: gaana gaate hue nahaata hai = il se douche en chantant. Like the gérondif, -te hue normally refers to the subject of the sentence.

docs.title: tout en — emphasis or contrast
docs.text:
Adding tout before the gérondif either stresses that two things happen at the same time, or marks a contrast (= although).

  • Il conduit tout en téléphonant — c’est dangereux ! — He drives while talking on the phone at the same time — it’s dangerous!
  • Tout en étant très riche, elle vit simplement. — Although she is very rich, she lives simply.

Careful

  • Wrong: En sortant de la maison, la pluie a commencé.
  • Right: En sortant de la maison, j’ai vu qu’il pleuvait.
  • Why: The gérondif’s subject must be the main subject. In the wrong version, it is "the rain" that leaves the house! Say instead: Quand je suis sorti, il a commencé à pleuvoir.

docs.title: 32.2 The participe présent (without en)
docs.text: Without en, the -ant form is the participe présent. It is mostly written and formal, and it is invariable. It has two main jobs.

docs.title: a) Instead of qui + verb
docs.text:
• Les candidats souhaitant participer doivent s’inscrire avant lundi. — Candidates wishing to take part must register before Monday. (= qui souhaitent)
  • Nous cherchons une personne parlant hindi et français. — We are looking for someone who speaks Hindi and French.

docs.title: b) To give a cause
docs.text:
• Étant malade, elle n’est pas venue. — Being ill, she didn’t come.
  • Ne sachant pas quoi dire, il s’est tu. — Not knowing what to say, he fell silent.
Figure 32.1. One little word changes who does the action: with en, the subject of the sentence; without en, the noun just before.

docs.title: 32.3 Participe présent or adjectif verbal?
docs.text:
Many -ant forms are also adjectives (une histoire amusante). As adjectives they describe a quality and agree; as participles they describe an action and never agree. Some pairs are even spelled differently — a classic trap in written exams.

Participe (action) Adjectif (quality) Spelling change fatiguant fatigant -guant → -gant intriguant intrigant -guant → -gant naviguant navigant -guant → -gant convainquant convaincant -quant → -cant provoquant provocant -quant → -cant communiquant communicant -quant → -cant différant différent -ant → -ent précédant précédent -ant → -ent négligeant négligent -geant → -gent excellant excellent -ant → -ent
  • Ce voyage était très fatigant. — This journey was very tiring. (adjective)
  • En fatiguant ses joueurs à l’entraînement, le coach les a rendus plus forts. — By tiring his players out in training, the coach made them stronger. (participle with an object)
  • Ses arguments sont convaincants. — Her arguments are convincing. (adjective, agrees)
  • Les jours précédant l’examen, il dormait mal. — In the days before the exam, he slept badly. (participle + object)

The quick test

Can you put très in front? → adjective (agrees, maybe a different spelling). Is it followed by an object or a complement? → participle (invariable, -ant).

docs.title: 32.4 Compound participles: ayant fini, étant arrivé
docs.text:
To show that one action was completed before the main one, use ayant / étant + past participle. With étant, the participle agrees with the subject, as in the passé composé.

  • Ayant fini ses devoirs, elle est sortie. — Having finished her homework, she went out.
  • Étant arrivée en retard, elle a raté le début. — Having arrived late, she missed the beginning.
  • Ayant toujours vécu en ville, il déteste la campagne. — Having always lived in the city, he hates the countryside.
  • S’étant trompés de route, ils sont arrivés à minuit. — Having taken the wrong road, they arrived at midnight.

docs.title: The bare past participle
docs.text:
In writing, étant is often dropped: the past participle alone opens the sentence and agrees with the subject. A noun + participle can also stand alone ("absolute construction").

  • Arrivée à la gare, elle a appelé sa mère. — Once she had arrived at the station, she called her mother.
  • Le repas terminé, tout le monde est allé se promener. — The meal over, everyone went for a walk.

docs.title: 32.5 Infinitive constructions
docs.text:
After a preposition, French uses the infinitive — never the -ant form (English "before leaving" = avant de partir**). Like the gérondif, these require the same subject.

Structure Meaning Example après avoir / être + p.p. after doing Après avoir mangé, on est sortis. avant de + inf. before doing Réfléchis avant de parler. sans + inf. without doing Il est parti sans dire au revoir. au lieu de + inf. instead of doing Au lieu de te plaindre, agis. pour + inf. passé for having done Il a été puni pour avoir menti.
  • Après avoir lu le contrat, je l’ai signé. — After reading the contract, I signed it.
  • Après être rentrée, elle s’est couchée. — After getting home, she went to bed. (être verb → agreement)
  • Après nous être reposés, nous sommes repartis. — After resting, we set off again. (reflexive pronoun matches the subject)
  • Lave-toi les mains avant de passer à table. — Wash your hands before sitting down to eat.
  • Elle a répondu sans hésiter. — She answered without hesitating.

Careful

  • Wrong: Après avoir arrivé, il a téléphoné.
  • Right: Après être arrivé, il a téléphoné.
  • Why: The infinitif passé uses the same auxiliary as the passé composé: arriver → être.

Careful

  • Wrong: Avant partant, ferme la fenêtre.
  • Right: Avant de partir, ferme la fenêtre.
  • Why: English "before leaving" uses -ing; French uses avant de + infinitive. The only preposition that takes the -ant form is en.

docs.title: 32.6 The causative: faire, laisser, se faire
docs.text:
faire + infinitive means "to have something done" or "to make someone do something". You are the cause; someone else does the action. English uses "have / get / make"; Hindi uses the causative verb forms like banwana (to have built) or karwana (to have done).

Figure 32.2. With faire + infinitive, the subject causes the action and someone else carries it out. Pronouns go before faire; fait never agrees.
  • Nous faisons construire une maison. — We are having a house built.
  • Le professeur fait lire le texte aux élèves. — The teacher has the students read the text. (the doer gets à when there is also an object)
  • Ce film m’a fait pleurer. — This film made me cry.
  • Je fais faire mes costumes chez un tailleur. — I have my suits made at a tailor’s.
  • Fais-les entrer, s’il te plaît. — Show them in, please.

Two causative rules

Object pronouns go before faire, not before the infinitive: je la fais réparer. In compound tenses, fait + infinitive never agrees: la voiture que j’ai fait réparer.

docs.title: laisser + infinitive — to let
docs.text:
• Laisse-moi parler ! — Let me speak!
  • Il a laissé tomber son téléphone. — He dropped his phone. (and in slang: Laisse tomber ! = forget it!)

docs.title: se faire + infinitive — it happens to me
docs.text:
• Je me suis fait couper les cheveux. — I had my hair cut.
  • Elle s’est fait voler son vélo. — She had her bike stolen. (see also Passive & reported speech)

Careful

  • Wrong: J’ai coupé mes cheveux chez le coiffeur.
  • Right: Je me suis fait couper les cheveux chez le coiffeur.
  • Why: "J’ai coupé mes cheveux" means you cut them yourself. When someone else does it for you → se faire + infinitive.

docs.title: 32.7 Mise en relief: c’est… qui / que
docs.text:
French cannot stress a word with the voice as English does ("I paid"). Instead it moves that word into a frame: c’est … qui for the subject, c’est … que for anything else.

  • C’est Paul qui a gagné, pas moi. — It’s Paul who won, not me.
  • C’est moi qui ai payé. — I’m the one who paid. (the verb agrees with moi → ai)
  • C’est à toi que je parle ! — It’s you I’m talking to!
  • C’est en 1789 que la Révolution a commencé. — It was in 1789 that the Revolution began.
  • Ce sont eux qui ont organisé la fête. — They are the ones who organised the party.

docs.title: ce qui…, c’est… / ce que…, c’est…
docs.text:
To build suspense, start with ce qui / ce que / ce dont (see Relative pronouns) and reveal the key element after c’est.

  • Ce qui me plaît chez elle, c’est son humour. — What I like about her is her sense of humour.
  • Ce que je veux, c’est dormir. — What I want is to sleep.
  • Ce dont j’ai besoin, c’est de vacances. — What I need is a holiday. (the de comes back after c’est)

Spoken emphasis: dislocation

In conversation, French also "pulls out" a word and repeats it with a pronoun: Moi, je pense que… · Ce film, je l’ai adoré. · Il est où, ton frère ? More in Real spoken French.

Careful

  • Wrong: C’est moi qui a raison.
  • Right: C’est moi qui ai raison.
  • Why: After qui, the verb agrees with the stressed pronoun: moi qui ai, toi qui as, nous qui avons.

Careful

  • Wrong: C’est à Paris où je suis né.
  • Right: C’est à Paris que je suis né.
  • Why: The frame is always c’est … que for non-subjects — even for places and times. (C’est Paris, la ville où je suis né is a different structure.)

À retenir

  • Take the nous form of the present, drop -ons, add -ant: nous parlons → parlant, nous finissons → finissant. Only three exceptions: étant (être), ayant (avoir), sachant (savoir).
  • Can you put très in front? → adjective (agrees, maybe a different spelling). Is it followed by an object or a complement? → participle (invariable, -ant).
  • Object pronouns go before faire, not before the infinitive: je la fais réparer. In compound tenses, fait + infinitive never agrees: la voiture que j’ai fait réparer.
  • In conversation, French also "pulls out" a word and repeats it with a pronoun: Moi, je pense que… · Ce film, je l’ai adoré. · Il est où, ton frère ? More in Real spoken French.
  • Describe your morning routine in four sentences using en + -ant, après avoir… and avant de…. Then read on: Literary & formal French.

docs.title: 32.8 Practice — Gérondif & participles
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Elle chante ___ la vaisselle.

  • en faisant
  • faisant
  • en fait
  • à faire

Hint: while doing

Answer

en faisant

Simultaneity → gérondif: en + faisant.

Exercise 2

___ malade, il est resté au lit.

  • Étant
  • En étant
  • Ayant
  • Été

Hint: cause, être

Answer

Étant

The participe présent étant gives the cause: being ill.

Exercise 3

C'est un argument très ___.

  • convainquant
  • convaincant
  • convaincu
  • convaincre

Hint: adjective

Answer

convaincant

The adjective is spelled convaincant (-cant); the participle is convainquant.

Exercise 4

Après ___ sortis, nous avons pris un taxi.

  • avoir
  • être
  • étant
  • ayant
Answer

être

sortir takes être → après être sortis.

Exercise 5

Je ___ réparer mon ordinateur chez un technicien.

  • fais
  • répare
  • laisse
  • suis

Hint: I'm having it repaired

Answer

fais

Causative: faire + infinitive = to have something done.

Exercise 6

C'est nous qui ___ gagné.

  • a
  • avons
  • ont
  • avez
Answer

avons

The verb agrees with the pronoun before qui: nous qui avons.

Exercise 7

___ (finir) son travail, elle est partie.

Hint: Having finished…

Answer

Ayant fini / ayant fini

Compound participle: ayant + past participle shows the earlier action.

Exercise 8

Il est parti sans ___ (dire) au revoir.

Answer

dire

After sans, French uses the infinitive.

Exercise 9

Réfléchis ___ parler !

Hint: before

Answer

avant de

before + -ing = avant de + infinitive.

Exercise 10

La maison que nous avons ___ construire est grande.

Hint: causative participle

Answer

fait

fait + infinitive never agrees.

Exercise 11

Pick the wrong word.

Après avoir arrivé à Paris, elle a appelé sa mère.

Answer

Wrong word: avoir.

Corrected: Après être arrivée à Paris, elle a appelé sa mère.

arriver takes être; with être, the participle agrees: arrivée.

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

C'est moi qui a fait le gâteau.

Answer

Wrong word: a.

Corrected: C'est moi qui ai fait le gâteau.

moi qui → first person: ai.

Exercise 13

Pick the wrong word.

Ce travail est vraiment fatiguant.

Answer

Wrong word: fatiguant.

Corrected: Ce travail est vraiment fatigant.

The adjective is fatigant (no u); fatiguant is the participle.

Exercise 14

Match the structure to its meaning.

A B en marchant before walking après avoir marché without walking avant de marcher while walking sans marcher after walking Answer

en marchant — while walking; après avoir marché — after walking; avant de marcher — before walking; sans marcher — without walking

Only en takes the -ant form; other prepositions take the infinitive.

Exercise 15

Match the causative.

A B faire réparer to drop laisser tomber to have one's hair cut se faire couper les cheveux to have something repaired Answer

faire réparer — to have something repaired; laisser tomber — to drop; se faire couper les cheveux — to have one's hair cut

faire / laisser / se faire + infinitive.

Exercise 16

Put the words in order: It's by forging that one becomes a blacksmith.

Words: devient / C'est / en / forgeant / qu'on / forgeron

Answer

C'est en forgeant qu'on devient forgeron

Mise en relief c'est … que around a gérondif.

Exercise 17

Put the words in order: What I need is a holiday.

Words: c'est / Ce / de / j'ai / dont / besoin / vacances

Answer

Ce dont j'ai besoin c'est de vacances

ce dont … c'est de + noun.

Exercise 18

Say it aloud.

Je me suis fait couper les cheveux

Answer

se faire + infinitive: someone else did it for me.

Exercise 19

Say it aloud.

J'apprends le français en écoutant des podcasts

Answer

Gérondif of means: en écoutant.

Next step

Describe your morning routine in four sentences using en + -ant, après avoir… and avant de…. Then read on: Literary & formal French.

docs.title: Chapter 24: Giving instructions
docs.text:
l’impératif

Viens ! Écoutez ! Allons-y ! The imperative is how you tell, invite or ask someone to do something. In French it is easy to form — it is the present tense without the subject — but it has three traps: a missing -s, a few irregular forms, and pronouns that change place. And because a bare command can sound rude, you will also learn the polite ways to ask.

In one line

Imperative = the present tense of tu, nous, vous without the subject: tu viens → Viens ! vous écoutez → Écoutez !

  • Viens ici ! — Come here! (to one friend) [vyɛ̃‿zee-SEE]
  • Écoutez bien. — Listen carefully. (to a group, or politely) [ay-koo-TAY BYɛ̃]
  • Allons-y ! — Let’s go! [a-lõ-ZEE]

docs.title: 24.1 Three forms: tu, nous, vous
docs.text:
There is no imperative for je or il. You choose the form by who you speak to:

Form Speaking to… Example tu one friend, child, family member Attends !Wait! nous a group including you — “let’s” Attendons !Let’s wait! vous several people, or one person politely Attendez !Wait!

Just like tum / aap in Hindi: use the tu form with people you call tu, and vous with everyone else.

Verb tu nous vous finir finis finissons finissez prendre prends prenons prenez faire fais faisons faites venir viens venons venez dire dis disons dites
  • Prends ton manteau, il fait froid. — Take your coat, it’s cold. [prã tõ man-TO]
  • Faites attention à la marche. — Mind the step. [fɛt‿za-tã-SYÕ]
  • Finissons ce travail avant midi. — Let’s finish this work before noon.
  • Dites-moi tout ! — Tell me everything! [deet-mwa TOO]

docs.title: 24.2 The missing -s of -er verbs
docs.text:
For -er verbs (and aller), the tu form drops the -s. You can’t hear it, but you must not write it. The same happens with verbs like ouvrir, offrir, cueillir, whose present ends in -es.

Present (tu) Imperative Meaning tu manges Mange ! Eat! tu écoutes Écoute ! Listen! tu vas Va ! Go! tu ouvres Ouvre la fenêtre ! Open the window! tu finis Finis ! Finish! (not -er: the -s stays)

Careful

  • Wrong: Manges ta soupe !
  • Right: Mange ta soupe !
  • Why: -er verbs lose the -s in the tu command. A very common spelling mistake, even among French children.

docs.title: …which comes back before y and en
docs.text:
To make a smooth liaison, the -s returns before y and en:

  • Va au marché ! → Vas-y ! — Go to the market! → Go (there)! / Go on! [va-ZEE]
  • Il reste du gâteau. Manges-en ! — There’s some cake left. Have some! [mãzh-ZÃ]
  • Ton projet ? Penses-y ! — Your project? Think about it!

The -s rule

-er verbs: tu manges → Mange ! (no -s) — but Vas-y ! Manges-en ! (-s back before y/en). All other verbs keep their -s: Finis ! Prends !

docs.title: 24.3 The four irregulars: sois, aie, sache, veuille
docs.text:
Only four verbs have special imperative forms. They come from the subjunctive (see The subjunctive), but for now just learn them — especially être and avoir.

Verb tu nous vous être sois [swa] soyons soyez [swa-YAY] avoir aie [ɛ] ayons ayez [ay-YAY] savoir sache [SASH] sachons sachez vouloir veuille (veuillons) veuillez [vuh-YAY]
  • Sois sage ! — Be good! (to a child) [swa SAZH]
  • Soyez les bienvenus ! — Welcome! (to a group)
  • N’aie pas peur. — Don’t be afraid. [nɛ pa PUHR]
  • Ayez la gentillesse de répondre rapidement. — Please be kind enough to reply quickly. (formal)
  • Sachez que le magasin est fermé lundi. — Please note that the shop is closed on Monday.
  • Veuillez patienter, s’il vous plaît. — Please hold / please wait. — the phone message you will hear a hundred times [vuh-yay pa-syã-TAY]

Careful

  • Wrong: Es calme !
  • Right: Sois calme !
  • Why: Être doesn’t use the present (tu es) for commands. It uses sois / soyons / soyez.

docs.title: 24.4 Negative commands: ne … pas around the verb
docs.text:
Put ne before the verb and pas (or jamais, plus, rien) after it.

  • Ne touche pas ! — Don’t touch! [nuh toosh PA]
  • N’oublie pas tes clés. — Don’t forget your keys. [noo-blee pa tay KLAY]
  • Ne soyez pas en retard demain. — Don’t be late tomorrow.
  • Ne dis rien à personne ! — Don’t say anything to anyone!
  • Ne parlons plus de ça. — Let’s not talk about that any more.

In fast speech

People often drop ne: Touche pas ! T’inquiète pas ! Recognise it — but write the full form. See Real spoken French.

docs.title: 24.5 Where the pronouns go
docs.text:
This is the real difficulty of the imperative. In a positive command, object pronouns move after the verb, joined with a hyphen — and me / te become moi / toi. In a negative command, everything goes back to the normal place, before the verb.

Figure 24.1. Positive commands flip the pronouns behind the verb; ne … pas flips them back in front.
  • Aide-moi, s’il te plaît. / Ne m’aide pas, je veux essayer seul. — Help me, please. / Don’t help me, I want to try on my own.
  • Ce gâteau ? Goûte-le ! / Ne le mange pas tout ! — This cake? Taste it! / Don’t eat it all!
  • Ton passeport ? Donne-le-moi. — Your passport? Give it to me. [don-luh-MWA]
  • Ta grand-mère ? Téléphone-lui ce soir. — Your grandmother? Phone her tonight.

docs.title: Reflexive verbs in commands
docs.text:
se lever Positive Negative tu Lève-toi ! Ne te lève pas ! nous Levons-nous ! Ne nous levons pas ! vous Levez-vous ! Ne vous levez pas !
  • Asseyez-vous, je vous en prie. — Please, do sit down. [a-say-yay-VOO]
  • Assieds-toi ! / Ne t’inquiète pas. — Sit down! / Don’t worry. [a-syay-TWA]
  • Dépêchons-nous, le magasin ferme ! — Let’s hurry, the shop is closing!
  • Va-t’en ! / Ne t’en va pas ! — Go away! / Don’t go! [va-TÃ]

Pronoun-position errors

  • Wrong: Donne-me le livre.
  • Right: Donne-moi le livre.

  • Why: After the verb, me becomes moi (and te becomes toi).

  • Wrong: Ne lève-toi pas !

  • Right: Ne te lève pas !
