  • Why: In a negative command, the pronoun goes back before the verb, in its normal form te.

  • Wrong: Donne-moi-le !

  • Right: Donne-le-moi !
  • Why: In positive commands: direct pronoun (le, la, les) first, then moi, lui, nous, leur. The full order is in Y, en & pronoun order.

Pronoun position

Positive: verb-pronoun (Regarde-moi !). Negative: ne + pronoun + verb + pas (Ne me regarde pas !).

docs.title: 24.6 Commands you will hear every day
docs.text:
Many short imperatives work as everyday expressions. Their meaning is often not literal.

French Literal Real meaning Tiens ! / Tenez ! hold! Here you are! / Oh, look! Allez ! go! Come on! (encouragement) Vas-y ! / Allez-y ! go there! Go ahead! Go on! Voyons… let’s see Let’s see… / Come now! Dis donc ! say then Wow! / Hey! Écoute… listen Look… (before an opinion) Arrête ! stop! Stop it! / No way! Entrez ! enter! Come in! Excusez-moi excuse me Excuse me (to get attention)
  • Tenez, voici votre monnaie. — Here you are, here’s your change. [tuh-NAY]
  • Allez, encore un effort ! — Come on, one more push!
  • Dis donc, tu as changé de coiffure ! — Hey, you’ve got a new haircut!

docs.title: 24.7 Polite alternatives: asking instead of ordering
docs.text:
A bare imperative is fine with friends, in instructions and in emergencies. But with strangers, staff or colleagues, French speakers usually soften it — or replace it with a question. Climb the ladder as the situation gets more formal:

Figure 24.2. The same request on six steps. Spoken French lives mostly on steps 2–4; steps 5–6 are for formal speech and writing.
  • Vous pouvez répéter, s’il vous plaît ? — Could you repeat that, please? — the learner’s best friend [voo poo-vay ray-pay-TAY]
  • Pourriez-vous m’indiquer la gare ? — Could you show me the way to the station? [poo-ryay-VOO]
  • Veuillez trouver ci-joint mon CV. — Please find my CV attached. (formal email)
  • Merci de ne pas fumer. — Please do not smoke. (sign)

The infinitive as a command

Recipes, signs and instructions often use the infinitive: Ne pas toucher. Ajouter le sel. Tirer / Pousser (on doors: pull / push).

Careful

  • Wrong: Donnez-moi un café. (to a waiter, with no softener)
  • Right: Je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.
  • Why: Grammatically fine, but it sounds abrupt. In shops and cafés, ask with je voudrais or vous pourriez — and always add s’il vous plaît.

docs.title: 24.8 In real life: asking the way
docs.text:
• — Excusez-moi, madame. Pourriez-vous m’aider ? Je cherche la place du Marché. — — Excuse me, madam. Could you help me? I’m looking for the market square.
  • — Bien sûr. Prenez la deuxième rue à gauche, puis continuez tout droit. — — Of course. Take the second street on the left, then carry straight on.
  • — Traversez le pont et tournez à droite après la pharmacie. — — Cross the bridge and turn right after the chemist’s.
  • — Mais faites attention, ne prenez pas la rue piétonne, elle est fermée aujourd’hui. — — But be careful, don’t take the pedestrian street, it’s closed today.
  • — Merci beaucoup ! — Je vous en prie. Passez une bonne journée ! — — Thank you very much! — You’re welcome. Have a nice day!

À retenir

  • Imperative = the present tense of tu, nous, vous without the subject: tu viens → Viens ! vous écoutez → Écoutez !
  • -er verbs: tu manges → Mange ! (no -s) — but Vas-y ! Manges-en ! (-s back before y/en). All other verbs keep their -s: Finis ! Prends !
  • Positive: verb-pronoun (Regarde-moi !). Negative: ne + pronoun + verb + pas (Ne me regarde pas !).
  • Recipes, signs and instructions often use the infinitive: Ne pas toucher. Ajouter le sel. Tirer / Pousser (on doors: pull / push).
  • Give yourself (or a friend) ten instructions today in French — five positive, five negative, at least two with a pronoun. Then move on to Comparing.

docs.title: 24.9 Practice — The imperative
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Tell a friend: 'Eat your vegetables!' ___ tes légumes !

  • Manges
  • Mange
  • Mangez
  • Mangeons
Answer

Mange

-er verbs drop the -s in the tu command.

Exercise 2

Tell a child: 'Be good!'

  • Es sage !
  • Sois sage !
  • Être sage !
  • Soit sage !
Answer

Sois sage !

être → sois, soyons, soyez.

Exercise 3

'Give it to me!' (le livre)

  • Donne-moi-le !
  • Donne-le-moi !
  • Me le donne !
  • Donne-le-me !
Answer

Donne-le-moi !

Positive command: verb, then le, then moi.

Exercise 4

'Don't get up!' (to a friend)

  • Ne lève-toi pas !
  • Ne te lève pas !
  • Lève-toi pas !
  • Ne toi lève pas !
Answer

Ne te lève pas !

Negative: ne + te + verb + pas.

Exercise 5

The most polite way to ask a stranger:

  • Répétez !
  • Répète, s'il te plaît.
  • Pourriez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?
  • Tu répètes ?
Answer

Pourriez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

Conditional question + s'il vous plaît = very polite.

Exercise 6

Va au parc ! → ___ ! (go there)

Hint: the -s comes back

Answer

Vas-y / vas-y

Before y, the -s returns: vas-y.

Exercise 7

N'___ pas peur ! (avoir, tu)

Answer

aie

avoir → aie, ayons, ayez.

Exercise 8

___ patienter, s'il vous plaît. (formal: please wait)

Answer

Veuillez / veuillez

veuillez + infinitive = formal 'please'.

Exercise 9

___-vous, je vous en prie. (sit down, vous)

Answer

Asseyez / asseyez

s'asseoir → asseyez-vous.

Exercise 10

Ne ___ pas ! (toucher, tu)

Answer

touche

Negative command: ne + touche + pas (no -s).

Exercise 11

Pick the wrong word.

Regardes la mer, c'est magnifique !

Answer

Wrong word: Regardes.

Corrected: Regarde la mer, c'est magnifique !

-er verb, tu command → no -s: Regarde.

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

Donne-me ton numéro de téléphone.

Answer

Wrong word: Donne-me.

Corrected: Donne-moi ton numéro de téléphone.

After the verb, me becomes moi.

Exercise 13

Pick the wrong word.

Es gentil avec ta sœur.

Answer

Wrong word: Es.

Corrected: Sois gentil avec ta sœur.

être has the special form sois.

Exercise 14

Put the words in order: Don't forget your keys.

Words: pas / N'oublie / tes / clés

Answer

N'oublie pas tes clés

ne + verb + pas; oublier is -er so no -s.

Exercise 15

Match the expression to its real meaning.

A B Tenez ! Wow! / Hey! Allez ! Go ahead! Dis donc ! Here you are! Allez-y ! Come on! Answer

Tenez ! — Here you are!; Allez ! — Come on!; Dis donc ! — Wow! / Hey!; Allez-y ! — Go ahead!

Everyday imperatives often have non-literal meanings.

Exercise 16

Say it aloud.

Vous pouvez répéter s'il vous plaît

Answer

The most useful polite request for a learner.

Exercise 17

Say it aloud.

Allons-y

Answer

allons-y: the s links to y — a-lõ-ZEE.

Next step

Give yourself (or a friend) ten instructions today in French — five positive, five negative, at least two with a pronoun. Then move on to Comparing.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Hello, please, thank you
docs.text:
Les premiers mots

With about forty words you can greet people, be polite, say who you are and survive when you do not understand. In France these little words matter a lot: a missing bonjour can feel rude. This chapter gives you the words, the right moment for each one, and the big choice every speaker makes: tu or vous?

Rule number one

Always start with Bonjour — in a shop, a bus, an office, before any question. Add Monsieur or Madame for a stranger.

  • Bonjour, Monsieur. — Hello, sir. [bõ-zhoor muh-SYÖ]
  • Bonjour, Madame. — Hello, madam. [bõ-zhoor ma-DAM]

docs.title: 5.1 Saying hello at every time of day
docs.text:
French has no separate “good morning” and “good afternoon”. Bonjour (literally “good day”) covers the whole day. In the evening it becomes bonsoir.

Figure 5.1. Bonne nuit is only for going to bed — never a greeting. When you leave, wish people a good rest of the day or evening. French When Bonjour [bõ-ZHOOR] Hello / good morning / good afternoon — polite, all day Bonsoir [bõ-SWAR] Good evening — arriving after about 6 pm Salut [sa-LEW] Hi / bye — friends, family, people your age Coucou [koo-KOO] Hiya — very casual, close friends, children, text messages Bonne nuit [bon NWEE] Good night — going to bed only

Careful

  • Wrong: (Arriving at a dinner at 8 pm) Bonne nuit !
  • Right: Bonsoir !
  • Why: Like English “good night”, bonne nuit means “sleep well”. To greet in the evening, say bonsoir.

Careful

  • Wrong: (To a bank manager) Salut !
  • Right: Bonjour, Madame.
  • Why: Salut is informal, like “hi” — fine with friends, too casual for strangers or at work.

docs.title: Monsieur, Madame — and the bise
docs.text: Use Monsieur [muh-SYÖ] and Madame [ma-DAM] alone, without a surname: Bonjour, Madame. Use Madame for any adult woman: Mademoiselle is now old-fashioned and has been dropped from official forms. Friends and family greet with la bise, light cheek kisses (two in Paris, more in some regions); at work and with strangers, a handshake or just a smile and a bonjour.

docs.title: 5.2 Saying goodbye
docs.text:
• Au revoir ! — Goodbye! — always correct [oh ruh-VWAR]
  • À bientôt ! — See you soon! [a byɛ̃-TOH]
  • À demain ! — See you tomorrow! [a duh-MƐ̃]
  • À tout à l’heure ! — See you later (today)! [a too-ta LÖR]
  • À plus tard ! / À plus ! — See you later! / Later! (casual — in texts: A+) [a plew TAR / a PLEWSS]
  • À la prochaine ! — Until next time! [a la pro-SHEN]

docs.title: Wishing a good day
docs.text:
When you leave a shop or end a call, add a wish. The answer is always Merci, vous aussi ! (Thanks, you too!) or, with a friend, Toi aussi !

  • Bonne journée ! — Merci, vous aussi ! — Have a nice day! — Thanks, you too! [bon zhoor-NAY … voo-zoh-SEE]
  • Bonne soirée ! Bon week-end ! — Have a nice evening! Have a good weekend! [bon swa-RAY, bõ wee-KEND]
  • Bon appétit ! Bon voyage ! — Enjoy your meal! Have a good trip! [bo-na-pay-TEE, bõ vwa-YAZH]

docs.title: 5.3 Please, thank you, you’re welcome
docs.text:
French English s’il vous plaît please (polite / plural) s’il te plaît please (to a friend) merci / merci beaucoup thank you / thank you very much merci bien / mille mercis thanks a lot / a thousand thanks de rien you’re welcome (everyday) je vous en prie / je t’en prie you’re welcome (polite / to a friend) avec plaisir with pleasure pas de quoi no problem (casual)
  • Un thé, s’il vous plaît. — Voilà. — Merci beaucoup ! — Je vous en prie. — A tea, please. — Here you are. — Thank you very much! — You're welcome.
  • Tu me passes le sel, s’il te plaît ? — Tiens. — Merci ! — De rien. — Can you pass me the salt, please? — Here. — Thanks! — No problem.

merci = no, thanks

When someone offers you something, Merci alone (often with a small hand gesture) can mean “no, thank you”. To accept, say Oui, merci or Avec plaisir.

Careful

  • Wrong: Merci très beaucoup.
  • Right: Merci beaucoup. / Merci mille fois.
  • Why: beaucoup already means “very much”. Never put très before it.

In Belgium, s’il vous plaît is also used to mean “here you are” when handing something over. In France, you say voilà or tenez (tiens to a friend).

docs.title: 5.4 Excuse me, sorry, pardon
docs.text:
French Use it to… Excusez-moi (Excuse-moi with tu) get attention before a question; apologise for a small thing Pardon ! bump into someone; squeeze past Pardon ? “Sorry, what did you say?” Je suis désolé / désolée say you are really sorry (regret)
  • Excusez-moi, Madame, où est la gare ? — Excuse me, madam, where is the station? [ex-kew-zay-MWA … oo eh la GAR]
  • Oh, pardon ! — Oh, sorry! (bumping into someone) [par-DÕ]
  • Je suis désolée, je suis en retard. — I'm sorry, I'm late. (a woman speaking: désolée) [day-zo-LAY … ã ruh-TAR]

Désolé agrees with the speaker: a man writes désolé, a woman désolée. Both sound exactly the same.

docs.title: 5.5 Tu or vous?
docs.text:
French has two words for “you”. Tu is informal and singular. Vous is polite (for one person) and the normal plural (for several people, polite or not). If you speak Hindi, you already know the idea:

Hindi French With whom tum tu friends, family, children, classmates aap vous strangers, elders, shops, work, officials tum log / aap log vous any group of two or more people

Careful: Hindi tu (very intimate, or rude) is stronger than French tu. French tu is closer to tum.

Figure 5.2. The tu/vous decision. Switching from vous to tu is called tutoyer ; the offer is On peut se tutoyer ? (“Shall we say tu?”).

tu vs vous

vous = one stranger (polite) or any group. tu = one friend, relative or child. Not sure? vous.

docs.title: The same question, two ways
docs.text:
With tu With vous Comment tu t’appelles ? Comment vous appelez-vous ? Ça va ? / Tu vas bien ? Comment allez-vous ? Tu es d’où ? Vous êtes d’où ? Et toi ? Et vous ? s’il te plaît s’il vous plaît

Careful

  • Wrong: (To a shop assistant) Tu as du lait ?
  • Right: Vous avez du lait ?
  • Why: Using tu with an adult stranger sounds rude or childish. The verb changes too: tu as → vous avez.

docs.title: Your name
docs.text:
• Je m’appelle Priya. — My name is Priya. (literally: I call myself Priya) [zhuh ma-PEL pree-YA]
  • Moi, c’est Arjun. — I'm Arjun. (relaxed, very common) [MWA, seh ar-JOON]
  • Enchanté ! / Enchantée ! — Nice to meet you! (a man writes enchanté, a woman enchantée — same sound) [ã-shã-TAY]

Careful

  • Wrong: Je m’appelle est Priya. / Mon nom est Priya.
  • Right: Je m’appelle Priya.
  • Why: je m’appelle is already a full verb: “I call myself”. Mon nom est… is grammatical but stiff; nobody says it.

docs.title: Nationality
docs.text:
Nationality adjectives change for gender (blue = said by or about a man, pink = a woman). They take no capital letter after je suis.

Masculine Feminine indien [ɛ̃-DYƐ̃] indienne [ɛ̃-DYEN] français [frã-SEH] française [frã-SEZ] anglais [ã-GLEH] anglaise [ã-GLEZ] américain [a-may-ree-KƐ̃] américaine [a-may-ree-KEN] canadien [ka-na-DYƐ̃] canadienne [ka-na-DYEN] pakistanais pakistanaise népalais népalaise britannique britannique
  • Je suis indien. — I am Indian. (a man) [zhuh swee ɛ̃-DYƐ̃]
  • Je suis indienne. — I am Indian. (a woman) — the nasal disappears, the n is heard [zhuh swee ɛ̃-DYEN]

Careful

  • Wrong: (Priya speaking) Je suis indien.
  • Right: Je suis indienne.
  • Why: The adjective agrees with the speaker. A woman is indienne, française, canadienne.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je suis Indien. Je parle Hindi.
  • Right: Je suis indien. Je parle hindi.
  • Why: French writes nationality adjectives and languages in small letters. Only the noun for a person takes a capital: les Indiens (Indian people).

docs.title: Where you live, what you do, what you speak
docs.text:
• J’habite à Pune, en Inde. — I live in Pune, in India. — à + city, en + most countries [zha-BEET a … ã-NƐ̃D]
  • Je viens de Chennai. — I come from Chennai. [zhuh vyɛ̃ duh …]
  • Je suis étudiant. / Je suis étudiante. — I am a student. (man / woman) [ay-tew-DYÃ / ay-tew-DYÃT]
  • Je suis ingénieur. Je suis médecin. — I am an engineer. I am a doctor. [ɛ̃-zhay-NYÖR, mayd-SƐ̃]
  • Je parle hindi, anglais et un peu français. — I speak Hindi, English and a little French. [zhuh parl een-DEE, ã-GLEH ay ɛ̃ pö frã-SEH]
  • J’ai vingt-cinq ans. — I am 25 (literally: I have 25 years). [zhay vɛ̃t-sɛ̃-KÃ]

Careful

  • Wrong: Je suis un ingénieur.
  • Right: Je suis ingénieur.
  • Why: After je suis, professions take no article. (But: C’est un ingénieur — with c’est, the article comes back.)

Careful

  • Wrong: J’habite en Mumbai.
  • Right: J’habite à Mumbai.
  • Why: Cities take à; most countries take en (en Inde, en France). More in Prepositions & places.

docs.title: 5.7 Ça va? — How are you?
docs.text:
Ça va ? (literally “it goes?”) is the everyday “how are you?”, and Ça va. is also the answer: “I’m fine.” Only the melody changes.

Answer Meaning Très bien, merci ! Very well, thanks! Ça va bien. I'm good. Pas mal. Not bad. Comme ci, comme ça. So-so. Bof… Meh… (casual) Pas terrible. Not great.

Always bounce it back

After your answer, return the question: Et toi ? (friend) or Et vous ? (polite). Leaving it out feels abrupt.

docs.title: Dialogue 1 — two students in Lyon (tu)
docs.text:
• Léa : Salut ! Moi, c’est Léa. Et toi ? — Hi! I'm Léa. And you?
  • Rohan : Salut, Léa ! Je m’appelle Rohan. — Hi, Léa! My name is Rohan.
  • Léa : Tu es d’où ? — Where are you from? [tew eh DOO]
  • Rohan : Je suis indien, je viens de Pune. Et toi ? — I'm Indian, I come from Pune. And you?
  • Léa : Moi, je suis française. J’habite ici, à Lyon. — I'm French. I live here, in Lyon.
  • Rohan : Enchanté ! — Léa : Enchantée ! — Nice to meet you! — Nice to meet you!
  • Léa : Bon, j’ai cours. À plus ! — Right, I have class. See you!
  • Rohan : Salut, à demain ! — Bye, see you tomorrow!

docs.title: Dialogue 2 — at a hotel reception (vous)
docs.text:
• Réceptionniste : Bonsoir, Monsieur. — Good evening, sir.
  • M. Mehta : Bonsoir, Madame. J’ai une réservation au nom de Mehta. — Good evening, madam. I have a reservation in the name of Mehta.
  • Réceptionniste : Vous pouvez épeler, s’il vous plaît ? — Can you spell it, please?
  • M. Mehta : Oui : M, E, H, T, A. — Yes: M-E-H-T-A.
  • Réceptionniste : Merci. Voici votre clé. Bonne soirée ! — Thank you. Here is your key. Have a nice evening!
  • M. Mehta : Merci beaucoup. Vous aussi ! — Thank you very much. You too!

docs.title: 5.8 Survival phrases
docs.text:
These sentences rescue any conversation. Learn them by heart this week — they are worth more than a hundred nouns.

  • Je ne comprends pas. — I don't understand. [zhuhn kõ-prã PA]
  • Vous pouvez répéter, s’il vous plaît ? — Can you repeat, please? [voo poo-vay ray-pay-TAY]
  • Plus lentement, s’il vous plaît. — More slowly, please. [plew lãt-MÃ]
  • Vous parlez anglais ? — Do you speak English? [voo par-lay ã-GLEH]
  • Je ne parle pas bien français. Je suis débutant. — I don't speak French well. I'm a beginner. (woman: débutante) [… day-bew-TÃ]
  • Comment dit-on « thank you » en français ? — How do you say “thank you” in French? [ko-mã dee-TÕ … ã frã-SEH]
  • Qu’est-ce que ça veut dire ? — What does that mean? [kes-kuh sa vö DEER]
  • Je ne sais pas. — I don't know. [zhuhn seh PA]
  • Où sont les toilettes, s’il vous plaît ? — Where are the toilets, please? [oo sõ lay twa-LET]
  • Je voudrais un verre d’eau. — I would like a glass of water. [zhuh voo-DREH ɛ̃ vehr DOH]
  • Oui. Non. D’accord. Peut-être. — Yes. No. OK. Maybe. [WEE, NÕ, da-KOR, pö-TETR]

Polite magic

Bonjour + excusez-moi + your question + s’il vous plaît + merci: this frame makes even broken French sound polite.

À retenir

  • Always start with Bonjour — in a shop, a bus, an office, before any question. Add Monsieur or Madame for a stranger.
  • When someone offers you something, Merci alone (often with a small hand gesture) can mean “no, thank you”. To accept, say Oui, merci or Avec plaisir.
  • vous = one stranger (polite) or any group. tu = one friend, relative or child. Not sure? vous.
  • After your answer, return the question: Et toi ? (friend) or Et vous ? (polite). Leaving it out feels abrupt.
  • Bonjour + excusez-moi + your question + s’il vous plaît + merci: this frame makes even broken French sound polite.
  • Introduce yourself aloud in four sentences: name, nationality, city, languages. Then go on to Numbers, dates & time — you will need them for your age, phone number and prices.

docs.title: 5.9 Practice — First words
docs.text:
Exercise 1

It's 9 pm. You walk into a restaurant. You say…

  • Bonjour
  • Bonsoir
  • Bonne nuit
  • Bonne journée
Answer

Bonsoir

Evening greeting = bonsoir. Bonne nuit is only for going to bed.

Exercise 2

When do you say 'Bonne nuit'?

  • Arriving in the evening
  • Going to bed
  • Leaving a shop at noon
  • Meeting a friend
Answer

Going to bed

Bonne nuit = sleep well. It is never a greeting.

Exercise 3

'Please', to a stranger:

  • s'il te plaît
  • s'il vous plaît
  • de rien
  • pardon
Answer

s'il vous plaît

vous = polite; s'il te plaît is for friends.

Exercise 4

Someone says 'Merci !'. You answer…

  • Merci
  • De rien
  • Pardon
  • Salut
Answer

De rien

de rien / je vous en prie = you're welcome.

Exercise 5

You bump into someone in the metro. You say…

  • Pardon !
  • Bonsoir !
  • De rien !
  • Enchanté !
Answer

Pardon !

Pardon for small bumps; excusez-moi to get attention; désolé for real regret.

Exercise 6

Tu or vous with a shop assistant you don't know?

  • tu
  • vous
Answer

vous

Strangers, shops, work, elders: vous.

Exercise 7

Hindi 'tum' is closest to French…

  • tu
  • vous
  • il
  • on
Answer

tu

tum ≈ tu (informal), aap ≈ vous (polite).

Exercise 8

Je m'___ Priya. (My name is Priya.)

Hint: from s'appeler

Answer

appelle

Je m'appelle = I call myself. Two p, two l.

Exercise 9

(Priya speaking) Je suis ___ . (Indian)

Hint: a woman

Answer

indienne

Feminine: indien → indienne. The nasal disappears: [ɛ̃-DYEN].

Exercise 10

Pick the extra word.

Je suis un ingénieur.

Answer

Wrong word: un.

Corrected: Je suis ingénieur.

No article for a profession after je suis.

Exercise 11

Pick the wrong word.

J'habite en Mumbai.

Answer

Wrong word: en.

Corrected: J'habite à Mumbai.

à + city; en + most countries (en Inde).

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

Merci très beaucoup !

Answer

Wrong word: très.

Corrected: Merci beaucoup !

beaucoup already means 'very much'.

Exercise 13

Match the goodbyes.

A B Au revoir See you tomorrow À bientôt Have a nice day À demain Goodbye Bonne journée See you soon Answer

Au revoir — Goodbye; À bientôt — See you soon; À demain — See you tomorrow; Bonne journée — Have a nice day

À + a time = see you then.

Exercise 14

Match the survival phrases.

A B Je ne comprends pas More slowly Vous pouvez répéter ? I don't know Plus lentement I don't understand Je ne sais pas Can you repeat? Answer

Je ne comprends pas — I don't understand; Vous pouvez répéter ? — Can you repeat?; Plus lentement — More slowly; Je ne sais pas — I don't know

Learn these by heart — they rescue any conversation.

Exercise 15

'Ça va ?' — the best informal answer:

  • Ça va, et toi ?
  • Je m'appelle Léa.
  • Bonne nuit.
  • De rien.
Answer

Ça va, et toi ?

Answer, then bounce the question back: et toi ? / et vous ?

Exercise 16

Who writes 'Enchantée' with -ée?

  • a man
  • a woman
  • a group
  • nobody
Answer

a woman

Enchanté (man), enchantée (woman) — same sound.

Exercise 17

Put the words in order: 'What is your name?' (polite)

Words: appelez-vous / vous / Comment

Answer

Comment vous appelez-vous

Comment + vous + appelez-vous: the polite inverted question.

Exercise 18

Put the words in order: 'I don't understand.'

Words: ne / pas / comprends / Je

Answer

Je ne comprends pas

ne + verb + pas: the negation sandwich.

Exercise 19

Say it aloud.

Vous pouvez répéter s'il vous plaît

Answer

voo poo-VAY ray-pay-TAY seel voo PLEH — the most useful sentence in this chapter.

Exercise 20

Say it aloud (change the name if you like).

Je m'appelle Arjun et je suis indien

Answer

zhuh ma-PEL … ay zhuh swee ɛ̃-DYƐ̃ (a woman: indienne).

Next step

Introduce yourself aloud in four sentences: name, nationality, city, languages. Then go on to Numbers, dates & time — you will need them for your age, phone number and prices.

docs.title: Chapter 1: How to use this book
docs.text:
Le mode d’emploi

This book takes you from your very first bonjour to confident, natural French at C2, the top level. It is not a book you only read. You will listen, speak and test yourself on every page.

The whole method in one line

20 minutes a day, out loud, every day — read, listen, repeat, quiz, review. Speaking aloud is not optional: it is how French moves from your eyes to your mouth.

  • Bonjour ! — Hello! / Good morning! [bõ-ZHOOR]
  • On commence ? — Shall we start? [õ ko-MÃSS]

docs.title: 1.1 The path: from A1 to C2
docs.text:
Language levels in Europe, and in most French exams, follow the CEFR (Common European Framework of Reference). It has six levels in three pairs: A = basic user, B = independent user, C = proficient user.

Level Name What you can do A1 Beginner Greet people, introduce yourself, ask simple questions, understand slow, clear speech. A2 Elementary Shop, order food, talk about your family, job and past weekend in simple sentences. B1 Threshold Travel alone, tell a story, give a simple opinion, follow the main points of the news. B2 Vantage Discuss and argue, watch most films without subtitles, work in French. C1 Advanced Speak fluently and precisely, write structured essays, understand implicit meaning. C2 Mastery Understand almost everything, play with style and register, sound educated and natural.

The book has seven parts. The order is the learning path: you cannot read French aloud until the silent letters and nasal sounds make sense, so Part 1 starts there. The parts on speaking, vocabulary and writing climb in level inside each part, so you can dip into their early chapters while you work through the grammar.

Figure 1.1. The road through the book. Parts 1–4 build the core; parts 5–7 add words, writing and polish. Each stop shows its CEFR range and number of chapters.

Where to start

Total beginner? Go in order. Already know some French? Still do Part 1 — pronunciation habits are hard to fix later — then use the quizzes to skip what you already know.

docs.title: 1.2 How each chapter works
docs.text:
Every chapter opens as a set of swipeable pages. You always meet the same steps, so you always know where you are.

Step What it does Cover Title, level and time. Map The sections of the chapter. Tap one to jump to it. Content pages Rules, examples with sound, tables, figures and typical mistakes. À retenir “To remember”: the key rules on one page. Practice A quiz of 12–20 questions, including speaking. Finish Your score and the next chapter.

docs.title: The colour code
docs.text:
French nouns are masculine or feminine, and that choice changes the words around them. So the book colours them everywhere, from page one to the last chapter.

  • le livre — the book — blue = masculine** [luh LEEVR]
  • la table — the table — pink = feminine** [la TABL]
  • les amis — the friends — violet = plural** [lay-za-MEE]
  • Je parle français. — I speak French. — the verb has its own colour [zhuh parl frã-SEH]

Two more marks help you read aloud. A greyed, struck letter is silent: petit, ils parlent. A tie mark shows that two words are linked in speech (a liaison): les‿amis. You will learn both in Silent letters & liaison.

docs.title: The pronunciation hints
docs.text: Under new words you will see a hint in square brackets, written for English readers: [bõ-ZHOOR]. CAPITALS mark the last syllable, which is slightly longer in French. The symbols ã õ ɛ̃ are the nasal vowels, and ew is the French u. They are explained, mouth by mouth, in The sounds of French.

docs.title: 1.3 The 20-minute daily routine
docs.text:
Short, daily practice beats a long session once a week. Your brain stores language during sleep, so seven small sessions give you seven nights of consolidation instead of one. Here is the routine that the whole book is built for.

Figure 1.2. Read a little, then spend most of the time with your ears and mouth. Finish with a quick look back at an older chapter. Step How to do it well 1. Read (6 min) One or two sections only. Understand the rule; do not try to memorise every example. 2. Listen (4 min) Look at the French while you listen. 3. Repeat aloud (5 min) Copy the melody, not just the words. 4. Quiz (3 min) Do part of the chapter quiz, or all of it at the end of the chapter. 5. Review (2 min) Open the “À retenir” page of an older chapter and say its examples aloud.

The routine in French — say these as you do each step:

  • Je lis. — I read. [zhuh LEE]
  • J’écoute. — I listen. [zhay-KOOT]
  • Je répète à voix haute. — I repeat out loud. [zhuh ray-PET a vwa OHT]
  • Je révise tous les jours. — I review every day. [zhuh ray-VEEZ too lay ZHOOR]

Shadowing

Do it three times per sentence.

docs.title: 1.4 Spaced review: beat the forgetting curve
docs.text:
You forget most of a new word within a day or two — unless you meet it again. Each time you review it just before you forget, the memory gets stronger and lasts longer. This is called spaced repetition.

Figure 1.3. Review a chapter 1, 3, 7 and 21 days after you first study it. Four short reviews are enough to make most of it permanent.

The review rule

Review each chapter after 1 day, 3 days, 1 week and 3 weeks — just the “À retenir” page and the quiz. A second quiz attempt the next day fixes it in memory.

Keep a small notebook (or a notes app) with one line per day: the date and the chapter. Then each morning you can see which chapters are due. Write new words with their article — une pomme, not just pomme — so you learn the gender at the same time.

docs.title: 1.5 How long will it take?
docs.text:
Honest numbers help you plan. The figures below are the usual estimates of total guided study hours to reach each level, as quoted by language schools such as the Alliance Française. They vary a lot from person to person; extra listening (films, podcasts, music) makes everything faster.

Level Total hours (approx.) At 20 min/day At 1 hour/day A1 60–100 h 6–10 months 2–3 months A2 160–200 h about 1.5 years about 6 months B1 350–400 h about 3 years about 1 year B2 550–650 h about 5 years 1.5–2 years C1 800–1000 h — 2.5–3 years C2 1000–1200 h+ — 3–4 years

So 20 minutes a day is the minimum that keeps you moving, not the fastest road. A good plan: the 20-minute routine with this book, plus 20–40 minutes of French you enjoy — a series with French subtitles, a podcast for learners, songs. English speakers have a head start: the US Foreign Service Institute puts French in its easiest group of languages for English speakers.

Measure, don’t guess

The official French exams are the DELF (A1–B2) and DALF (C1–C2), offered in India by the Alliance Française centres. See DELF, DALF & your level in Part 7.

docs.title: 1.6 Tips for Indian and English-speaking learners
docs.text:
You already know far more French than you think. A large part of English vocabulary comes from French. Many words are almost the same — only the pronunciation changes.

  • la nation, l’information, la question — nation, information, question — same words, French sound [na-SYÕ, ɛ̃-for-ma-SYÕ, kes-TYÕ]
  • le restaurant, le train, le chocolat — restaurant, train, chocolate [res-to-RÃ, trɛ̃, sho-ko-LA]
  • l’hôtel, le taxi, le bus — hotel, taxi, bus [lo-TEL, tak-SEE, BEWSS]
  • la police, la banque, la pharmacie — police, bank, pharmacy [po-LEESS, BÃK, far-ma-SEE]
  • C’est possible ? C’est important ! — Is it possible? It's important! [seh po-SEEBL … seh-tɛ̃-por-TÃ]

Same spelling, French sound

A shared word is only free if you say it the French way: hôtel is [o-TEL], not “HO-tel”; important ends in a nasal, with no t. Some look-alikes are traps (false friends) — see Cognates & false friends.

docs.title: What Hindi gives you
docs.text: Hindi helps with… Why Gender Hindi nouns are masculine or feminine too (kitaab is feminine). The idea is familiar — but the genders do not match the French ones, so learn each word with its article. Nasal vowels The nasal sound in maan (माँ) or haan (हाँ) is very close to French an in enfant. t, d, p, k French t and d are dental, like Hindi त and द, not like English t and d. French p, t, k have no puff of air, like Hindi प, त, क. tu / vous Like tum / aap: vous is the polite form. See Hello, please, thank you. The French R It is made in the throat, close to the Urdu sound ग़ in ghazal — not the tapped Hindi र.

docs.title: Traps for English speakers
docs.text:
Careful

  • Wrong: Reading Paris as “PA-ris”, with the s.
  • Right: Paris = [pa-REE]: the s is silent and the last syllable is stressed.
  • Why: French final consonants are usually silent, and French stresses the end of the word, not the beginning.

Careful

  • Wrong: Learning “pomme = apple”.
  • Right: Learning “une pomme = an apple”.
  • Why: Gender is part of every noun. Learn it with the word from day one — later it is much harder.

Careful

  • Wrong: Reading silently, in your head.
  • Right: Reading every example aloud, at normal volume.
  • Why: Your mouth needs practice as much as your memory. Silent study gives you a reading French, not a speaking French.

Careful

  • Wrong: Waiting to speak until you are “ready”.
  • Right: Speaking from the first day, with mistakes.
  • Why: Mistakes are how you learn. French people are usually happy you try — start every exchange with bonjour.

docs.title: 1.7 Your first French words
docs.text:
Before the next chapter, here are six words you will use every single day.

  • oui — yes [WEE]
  • non — no [NÕ]
  • merci — thank you [mehr-SEE]
  • s’il vous plaît — please (polite) [seel voo PLEH]
  • d’accord — OK, agreed [da-KOR]
  • au revoir — goodbye [oh ruh-VWAR]

docs.title: A first mini-dialogue
docs.text:
• — Bonjour, Madame ! — — Hello, madam! [bõ-zhoor ma-DAM]
  • — Bonjour ! Un café, s’il vous plaît ? — — Hello! A coffee, please? [ɛ̃ ka-FAY seel voo PLEH]
  • — Oui, d’accord. — — Yes, OK.
  • — Merci ! Au revoir ! — — Thank you! Goodbye!

Notice Madame after bonjour: in France it is polite to add Monsieur or Madame when you greet someone you do not know. More in Hello, please, thank you.

À retenir

  • 20 minutes a day, out loud, every day — read, listen, repeat, quiz, review. Speaking aloud is not optional: it is how French moves from your eyes to your mouth.
  • Total beginner? Go in order. Already know some French? Still do Part 1 — pronunciation habits are hard to fix later — then use the quizzes to skip what you already know.
  • Do it three times per sentence.
  • Review each chapter after 1 day, 3 days, 1 week and 3 weeks — just the “À retenir” page and the quiz. A second quiz attempt the next day fixes it in memory.
  • The official French exams are the DELF (A1–B2) and DALF (C1–C2), offered in India by the Alliance Française centres. See DELF, DALF & your level in Part 7.
  • Go on to Alphabet & accents. That is your first day of French — bravo !

docs.title: 1.8 Practice — The method
docs.text:
Exercise 1

How many CEFR levels are there?

  • 4
  • 5
  • 6
  • 8
Answer

6

A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2 — three pairs: basic, independent, proficient.

Exercise 2

What is the top CEFR level?

  • A1
  • B2
  • C1
  • C2
Answer

C2

C2 = mastery. This book aims to take you all the way there.

Exercise 3

What does the daily routine ask you to do with every example?

  • Copy it into a notebook
  • Say it aloud
  • Translate it into Hindi
  • Skip it
Answer

Say it aloud

Speaking aloud moves French from your eyes to your mouth. Silent reading is not enough.

Exercise 4

How long is the core daily routine?

  • 5 minutes
  • 20 minutes
  • 1 hour
  • 2 hours
Answer

20 minutes

20 minutes every day: read, listen, repeat aloud, quiz, review.

Exercise 5

In this book, a noun in blue is…

  • masculine
  • feminine
  • plural
  • a verb

Hint: le livre

Answer

masculine

Blue = masculine, pink = feminine, violet = plural.

Exercise 6

In the hint [bõ-ZHOOR], what do the capitals show?

  • A loud shout
  • The last, slightly longer syllable
  • A silent part
  • An English word
Answer

The last, slightly longer syllable

French stresses the end of a word or group: bon-JOUR.

Exercise 7

Review a chapter after 1 day, 3 days, 1 week and ___ weeks.

Hint: a number

Answer

3 / three / trois

1 – 3 – 7 – 21 days: each gap is longer than the one before.

Exercise 8

Pick the bad study habit.

Learn every noun silently with its article.

Answer

Wrong word: silently.

Corrected: Learn every noun aloud with its article.

Always say words aloud — and yes, always with the article.

Exercise 9

Match the exam to its levels.

A B DELF C1 to C2 DALF the six-level scale CEFR A1 to B2 Answer

DELF — A1 to B2; DALF — C1 to C2; CEFR — the six-level scale

DELF covers A1–B2, DALF covers C1–C2; the CEFR is the scale they use.

Exercise 10

Match the French to the English.

A B oui thank you non goodbye merci yes au revoir no Answer

oui — yes; non — no; merci — thank you; au revoir — goodbye

Four words you will use every day.

Exercise 11

Which sound is closest to the French R?

  • र as in raja
  • ग़ as in ghazal
  • ड as in dal
  • the English r in red
Answer

ग़ as in ghazal

The French R is made at the back of the throat, like ग़ — not tapped like र, not curled like English r.

Exercise 12

"S'il vous plaît" means…

  • thank you
  • please
  • hello
  • sorry
Answer

please

s'il vous plaît = please (literally 'if it pleases you').

Exercise 13

Un café, s'il vous ___ .

Hint: please = s'il vous …

Answer

plaît / plait

s'il vous plaît — the t is silent: [seel voo PLEH].

Exercise 14

Put the words in order: 'I speak a little French.'

Words: français / parle / Je / un / peu

Answer

Je parle un peu français

Je (I) + parle (speak) + un peu (a little) + français.

Exercise 15

Say it aloud.

Bonjour Madame

Answer

bon-JOUR ma-DAME: add Monsieur or Madame when greeting a stranger.

Exercise 16

Say it aloud.

J'apprends le français

Answer

zha-PRAN luh fran-SEH — the final s of français is silent.

Next step

Go on to Alphabet & accents. That is your first day of French — bravo !

docs.title: Chapter 47: Idioms & expressions
docs.text:
Les expressions idiomatiques

French people don’t say “I’m tired and can’t be bothered” — they say j’ai la flemme. They don’t get stood up — someone “puts a rabbit” on them. Idioms are where French is most colourful and most impossible to guess. Here are sixty that you will really hear, sorted by theme, each with its literal picture, its real meaning and an example.

How to read this chapter

Each idiom has three layers: Lit. (the word-for-word picture) → real meaning → an example. Remember the picture; it is what makes the idiom stick.

docs.title: 47.1 How idioms work
docs.text:
An idiom is a fixed group of words whose meaning is not the sum of its parts. You cannot change the words (il pleut des cordes, never des ficelles), but you do conjugate the verb and change the possessives: je me creuse la tête, elle se creuse la tête.

Figure 47.1. Picture cards: learn each idiom as a silly image, then attach the real meaning to it.

Watch the register

Many idioms are familier (marked fam.): perfect with friends, wrong in a job interview or an essay. For the full scale of registers and slang, see Registers & slang.

Don’t overdo it

One well-placed idiom makes you sound natural; five in one sentence sounds like a textbook. Use them when the situation calls for them.

docs.title: 47.2 À table ! Food idioms
docs.text:
French is a food culture, and its idioms prove it: apples, beans, onions, cheese and bread everywhere.

  • avoir la pêche (fam.) — Ce matin, j’ai la pêche ! — Lit. to have the peach → to be full of energy. — This morning I feel great!
  • tomber dans les pommes — Avec la chaleur, elle est tombée dans les pommes. — Lit. to fall into the apples → to faint. — With the heat, she fainted.
  • raconter des salades (fam.) — Arrête de me raconter des salades. — Lit. to tell salads → to tell fibs. — Stop telling me stories.
  • c’est la fin des haricots — Plus de café au bureau ? C’est la fin des haricots ! — Lit. it’s the end of the beans → all is lost (usually joking). — No more coffee at the office? It’s the end of the world!
  • mettre son grain de sel — Il faut toujours qu’il mette son grain de sel. — Lit. to put in one’s grain of salt → to butt in with an opinion. — He always has to stick his oar in.
  • avoir du pain sur la planche — Cette semaine, j’ai du pain sur la planche. — Lit. to have bread on the board → to have a lot of work ahead. — This week I’ve got my work cut out.
  • occupe-toi de tes oignons (fam.) — Ma vie privée ? Occupe-toi de tes oignons ! — Lit. look after your onions → mind your own business. — My private life? Mind your own business!
  • en faire tout un fromage (fam.) — C’est une petite tache, n’en fais pas tout un fromage ! — Lit. to make a whole cheese of it → to make a fuss about nothing. — It’s a tiny stain, don’t make a mountain out of a molehill!
  • les carottes sont cuites — On perd 3-0 à la 85e minute : les carottes sont cuites. — Lit. the carrots are cooked → it’s all over. — We’re losing 3–0 in the 85th minute: it’s game over.
  • c’est du gâteau (fam.) — Cet exercice ? C’est du gâteau. — Lit. it’s cake → it’s a piece of cake. — This exercise? Easy. (And ce n’est pas du gâteau = it’s no picnic.)

docs.title: 47.3 Animal idioms
docs.text:
Cats are the stars of French idioms — and rabbits, hens, sheep and wolves are not far behind.

  • poser un lapin à quelqu’un — Elle m’a posé un lapin : je l’ai attendue une heure ! — Lit. to put a rabbit on someone → to stand someone up. — She stood me up: I waited an hour for her!
  • avoir d’autres chats à fouetter — Désolé, j’ai d’autres chats à fouetter. — Lit. to have other cats to whip → to have bigger fish to fry. — Sorry, I’ve got more important things to do.
  • appeler un chat un chat — Appelons un chat un chat : c’est un échec. — Lit. to call a cat a cat → to call a spade a spade. — Let’s be honest: it’s a failure.
  • avoir un chat dans la gorge — Pardon, j’ai un chat dans la gorge. — Lit. to have a cat in the throat → to have a frog in one’s throat. — Sorry, I’ve got a frog in my throat.
  • donner sa langue au chat — Je ne trouve pas la réponse, je donne ma langue au chat. — Lit. to give one’s tongue to the cat → to give up guessing. — I can’t find the answer, I give up — tell me.
  • quand les poules auront des dents — Il rangera sa chambre quand les poules auront des dents. — Lit. when hens have teeth → never; when pigs fly. — He’ll tidy his room when pigs fly.
  • avoir la chair de poule — Cette musique me donne la chair de poule. — Lit. to have hen’s flesh → to have goosebumps. — This music gives me goosebumps.
  • revenons à nos moutons — Bon, revenons à nos moutons : le budget. — Lit. let’s get back to our sheep → let’s get back to the point. — Right, back to the subject: the budget.
  • avoir une faim de loup — Après le match, j’ai une faim de loup. — Lit. to have a wolf’s hunger → to be starving. — After the match I’m ravenous.
  • quand on parle du loup… — Tiens, voilà Karim ! Quand on parle du loup… — Lit. when you talk about the wolf (you see its tail) → speak of the devil. — Look, here’s Karim! Speak of the devil…

docs.title: 47.4 The body: head, eyes, hands and feet
docs.text:
Almost every part of the body has an idiom. The map below gathers the most common ones.

Figure 47.2. The idiom body: ten body parts, ten everyday expressions.
  • casser les pieds à quelqu’un (fam.) — Ces réunions me cassent les pieds. — Lit. to break someone’s feet → to annoy, to bore stiff. — These meetings drive me mad. (A casse-pieds = a pain in the neck.)
  • casser les oreilles — Baisse la musique, tu me casses les oreilles ! — Lit. to break the ears → to be deafeningly loud. — Turn the music down, you’re deafening me!
  • mettre les pieds dans le plat — Il a mis les pieds dans le plat en parlant de son ex. — Lit. to put one’s feet in the dish → to put one’s foot in it; to raise an awkward subject bluntly. — He put his foot in it by mentioning her ex.
  • avoir le cœur sur la main — Ma grand-mère a le cœur sur la main. — Lit. to have the heart on the hand → to be very generous. — My grandmother would give you anything.
  • tirer les vers du nez à quelqu’un — Il ne voulait rien dire, mais je lui ai tiré les vers du nez. — Lit. to pull the worms out of someone’s nose → to worm information out of someone. — He didn’t want to say anything, but I got it out of him.
  • se creuser la tête — Je me suis creusé la tête pendant une heure. — Lit. to dig one’s head → to rack one’s brains. — I racked my brains for an hour.
  • avoir la grosse tête (fam.) — Depuis sa promotion, il a la grosse tête. — Lit. to have the big head → to be big-headed. — Since his promotion he’s been full of himself.
  • mon œil ! (fam.) — Tu as fini tes devoirs ? Mon œil ! — Lit. my eye! → yeah, right! — You’ve finished your homework? Yeah, right!
  • avoir quelque chose sur le bout de la langue — Son nom ? Je l’ai sur le bout de la langue. — Lit. on the tip of the tongue → same as English. — His name? It’s on the tip of my tongue.
  • ne pas avoir froid aux yeux — Elle a traversé l’Afrique seule : elle n’a pas froid aux yeux ! — Lit. not to have cold eyes → to be fearless, daring. — She crossed Africa alone: she’s got guts!
  • les doigts dans le nez (fam.) — Il a gagné la course les doigts dans le nez. — Lit. with fingers in the nose → effortlessly, hands down. — He won the race without even trying.

docs.title: 47.5 Weather and nature
docs.text:
• il pleut des cordes — Prends un parapluie, il pleut des cordes ! — Lit. it’s raining ropes → it’s raining cats and dogs. — Take an umbrella, it’s pouring! (also: il pleut à verse)
  • il fait un froid de canard — Couvre-toi, il fait un froid de canard. — Lit. it’s duck cold (probably from winter duck-hunting) → it’s freezing. — Wrap up, it’s bitterly cold.
  • un temps de chien — Quel temps de chien aujourd’hui ! — Lit. dog’s weather → awful weather. — What foul weather today!
  • être dans la lune — Pardon, tu disais ? J’étais dans la lune. — Lit. to be in the moon → to be daydreaming, miles away. — Sorry, what were you saying? I was miles away.
  • ce n’est pas la mer à boire — Trois pages à lire, ce n’est pas la mer à boire. — Lit. it’s not the sea to drink → it’s not that hard. — Three pages to read — it’s hardly the end of the world.
  • ne pas être né de la dernière pluie — Je ne suis pas né de la dernière pluie ! — Lit. not to be born from the last rain → not to be born yesterday. — I wasn’t born yesterday!
  • tomber à l’eau — Notre projet de voyage est tombé à l’eau. — Lit. to fall into the water → to fall through. — Our travel plans fell through.

docs.title: 47.6 Feelings and moods
docs.text:
• avoir le cafard — Le dimanche soir, j’ai souvent le cafard. — Lit. to have the cockroach → to feel down, to have the blues. — On Sunday evenings I often feel low.
  • en avoir marre (fam.) — J’en ai marre de ce bruit ! — Marre* has no meaning alone; ≈ to have had enough of it → to be fed up*. — I’m sick of this noise!
  • ne pas être dans son assiette — Je ne suis pas dans mon assiette aujourd’hui. — Lit. not to be in one’s plate → to feel under the weather, not oneself. — I’m not feeling myself today.
  • être aux anges — Elle a eu son bac : elle est aux anges. — Lit. to be with the angels → to be over the moon. — She passed her baccalauréat: she’s thrilled.
  • être sur un petit nuage — Depuis leur mariage, ils sont sur un petit nuage. — Lit. to be on a little cloud → to be on cloud nine. — Since their wedding they’ve been walking on air.
  • faire la tête — Pourquoi tu fais la tête ? J’ai dit quelque chose ? — Lit. to make the head → to sulk. — Why are you sulking? Did I say something?
  • péter les plombs (fam.) — Avec tout ce stress, il a fini par péter les plombs. — Lit. to blow the fuses → to lose it, to snap. — With all that stress, he finally flipped.

docs.title: Love and talking
docs.text:
• avoir un coup de foudre — Quand ils se sont rencontrés, ça a été le coup de foudre. — Lit. a lightning strike → love at first sight. — When they met, it was love at first sight. (Also for things: j’ai eu un coup de foudre pour cette maison.)
  • tourner autour du pot — Arrête de tourner autour du pot et dis-moi la vérité. — Lit. to turn around the pot → to beat around the bush. — Stop beating around the bush and tell me the truth.

docs.title: Money
docs.text:
• coûter les yeux de la tête — Ce sac coûte les yeux de la tête. — Lit. to cost the eyes of the head → to cost an arm and a leg. — This bag costs a fortune.
  • coûter un bras (fam.) — Ce téléphone m’a coûté un bras. — Lit. to cost an arm → to be very expensive. — This phone cost me an arm and a leg. (Only one arm — and no leg!)
  • jeter l’argent par les fenêtres — Un troisième vélo ? Tu jettes l’argent par les fenêtres. — Lit. to throw money out of the windows → to waste money. — A third bike? You’re throwing money down the drain.
  • être fauché comme les blés (fam.) — Je ne sors pas ce soir, je suis fauché comme les blés. — Lit. to be mown like wheat → to be flat broke. — I’m not going out tonight, I’m skint.

docs.title: Time, work and laziness
docs.text:
• avoir la flemme (fam.) — J’ai la flemme de faire la vaisselle. — Lit. to have the laziness → can’t be bothered. — I can’t be bothered to do the dishes.
  • faire la grasse matinée — Dimanche, je fais la grasse matinée. — Lit. to do the fat morning → to sleep in, have a lie-in. — On Sunday I’m sleeping in. (fam.: la grasse mat’)
  • avoir un poil dans la main — Ton frère ne fait rien : il a un poil dans la main ! — Lit. to have a hair in the palm of one’s hand → to be bone idle. — Your brother does nothing: he’s bone idle!
  • se tourner les pouces — Au bureau, il se tourne les pouces toute la journée. — Lit. to turn one’s thumbs → to twiddle one’s thumbs. — At the office he does nothing all day.
  • mettre la main à la pâte — Pour la fête, tout le monde a mis la main à la pâte. — Lit. to put one’s hand in the dough → to pitch in, lend a hand. — For the party, everyone pitched in.
  • en un clin d’œil — Elle a réparé l’ordinateur en un clin d’œil. — Lit. in a wink → in the blink of an eye. — She fixed the computer in no time.

docs.title: 47.8 Proverbs everyone quotes
docs.text:
• L’habit ne fait pas le moine. — Lit. the habit doesn’t make the monk → don’t judge a book by its cover.
  • Petit à petit, l’oiseau fait son nid. — Lit. little by little the bird builds its nest → slowly but surely — a perfect motto for learning French.
  • Après la pluie, le beau temps. — Lit. after the rain, fine weather → every cloud has a silver lining; things will get better.
  • Les murs ont des oreilles. — Lit. and real: the walls have ears — be careful what you say.
  • Il ne faut pas vendre la peau de l’ours avant de l’avoir tué. — Lit. don’t sell the bear’s skin before killing it → don’t count your chickens before they hatch.
  • L’appétit vient en mangeant. — Lit. appetite comes while eating → the more you have, the more you want; once you start, you get into it.

Proverbs are often cut short

French speakers often say only the first half and let you finish it: Quand on parle du loup… · Petit à petit… Knowing the whole proverb lets you catch the allusion.

docs.title: 47.9 Never translate an English idiom word for word
docs.text:
An English idiom translated literally is either nonsense or, worse, means something else. Find the French equivalent, not the translation. These are the classics.

Careful

  • Wrong: Il pleut des chats et des chiens.
  • Right: Il pleut des cordes. / Il pleut à verse.
  • Why: French rain is made of ropes, not pets.

Careful

  • Wrong: C’est un morceau de gâteau.
  • Right: C’est du gâteau. / C’est simple comme bonjour.
  • Why: The French idiom uses the partitive: du gâteau. “Un morceau de gâteau” is just a slice of cake.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je suis sous le temps aujourd’hui.
  • Right: Je ne suis pas dans mon assiette aujourd’hui.
  • Why: “Under the weather” = not in your plate. Sous le temps means nothing.

Careful

  • Wrong: Ça coûte un bras et une jambe.
  • Right: Ça coûte les yeux de la tête. / Ça coûte un bras.
  • Why: French charges your eyes — or, informally, a single arm.

Careful

  • Wrong: J’ai une grenouille dans la gorge.
  • Right: J’ai un chat dans la gorge.
  • Why: In French throats, the frog becomes a cat.

Careful

  • Wrong: Tuer deux oiseaux avec une pierre.
  • Right: Faire d’une pierre deux coups.
  • Why: Lit. “to make two hits with one stone” — no birds are harmed in French.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je suis sur le nuage neuf !
  • Right: Je suis sur un petit nuage ! / Je suis aux anges !
  • Why: The French cloud has no number; it is just “little”.

Careful

  • Wrong: (to an actor) Casse une jambe !
  • Right: Bonne chance ! — in the theatre, actors say Merde !
  • Why: French theatre people wish luck with a rude word (and you don’t say thank you). Outside the theatre, keep to bonne chance.

docs.title: In real life: idioms in conversation
docs.text:
• — Alors, ton rendez-vous d’hier ? — — So, how was your date yesterday?
  • — Ne m’en parle pas ! Il m’a posé un lapin, et il pleuvait des cordes. — — Don’t talk to me about it! He stood me up, and it was pouring.
  • — Oh non… Tu as le cafard ? — — Oh no… Are you feeling down?
  • — Un peu. Mais bon, ce n’est pas la fin des haricots. Après la pluie, le beau temps ! — — A bit. But hey, it’s not the end of the world. Things will get better!

Learn three a week

Pick three idioms, picture them, and use each one in a real sentence this week. Petit à petit, l’oiseau fait son nid.

À retenir

  • Each idiom has three layers: Lit. (the word-for-word picture) → real meaning → an example. Remember the picture; it is what makes the idiom stick.
  • One well-placed idiom makes you sound natural; five in one sentence sounds like a textbook. Use them when the situation calls for them.
  • French speakers often say only the first half and let you finish it: Quand on parle du loup… · Petit à petit… Knowing the whole proverb lets you catch the allusion.
  • Pick three idioms, picture them, and use each one in a real sentence this week. Petit à petit, l’oiseau fait son nid.
  • Many of these idioms are familier. Learn exactly where each register belongs — and the slang and verlan young French people use — in Registers & slang.

docs.title: 47.10 Practice — idioms & expressions
docs.text:
Exercise 1

'Elle m'a posé un lapin' means…

  • She gave me a rabbit.
  • She stood me up.
  • She cooked me rabbit.
  • She told me a lie.
Answer

She stood me up.

Poser un lapin à quelqu'un = not turn up to a date.

Exercise 2

'It's raining cats and dogs' in French:

  • Il pleut des chats et des chiens.
  • Il pleut des cordes.
  • Il fait un froid de canard.
  • Il fait la tête.
Answer

Il pleut des cordes.

French rain falls in ropes: il pleut des cordes (or à verse).

Exercise 3

'J'ai la flemme' means…

  • I'm on fire.
  • I can't be bothered.
  • I'm in love.
  • I'm starving.
Answer

I can't be bothered.

Avoir la flemme (fam.) = to feel too lazy to do something.

Exercise 4

Which idiom means 'to faint'?

  • tomber dans les pommes
  • avoir la pêche
  • raconter des salades
  • mettre son grain de sel
Answer

tomber dans les pommes

Lit. to fall into the apples.

Exercise 5

Ce sac coûte ___ de la tête.

  • les yeux
  • les bras
  • les pieds
  • les oreilles
Answer

les yeux

Coûter les yeux de la tête = to cost a fortune.

Exercise 6

Il ne fait rien, il a un ___ dans la main.

Answer

poil

Avoir un poil dans la main = to be very lazy.

Exercise 7

Je ne trouve pas la réponse, je donne ma langue au ___.

Answer

chat

Donner sa langue au chat = to give up guessing.

Exercise 8

Il rangera sa chambre quand les poules auront des ___.

Answer

dents

Quand les poules auront des dents = never (when pigs fly).

Exercise 9

Quand ils se sont vus, ça a été le coup de ___.

Answer

foudre

Le coup de foudre = love at first sight.

Exercise 10

Pick the word that turns this into a literal translation.

J'ai une grenouille dans la gorge.

Answer

Wrong word: grenouille.

Corrected: J'ai un chat dans la gorge.

The English frog becomes a French cat.

Exercise 11

Pick the wrong word.

Ça coûte les oreilles de la tête.

Answer

Wrong word: oreilles.

Corrected: Ça coûte les yeux de la tête.

It's the eyes, not the ears.

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

Bon, revenons à nos chèvres.

Answer

Wrong word: chèvres.

Corrected: Bon, revenons à nos moutons.

Revenons à nos moutons = let's get back to the point.

Exercise 13

Match the mood idiom to its meaning.

A B avoir le cafard to sulk être aux anges to be fed up faire la tête to be full of energy en avoir marre to feel down avoir la pêche to be over the moon Answer

avoir le cafard — to feel down; être aux anges — to be over the moon; faire la tête — to sulk; en avoir marre — to be fed up; avoir la pêche — to be full of energy

Feelings idioms are the most frequent in daily talk.

Exercise 14

Match each French idiom to its English equivalent.

A B tourner autour du pot to have bigger fish to fry appeler un chat un chat to kill two birds with one stone avoir d'autres chats à fouetter to beat around the bush faire d'une pierre deux coups to call a spade a spade Answer

tourner autour du pot — to beat around the bush; appeler un chat un chat — to call a spade a spade; avoir d'autres chats à fouetter — to have bigger fish to fry; faire d'une pierre deux coups — to kill two birds with one stone

Equivalents, not translations.

Exercise 15

Put the words in order: 'I'm feeling under the weather.'

Words: mon / dans / pas / suis / ne / assiette / Je

Answer

Je ne suis pas dans mon assiette

ne… pas around the verb, then dans mon assiette.

Exercise 16

Put the words in order: 'It's freezing cold.'

Words: de / Il / fait / un / froid / canard

Answer

Il fait un froid de canard

Weather uses il fait.

Exercise 17

Say it aloud.

Ce n'est pas la mer à boire

Answer

It's not that hard.

Exercise 18

Say it aloud.

Arrête de tourner autour du pot

Answer

Stop beating around the bush.

Next step

Many of these idioms are familier. Learn exactly where each register belongs — and the slang and verlan young French people use — in Registers & slang.

docs.title: Chapter 22: Imparfait vs passé composé
docs.text:
l’imparfait

A story has two layers: the scene (it was raining, I was tired, people were waiting) and the events (suddenly the door opened, someone shouted). French gives each layer its own tense. The passé composé tells the events; the imparfait paints the scene. Learn the easiest conjugation in French, then learn to choose.

In one line

Imparfait = the scene, the habit, what was going on. Passé composé = the event, what happened.

  • Il pleuvait et j’étais fatigué. — It was raining and I was tired. (scene) [eel pluh-Vɛ]
  • Quand j’étais petit, je jouais au cricket. — When I was little, I used to play cricket. (habit) [zhay-Tɛ puh-TEE]
  • Je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné. — I was sleeping when the phone rang. (background + event)

docs.title: 22.1 Forming the imparfait: one stem, one set of endings
docs.text:
Take the nous form of the present tense, remove -ons, and add the endings. This works for every verb in French except one (être, section 2).

Infinitive nous (present) Imparfait stem parler nous parlons parl- finir nous finissons finiss- faire nous faisons fais- [fuh-Z…] avoir nous avons av- prendre nous prenons pren- boire nous buvons buv- aller nous allons all- Subject Ending parler avoir je -ais je parlais j’avais tu -ais tu parlais tu avais il / elle / on -ait il parlait elle avait nous -ions nous parlions nous avions vous -iez vous parliez vous aviez ils / elles -aient ils parlaient elles avaient

Five endings, one sound

-ais, -ais, -ait, -aient all sound exactly the same: [ɛ], like “e” in “bed”. je parlais, il parlait, ils parlaient = [par-Lɛ]. Only nous and vous sound different.

  • Nous habitions à Kolkata. — We lived (used to live) in Kolkata. [noo‿za-bee-TYÕ]
  • Ils faisaient du bruit. — They were making noise. [eel fuh-Zɛ]
  • Tu prenais le métro tous les jours ? — Did you take the metro every day?

docs.title: Small spelling adjustments
docs.text: Verbs in -ger keep an e before a (je mangeais, but nous mangions); verbs in -cer take ç before a (je commençais, but nous commencions). Verbs in -ier get a double i: nous étudiions, vous étudiiez. These keep the sound regular.

docs.title: 22.2 The one irregular: être → ét-
docs.text:
Nous sommes has no -ons to remove, so être has its own stem: ét-. The endings are the same.

Subject être Example je / j’ j’étais J’étais content. tu tu étais Tu étais où ? il / elle / on il était C’était génial ! nous nous étions Nous étions en retard. vous vous étiez Vous étiez à la réunion ? ils / elles ils étaient Elles étaient sœurs.
  • C’était comment, le concert ? — C’était génial ! — How was the concert? — It was brilliant! [say-Tɛ zhay-nyal]

docs.title: Impersonal verbs you will use constantly
docs.text:
Present Imparfait Meaning il y a il y avait there was / there were il fait beau il faisait beau the weather was nice il pleut il pleuvait it was raining il faut il fallait it was necessary, we had to c’est c’était it was
  • Il y avait beaucoup de monde au marché. — There were lots of people at the market. [eel-ya-VɛT]

docs.title: 22.3 Use 1 — description: the scene
docs.text:
Use the imparfait to describe how things were: weather, time, age, appearance, feelings, states of mind. These have no clear beginning or end in the story.

  • Il était huit heures du soir. Il faisait froid. — It was eight in the evening. It was cold.
  • J’avais dix-huit ans et je ne connaissais personne à Paris. — I was eighteen and I didn’t know anyone in Paris.
  • La maison était grande et le jardin sentait les roses. — The house was big and the garden smelled of roses.
  • Elle avait les cheveux longs et elle portait un sari bleu. — She had long hair and she was wearing a blue sari.
  • J’avais faim, mais je voulais finir mon travail. — I was hungry, but I wanted to finish my work.

Careful

  • Wrong: Quand j’ai été petit, j’ai habité à Goa.
  • Right: Quand j’étais petit, j’habitais à Goa.
  • Why: Childhood is a background period, not an event. Quand j’étais petit(e) is always imparfait.

docs.title: 22.4 Use 2 — habits: “used to” and “would”
docs.text:
English says “I used to walk to school” or “every summer we would go to the village”. French simply uses the imparfait. Hindi does something similar: “main school paidal jaata tha”.

  • Tous les étés, on allait chez ma grand-mère. — Every summer we would go to my grandmother’s.
  • D’habitude, je me levais à cinq heures. — I usually got up at five.
  • Le dimanche, mon père préparait des dosas pour tout le monde. — On Sundays my father used to make dosas for everyone.
  • À l’époque, on n’avait pas de portable. — Back then, we didn’t have mobile phones.

Signal words for the imparfait

d’habitude, souvent, toujours, tous les jours, chaque été, le lundi, autrefois, à l’époque, quand j’étais petit(e), pendant que — repetition or background.

docs.title: 22.5 Use 3 — the action in progress: “was doing”
docs.text:
The imparfait describes an action that was going on at a moment in the past — often when something else (an event, in passé composé) interrupts it.

Figure 22.1. The wave keeps going; the lightning bolt happens once. Imparfait is the wave, passé composé is the bolt.
  • Je prenais ma douche quand tu as appelé. — I was having a shower when you called.
  • Pendant que les enfants dormaient, nous préparions la fête. — While the children were sleeping, we were getting the party ready. (two backgrounds)
  • Il traversait la rue quand il est tombé. — He was crossing the road when he fell.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je lisais quand soudain le téléphone sonnait.
  • Right: Je lisais quand soudain le téléphone a sonné.
  • Why: Soudain announces a single event that breaks in: passé composé.

docs.title: 22.6 Choosing: imparfait or passé composé?
docs.text:
Ask yourself one question about each verb: is this an event that moves the story forward, or a description of the situation?

Figure 22.2. Events push the story forward (passé composé). Descriptions, habits and actions in progress hold it still (imparfait).

The closed period

A duration with a clear limit takes the passé composé, even if it was long: J’ai habité à Delhi pendant cinq ans. Without the limit, it is background: J’habitais à Delhi.

docs.title: Same verb, different meaning
docs.text:
Some verbs change meaning slightly between the two tenses — the imparfait gives a state, the passé composé a moment of change.

Imparfait (state) Passé composé (moment) J’avais peur.I was afraid. J’ai eu peur.I got a fright. Je savais la vérité.I knew the truth. J’ai su la vérité.I found out the truth. Je connaissais Paul.I knew Paul. J’ai connu Paul en 2015.I met Paul in 2015. Il devait venir.He was supposed to come. Il a dû partir.He had to leave (and did). Je pouvais le faire.I was able to (in general). J’ai pu le faire.I managed to do it.

Typical choices that go wrong

  • Wrong: L’année dernière, j’allais en France trois fois.
  • Right: L’année dernière, je suis allé en France trois fois.

  • Why: A counted number of times = a series of events → passé composé. (Souvent, without counting, would give imparfait.)

  • Wrong: Hier il a fait beau, alors on se promenait au parc.

  • Right: Hier il faisait beau, alors on s’est promené au parc.

  • Why: The weather is the scene (imparfait); the walk is what you did (passé composé).

  • Wrong: Le film a été long, mais je l’aimais beaucoup.

  • Right: Le film était long, mais il m’a beaucoup plu.
  • Why: Describing the film = imparfait. Your overall reaction to a finished film = passé composé.

docs.title: 22.7 Telling a story with both tenses
docs.text:
Read this short story. Verbs in the imparfait (in italics) build the scene; verbs in the passé composé (in bold) are the events. Read the passé composé verbs alone — you get the plot. Read the imparfait verbs alone — you get the picture.

  • C’était un samedi de juillet. Il faisait très chaud et la plage était pleine. — It was a Saturday in July. It was very hot and the beach was full. (scene)
  • Les enfants jouaient dans l’eau et je lisais sous un parasol. — The children were playing in the water and I was reading under a parasol. (scene)
  • Tout à coup, un chien est arrivé en courant. Il a pris mon sandwich et il est reparti. — Suddenly a dog came running. It took my sandwich and ran off again. (events)
  • Tout le monde a ri. Moi, j’avais encore faim, mais l’histoire était trop drôle. — Everyone laughed. As for me, I was still hungry, but the story was too funny.

The film test

Imagine filming your story. The set and the background action (sun, crowd, children playing) are imparfait. Each new shot where something happens is passé composé.

docs.title: 22.8 Just did, was doing: venir de and être en train de
venir de + infinitive: the recent past
docs.text:
Venir de + infinitive means “to have just done”. In the present it is very common in conversation; in the imparfait it means “had just done”.

  • Je viens de manger, merci. — I’ve just eaten, thanks. [zhuh vyɛ̃ duh mã-ZHAY]
  • Le train vient de partir ! — The train has just left!
  • Je venais de rentrer quand il a appelé. — I had just got home when he called.

Careful

  • Wrong: J’ai juste mangé. (meaning “I’ve just eaten”)
  • Right: Je viens de manger.
  • Why: J’ai juste mangé sounds like “I only ate”. For “just now”, French uses venir de.

docs.title: être en train de + infinitive: in the middle of
docs.text:
To insist that an action is in progress, use être en train de — in the present or the imparfait.

  • Je ne peux pas parler, je suis en train de conduire. — I can’t talk, I’m driving. [ã trɛ̃ duh]
  • On était en train de dîner quand la lumière s’est éteinte. — We were in the middle of dinner when the lights went out.

docs.title: Two polite bonuses
docs.text:
• Si on allait au cinéma ce soir ? — How about going to the cinema tonight? (si + imparfait = a suggestion)
  • Bonjour, je voulais savoir si vous aviez des chambres libres. — Hello, I wanted to know if you had any rooms free. (softer than “je veux”)

docs.title: 22.9 In real life: childhood memories
docs.text:
• — Tu habitais où quand tu étais petite ? — — Where did you live when you were little?
  • — À Jaipur. On avait une grande maison avec une terrasse. Le soir, on y dormait quand il faisait trop chaud. — — In Jaipur. We had a big house with a terrace. In the evening we slept there when it was too hot.
  • — Et pourquoi tu es partie ? — — And why did you leave?
  • — Mon père a trouvé un travail à Bangalore. J’avais douze ans. Au début, j’étais triste, mais je me suis vite fait des amis. — — My father found a job in Bangalore. I was twelve. At first I was sad, but I quickly made friends.

Events: a trouvé, es partie, me suis fait. Scene and habits: habitais, avait, dormait, faisait, avais, étais.

À retenir

  • Imparfait = the scene, the habit, what was going on. Passé composé = the event, what happened.
  • -ais, -ais, -ait, -aient all sound exactly the same: [ɛ], like “e” in “bed”. je parlais, il parlait, ils parlaient = [par-Lɛ]. Only nous and vous sound different.
  • d’habitude, souvent, toujours, tous les jours, chaque été, le lundi, autrefois, à l’époque, quand j’étais petit(e), pendant que — repetition or background.
  • A duration with a clear limit takes the passé composé, even if it was long: J’ai habité à Delhi pendant cinq ans. Without the limit, it is background: J’habitais à Delhi.
  • Imagine filming your story. The set and the background action (sun, crowd, children playing) are imparfait. Each new shot where something happens is passé composé.
  • Tell a five-sentence story about something that happened to you: two imparfait sentences for the scene, three passé composé sentences for the events. Then turn to The future.

docs.title: 22.10 Practice — Imparfait vs passé composé
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Imparfait of nous finissons → je ___

  • finis
  • finissais
  • finirais
  • finissai
Answer

finissais

Stem finiss- (from nous finissons) + -ais.

Exercise 2

Imparfait of être, ils:

  • ils étaient
  • ils êtaient
  • ils sontaient
  • ils étiont
Answer

ils étaient

être has the irregular stem ét- + -aient.

Exercise 3

Quand j'___ petit, j'habitais à Goa.

  • ai été
  • étais
  • suis
  • serai
Answer

étais

Childhood is background: quand j'étais petit.

Exercise 4

Je regardais la télé quand mon frère ___.

  • arrivait
  • est arrivé
  • arrive
  • arrivera
Answer

est arrivé

The event that interrupts the background → passé composé.

Exercise 5

L'année dernière, je ___ à Paris trois fois.

  • allais
  • suis allé
  • vais
  • allait
Answer

suis allé

A counted number of times → passé composé.

Exercise 6

J'ai connu ma femme en 2010 means:

  • I knew my wife in 2010.
  • I met my wife in 2010.
  • I used to know my wife.
  • I know my wife since 2010.
Answer

I met my wife in 2010.

connaître in the passé composé = to meet for the first time.

Exercise 7

Il ___ (faire) très beau ce jour-là.

Hint: weather = scene

Answer

faisait

Description of the weather → imparfait: il faisait.

Exercise 8

Tous les dimanches, nous ___ (manger) chez mes grands-parents.

Hint: nous, habit

Answer

mangions

Habit → imparfait; -ger verb: nous mangions (no e before i).

Exercise 9

Le train ___ de partir ! (has just left)

Answer

vient

venir de + infinitive = to have just done.

Exercise 10

Il y ___ beaucoup de monde. (there were)

Answer

avait

il y a → il y avait in the imparfait.

Exercise 11

Pick the wrong word.

Je lisais quand soudain le téléphone sonnait.

Answer

Wrong word: sonnait.

Corrected: Je lisais quand soudain le téléphone a sonné.

soudain introduces a single event → passé composé.

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

Quand j'ai été jeune, je jouais au foot.

Answer

Wrong word: été.

Corrected: Quand j'étais jeune, je jouais au foot.

quand j'étais jeune: background → imparfait.

Exercise 13

Put the words in order: I was sleeping when you called.

Words: appelé / Je / quand / dormais / as / tu

Answer

Je dormais quand tu as appelé

Background (imparfait) + interrupting event (passé composé).

Exercise 14

Match each sentence to its use.

A B Il pleuvait. event Je jouais au tennis le samedi. had just done Soudain, il est parti. description Je venais de rentrer. habit Answer

Il pleuvait. — description; Je jouais au tennis le samedi. — habit; Soudain, il est parti. — event; Je venais de rentrer. — had just done

Imparfait for scene and habit; passé composé for the event; venir de for the recent past.

Exercise 15

Say it aloud.

Quand j'étais petit je jouais au cricket

Answer

étais and jouais end in the same sound: ɛ.

Exercise 16

Say it aloud.

C'était génial

Answer

The phrase for any good memory: say-Tɛ zhay-NYAL.

Exercise 17

Say it aloud.

Je viens de manger merci

Answer

venir de = have just done.

Next step

Tell a five-sentence story about something that happened to you: two imparfait sentences for the scene, three passé composé sentences for the events. Then turn to The future.

docs.title: Chapter 46: Linking words
docs.text:
Les connecteurs

Connectors are the joints of a sentence: mais, donc, parce que, pourtant. With them, your French stops sounding like a list and starts sounding like thinking. This chapter sorts them by job (adding, contrasting, explaining…), by register (spoken, everyday, formal) — and shows the one thing learners forget: what comes after each one.

Two questions for every connector

1. What is its job and its register? 2. What follows it — an indicative verb, a subjunctive, an infinitive or a noun?

  • Il pleut, mais je sors. — It’s raining, but I’m going out.
  • Il pleut, donc je reste. — It’s raining, so I’m staying in.
  • Bien qu’il pleuve, je sors. — Although it’s raining, I’m going out. (subjunctive after bien que)

docs.title: 46.1 One job, three registers
docs.text:
French often has three connectors for the same job: one for speaking with friends, one neutral one for everyday use, and one formal one for essays, reports and speeches. Using du coup in an exam essay sounds as odd as using par conséquent with your friends at a café.

Figure 46.1. The register grid. Read a row from left to right to “dress up” an idea; mais and donc work in every column.

The safe pair

mais (but) and donc (so) are correct in every register — from a text message to a thesis.

docs.title: 46.2 Adding ideas and giving examples
docs.text:
To add a point, climb the ladder: et → aussi → en plus (spoken) → de plus → en outre / par ailleurs (formal). D’ailleurs adds a point that supports what you just said (“besides, in fact”).

  • Ce quartier est calme. En plus, il y a un grand parc. — This area is quiet. Plus, there’s a big park. (spoken)
  • Le loyer est raisonnable. De plus, l’appartement est lumineux. — The rent is reasonable. What’s more, the flat is bright.
  • Le projet coûte cher. En outre, il prendra trois ans. — The project is expensive. Furthermore, it will take three years. (formal)
  • Je n’ai pas envie de sortir. D’ailleurs, il pleut. — I don’t feel like going out. Besides, it’s raining.
  • Elle parle non seulement anglais, mais aussi hindi et français. — She speaks not only English but also Hindi and French.

To give examples: par exemple, comme (such as), notamment (in particular), tel que (such as — agrees: telle que, tels que, telles que), surtout (above all).

  • J’aime les fruits rouges, notamment les fraises. — I like red berries, especially strawberries.
  • Dans plusieurs pays, comme le Sénégal ou la Belgique, on parle français. — In several countries, such as Senegal or Belgium, people speak French.

Aussi at the start = “therefore”

In the middle, aussi means “also”: Je viens aussi. At the start of a formal sentence, with inversion, it means “so, therefore”: Aussi a-t-il démissionné. To say “Also, …” at the start, use De plus or En plus.

docs.title: 46.3 Contrast: mais, pourtant, cependant…
docs.text:
Connector Meaning Register mais but all par contre on the other hand spoken (purists prefer en revanche) pourtant and yet (surprise!) everyday en revanche on the other hand everyday / formal cependant, toutefois however formal néanmoins nevertheless formal alors que, tandis que whereas, while (+ indicative) all / formal au contraire on the contrary all or now, yet (a new fact in an argument) formal
  • Il est riche, mais il n’est pas heureux. — He is rich, but he isn’t happy.
  • Il a beaucoup travaillé ; pourtant, il a raté l’examen. — He worked hard; and yet he failed the exam.
  • Le plan est intéressant. Cependant, il coûte trop cher. — The plan is interesting. However, it costs too much.
  • C’était difficile ; nous avons néanmoins réussi. — It was difficult; we nevertheless succeeded.
  • La cuisine est excellente ; le service, en revanche, est très lent. — The food is excellent; the service, on the other hand, is very slow.
  • J’adore le thé. Par contre, je déteste le café. — I love tea. Coffee, on the other hand, I hate.
  • Mon frère est grand, alors que ma sœur est petite. — My brother is tall, whereas my sister is short.
  • Tous les hommes sont mortels. Or, Socrate est un homme. Donc Socrate est mortel. — All men are mortal. Now, Socrates is a man. So Socrates is mortal.

Where they sit

mais always opens its clause. pourtant, cependant, toutefois, néanmoins, en revanche can open the sentence or sit after the verb: Il a, cependant, refusé.

Careful

  • Wrong: Tu veux du thé or du café ?
  • Right: Tu veux du thé ou du café ?
  • Why: English “or” is ou. French or is a formal connector meaning “now, yet” in an argument.

docs.title: 46.4 Cause: parce que, car, puisque, comme
docs.text:
All four mean roughly “because”, but each has its own place in the sentence and its own nuance. All take the indicative.

Connector Use it… Example parce que to answer “pourquoi ?”; new information Parce que j’ai faim. car mid-sentence, mostly in writing; never to answer …, car il est tard. puisque cause the listener already knows Puisque tu es là… comme at the start of the sentence Comme il pleuvait, … vu que / étant donné que given that (spoken / formal) Vu qu’il est tard, … en effet new sentence that explains: “indeed, you see” … En effet, il est malade.
  • — Pourquoi tu ne manges pas ? — Parce que je n’ai pas faim. — — Why aren’t you eating? — Because I’m not hungry.
  • Il faut partir tôt, car la route est longue. — We must leave early, for the road is long.
  • Puisque tu es là, aide-moi ! — Since you’re here, help me!
  • Comme il pleuvait, nous sommes restés à l’intérieur. — As it was raining, we stayed inside.
  • Étant donné que les prix augmentent, les gens consomment moins. — Given that prices are rising, people are buying less.
  • Paul ne viendra pas. En effet, il est en déplacement à Lyon. — Paul won’t come. You see, he’s away on business in Lyon.

docs.title: Cause + noun: grâce à, à cause de, en raison de
docs.text:
• J’ai trouvé ce travail grâce à mon oncle. — I found this job thanks to my uncle. (good result)
  • Le match est annulé à cause de la pluie. — The match is cancelled because of the rain. (bad result)
  • Le vol est retardé en raison du brouillard. — The flight is delayed owing to fog. (neutral, official)
  • Faute de temps, je n’ai pas fini. — For lack of time, I didn’t finish.

Careful

  • Wrong: — Pourquoi tu pars ? — Car je suis fatigué.
  • Right: — Pourquoi tu pars ? — Parce que je suis fatigué.
  • Why: Car joins two parts of one sentence. It cannot answer a question or open a sentence; in speech, prefer parce que.

Careful

  • Wrong: J’ai réussi à cause de mon professeur.
  • Right: J’ai réussi grâce à mon professeur.
  • Why: À cause de blames. For a good result, give credit with grâce à.

Careful

  • Wrong: Il dit qu’il est riche. En effet, il n’a pas un sou.
  • Right: Il dit qu’il est riche. En fait, il n’a pas un sou.
  • Why: En effet confirms (“indeed”); en fait contradicts (“actually”). And au fait = “by the way”.

docs.title: 46.5 Consequence: donc, alors, du coup…
docs.text:
• Je pense, donc je suis. — I think, therefore I am. (Descartes)
  • Il n’y avait plus de bus, alors on a pris un taxi. — There were no more buses, so we took a taxi.
  • J’ai raté le train, du coup je suis arrivé en retard. — I missed the train, so I was late. (very spoken — see Real spoken French)
