A B sur in front of sous behind devant between derrière on entre under Answer

sur — on; sous — under; devant — in front of; derrière — behind; entre — between

The core place prepositions.

Exercise 14

Match the time words.

A B il y a deux ans two years from now depuis deux ans for two years (finished) dans deux ans two years ago pendant deux ans for two years (still now) Answer

il y a deux ans — two years ago; depuis deux ans — for two years (still now); dans deux ans — two years from now; pendant deux ans — for two years (finished)

Each word gives a different shape of time.

Exercise 15

Put the words in order.

Words: banque / en / la / face / La / de / poste / est

Answer

La banque est en face de la poste

en face de + place.

Exercise 16

Put the words in order.

Words: en / Je / vais / au / Canada / avion

Answer

Je vais au Canada en avion

au + masculine country; en + transport you sit in.

Exercise 17

Say where you are from.

Je viens d'Inde et j'habite à Paris

Answer

d'Inde (feminine country, vowel); à + city.

Exercise 18

Say it aloud.

La pharmacie est à côté de la banque

Answer

à côté de = next to.

Next step

You have finished Les bases. Next comes Object pronouns — le, la, lui, leur — the first step of building longer sentences. Today, describe where five things in your room are, using sur, sous, devant, à côté de and entre.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Present tense: -er verbs
docs.text:
Le présent des verbes en -er

Around nine French verbs out of ten end in -er: parler, aimer, habiter, travailler… They all follow one pattern, and every new verb French invents (googler, liker) joins this family. Learn this one table and you can use thousands of verbs today. Even better: most of the endings are silent.

In one line

Remove -er and add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent.

docs.title: 10.1 Stem + ending
docs.text:
Every French verb has an infinitive (the dictionary form): parler = to speak. To conjugate, cut off -er to get the stem (parl-), then add the ending that matches the subject.

Subject Ending Parler Sounds like je -e je parle [zhuh PARL] tu -es tu parles [tew PARL] il / elle / on -e il parle [eel PARL] nous -ons nous parlons [noo par-LÕ] vous -ez vous parlez [voo par-LAY] ils / elles -ent ils parlent [eel PARL]
  • Je parle hindi et anglais. — I speak Hindi and English. [zhuh parl een-DEE ay ã-GLEH]
  • Tu parles français ? — Do you speak French? [tew parl frã-SEH]
  • Nous parlons avec le directeur. — We are talking with the director. [noo par-LÕ a-vek luh dee-rek-TUHR]
  • Vous parlez trop vite ! — You speak too fast! [voo par-LAY troh VEET]
  • Elles parlent au téléphone. — They are talking on the phone. [el PARL oh tay-lay-FON]

docs.title: 10.2 Six spellings, only three sounds
docs.text:
Here is the great secret of French verbs: the endings -e, -es, -e, -ent are all silent. So je parle, tu parles, il parle, ils parlent sound exactly the same — and so do elle parle, on parle, elles parlent. Of all the persons, only nous and vous have an ending you can hear.

Figure 10.1. Grey letters are written but never spoken. The -ent of ils parlent is silent — never say “parl-ENT”.

Speaking is easier than writing

To speak, you only need three sounds per verb: the stem [parl], nous [-õ] and vous [-ay]. The silent letters matter only when you write.

docs.title: Verbs that start with a vowel
docs.text:
With aimer, habiter, écouter, arriver…, je becomes j’, and you get a liaison with nous, vous, ils, elles. Here the plural is audible: il aime [ee-LEM] vs ils‿aiment [eel-ZEM].

  • J’habite à Delhi. — I live in Delhi. [zha-BEET a deh-LEE]
  • Nous‿aimons le cinéma. — We love cinema. [noo-zeh-MÕ luh see-nay-MA]
  • Ils‿écoutent de la musique. — They are listening to music. [eel-zay-KOOT duh la mew-ZEEK]
  • Elle arrive ce soir. — She arrives this evening. [eh-la-REEV suh SWAR]

docs.title: 10.3 Thirty -er verbs to start with
docs.text:
Verb English Verb English parler to speak aimer to like, love habiter to live (in) travailler to work regarder to watch, look at écouter to listen to chercher to look for trouver to find donner to give demander to ask penser to think oublier to forget arriver to arrive rester to stay entrer to go in rentrer to go home jouer to play étudier to study cuisiner to cook marcher to walk, to work (a machine) fermer to close commander to order aider to help visiter to visit (a place) téléphoner (à) to phone coûter to cost porter to wear, carry laver to wash danser to dance chanter to sing

Only one -er verb is irregular: aller (to go) — see Present tense: the rest.

  • Je cherche la gare. — I’m looking for the station. (chercher — no “for” in French) [zhuh SHERSH la GAR]
  • Tu regardes la télé ? — Are you watching TV? [tew ruh-GARD la tay-LAY]
  • Mon frère travaille dans une banque. — My brother works in a bank. [mõ FREHR tra-VAÏ dã-zewn BÃK]
  • Les enfants jouent au cricket. — The children play cricket. (jouer à + sport) [lay-zã-FÃ ZHOO oh kree-KET]
  • Vous étudiez le français depuis quand ? — How long have you been studying French? [voo-zay-tew-DYAY … duh-pwee KÃ]
  • Ça coûte combien ? — How much does it cost? [sa KOOT kõ-BYɛ̃]

No extra preposition

chercher = look for, écouter = listen to, regarder = look at, attendre = wait for: the English preposition is already inside the French verb. J’écoute la radio, not “j’écoute à la radio”.

docs.title: 10.4 Spelling-change verbs: the “boot”
docs.text:
Some -er verbs are regular in sound but change their spelling to keep the pronunciation right. Most changes happen in the four silent-ending forms — je, tu, il, ils — the shape of a boot. Nous and vous stay outside.

Figure 10.2. The same boot works for acheter (è), appeler (ll), préférer (è) and payer (i).

docs.title: Type 1: -ger and -cer — only nous changes
docs.text:
These are the exception to the boot. Before -ons, a g would sound hard [g] and a c would sound like [k]. So French adds an e after g and turns c into ç — only in the nous form.

Verb je / il / ils nous Also manger (eat) je mange nous mangeons nager, voyager, changer, partager commencer (begin) je commence nous commençons lancer, placer, avancer
  • Nous mangeons à midi. — We eat at noon. [noo mã-ZHÕ a mee-DEE]
  • Nous commençons à neuf heures. — We start at nine o’clock. [noo ko-mã-SÕ a nuh-VUHR]
  • Nous voyageons en Inde chaque année. — We travel to India every year. [noo vwa-ya-ZHÕ ã-Nɛ̃D]

docs.title: Type 2: e → è (acheter) and é → è (préférer)
docs.text:
Verb Inside the boot nous / vous Also acheter (buy) j’achète, ils achètent nous achetons lever, emmener, se promener préférer (prefer) je préfère, ils préfèrent nous préférons espérer, répéter, compléter
  • J’achète du pain tous les matins. — I buy bread every morning. [zha-SHET dew Pɛ̃]
  • Vous achetez les billets ? — Are you buying the tickets? [voo-zash-TAY lay bee-YEH]
  • Je préfère le thé, mais nous préférons tous le café. — I prefer tea, but we all prefer coffee. [zhuh pray-FEHR … noo pray-fay-RÕ]
  • J’espère que tu vas bien. — I hope you’re well. [zhes-PEHR kuh tew va BYɛ̃]

docs.title: Type 3: double consonant (appeler, jeter)
docs.text:
Verb Inside the boot nous / vous appeler (call) j’appelle, tu appelles, ils appellent nous appelons, vous appelez jeter (throw) je jette, ils jettent nous jetons, vous jetez
  • Je t’appelle ce soir. — I’ll call you tonight. (present for a near future) [zhuh ta-PEL suh SWAR]
  • Comment vous vous appelez ? — Je m’appelle Rohan. — What’s your name? — My name is Rohan. (s’appeler is reflexive — see Reflexive verbs) [voo voo-za-PLAY … zhuh ma-PEL]

docs.title: Type 4: -yer → -ie (payer, envoyer, nettoyer)
docs.text:
Inside the boot, y becomes i: j’envoie, je nettoie, j’essaie. With -ayer verbs both spellings are correct: je paie or je paye.

  • Je paie par carte. — I’m paying by card. [zhuh PEH par KART]
  • Nous payons en liquide. — We’re paying in cash. [noo peh-YÕ ã lee-KEED]
  • Elle envoie un message à sa mère. — She’s sending a message to her mother. [eh-lã-VWA ɛ̃ meh-SAZH]

The boot rule

Spelling changes (achète, appelle, préfère, paie) happen in je, tu, il, ils; nous and vous keep the infinitive stem — except mangeons, commençons.

docs.title: 10.5 What the present tense means
docs.text:
French has one present tense where English has two. Je mange means both “I eat” and “I am eating”. There is no “-ing” form to add — and you never use être to make one.

Use French English right now Je regarde un film. I’m watching a film. habit Je regarde un film le vendredi. I watch a film on Fridays. general truth Les Français mangent tard. The French eat late. near future Je rentre demain. I’m coming home tomorrow. since + still true J’habite ici depuis 2020. I’ve lived here since 2020.
  • Chut ! Le bébé dort et je travaille. — Shh! The baby is sleeping and I’m working. [SHEWT … zhuh tra-VAÏ]
  • Je suis en train de cuisiner. — I’m (busy) cooking right now. — être en train de + infinitive stresses “in the middle of” [zhuh swee-zã TRɛ̃ duh kwee-zee-NAY]

docs.title: Depuis: present tense for “have been”
docs.text:
For an action that started in the past and is still going on, French uses the present with depuis. English uses “have been … for/since”. Hindi works exactly like French here: main do saal se French seekh raha hoon — present tense + “se”.

  • J’étudie le français depuis deux ans. — I have been studying French for two years. [zhay-tew-DEE … duh-PWEE duh-ZÃ]
  • Elle habite à Paris depuis 2019. — She has lived in Paris since 2019.
  • Tu m’attends depuis longtemps ? — Non, depuis cinq minutes. — Have you been waiting for me long? — No, for five minutes. (attendre is an -re verb)

Depuis + present

Still true now? Use present + depuis: j’habite ici depuis trois ans = I have lived here for three years.

docs.title: 10.6 Mistakes learners really make
docs.text:
The -er traps

  • Wrong: Je suis parle au téléphone.
  • Right: Je parle au téléphone.

  • Why: French has no “am + -ing”. The simple present already means “I am talking”.

  • Wrong: Nous mangons ensemble.

  • Right: Nous mangeons ensemble.

  • Why: Keep the soft g sound before -ons: mangeons, voyageons, nageons.

  • Wrong: Ils parlent [par-LÃ] anglais.

  • Right: Ils parlent [PARL] anglais.

  • Why: The verb ending -ent is completely silent. (It is pronounced only in nouns/adverbs like le moment, lentement.)

  • Wrong: J’achete une robe. / Je m’apelle Anil.

  • Right: J’achète une robe. / Je m’appelle Anil.

  • Why: Inside the boot: acheter → achète (è), appeler → appelle (ll).

  • Wrong: J’ai habité ici depuis cinq ans. (still living here)

  • Right: J’habite ici depuis cinq ans.

  • Why: If it is still true, French uses the present with depuis — not a past tense.

  • Wrong: Je cherche pour mes clés.

  • Right: Je cherche mes clés.

  • Why: chercher already means “look for”. No pour.

  • Wrong: Je aime le cricket.

  • Right: J’aime le cricket.
  • Why: je → j’ before a vowel or silent h: j’aime, j’habite, j’écoute.

docs.title: 10.7 In real life — a typical day
docs.text:
Read it aloud. Every verb is a regular -er verb (except one — can you find it?).

  • Le matin, je commence à huit heures. — In the morning, I start at eight.
  • Je travaille dans un bureau et je parle souvent anglais. — I work in an office and I often speak English.
  • À midi, mes collègues et moi, nous mangeons ensemble. — At noon, my colleagues and I eat together.
  • Le soir, je rentre à pied et j’achète des légumes. — In the evening, I walk home and buy vegetables.
  • Ma femme cuisine, et moi, je fais la vaisselle. — My wife cooks, and I do the washing-up. (faire is the irregular one!)
  • Après, on regarde une série et on appelle nos parents en Inde. — Afterwards, we watch a series and call our parents in India.

À retenir

  • Remove -er and add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent.
  • To speak, you only need three sounds per verb: the stem [parl], nous [-õ] and vous [-ay]. The silent letters matter only when you write.
  • Spelling changes (achète, appelle, préfère, paie) happen in je, tu, il, ils; nous and vous keep the infinitive stem — except mangeons, commençons.
  • Still true now? Use present + depuis: j’habite ici depuis trois ans = I have lived here for three years.
  • You have the regular pattern. The other verbs — finir, vendre, aller, faire, prendre and friends — are in Present tense: the rest. Today, describe your day in five -er verbs.

docs.title: 10.8 Practice — -er verbs
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Vous ___ (habiter) à Lyon ?

  • habite
  • habitez
  • habitons
  • habitent
Answer

habitez

vous → -ez: vous habitez.

Exercise 2

Which form is NOT pronounced [PARL]?

  • je parle
  • tu parles
  • ils parlent
  • vous parlez
Answer

vous parlez

vous parlez = [par-LAY]. The others all sound [PARL].

Exercise 3

Nous ___ (manger) au restaurant.

  • mangons
  • mangeons
  • mangez
  • mangent
Answer

mangeons

-ger verbs keep an e before -ons: mangeons.

Exercise 4

Tu ___ (acheter) le pain ?

  • acheter
  • achetes
  • achètes
  • achètez
Answer

achètes

Inside the boot (tu), e → è: tu achètes.

Exercise 5

'I have been working here for six months.'

  • J'ai travaillé ici depuis six mois.
  • Je travaille ici depuis six mois.
  • Je suis travaille ici six mois.
  • Je travaille ici pour six mois.
Answer

Je travaille ici depuis six mois.

Still true now → present + depuis.

Exercise 6

Nous ___ (commencer) à neuf heures.

Hint: c before -ons

Answer

commençons

c → ç before o: commençons.

Exercise 7

Je m'___ (appeler) Sara.

Hint: double consonant

Answer

appelle

appeler → j'appelle (ll inside the boot).

Exercise 8

Elles ___ (préférer) le train.

Hint: é → è in the boot

Answer

préfèrent / preferent

ils/elles préfèrent — è inside the boot.

Exercise 9

Je ___ (payer) par carte.

Hint: y → i (or keep y)

Answer

paie / paye

Both je paie and je paye are correct.

Exercise 10

Ils ___ (écouter) la radio.

Answer

écoutent / ecoutent

ils → -ent (silent): ils écoutent, with liaison ils‿écoutent.

Exercise 11

Pick the wrong word.

Je suis regarde la télé.

Answer

Wrong word: suis.

Corrected: Je regarde la télé.

No être + verb for '-ing'. The present alone is enough.

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

Nous nagons dans la mer.

Answer

Wrong word: nagons.

Corrected: Nous nageons dans la mer.

-ger verbs: nageons.

Exercise 13

Match the verb to its meaning.

A B chercher to listen to regarder to find écouter to look for trouver to look at, watch Answer

chercher — to look for; regarder — to look at, watch; écouter — to listen to; trouver — to find

The English preposition is built into the French verb.

Exercise 14

Put the words in order.

Words: à / ans / depuis / J'habite / Mumbai / dix

Answer

J'habite à Mumbai depuis dix ans

present + depuis + duration.

Exercise 15

Put the words in order.

Words: ensemble / le / dimanche / mangeons / Nous

Answer

Nous mangeons ensemble le dimanche

le dimanche = every Sunday.

Exercise 16

Say it aloud — keep -ent silent.

Ils parlent français et ils aiment Paris

Answer

parlent [PARL]; ils‿aiment [eel-ZEM].

Exercise 17

Say it aloud.

J'étudie le français depuis trois mois

Answer

Present + depuis for an action still going on.

Next step

You have the regular pattern. The other verbs — finir, vendre, aller, faire, prendre and friends — are in Present tense: the rest. Today, describe your day in five -er verbs.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Present tense: the rest
docs.text:
Le présent : -ir, -re et irréguliers

The -er verbs are the big regular family. The verbs in this chapter are fewer — but they are the ones you say fifty times a day: je vais, je fais, je peux, je veux, je prends. They look chaotic at first. They are not: a handful of patterns covers almost all of them, and this chapter shows you those patterns.

In one line

Most non -er verbs end in -s, -s, -t in the singular and -ons, -ez, -ent in the plural; what changes is the stem.

docs.title: 11.1 The two other regular families: finir and vendre
-ir verbs like finir (they add -iss- in the plural)
docs.text: About 300 verbs in -ir follow finir. The singular is short; the plural adds -iss-. Others: choisir (choose), réussir (succeed, pass), grandir (grow up), réfléchir (think it over), remplir (fill), obéir à (obey).

docs.title: -re verbs like vendre (no ending at all for il)
docs.text:
vendre (sell) has the classic endings, and nothing for il/elle: il vend. Others: attendre (wait for), entendre (hear), répondre (answer), perdre (lose), descendre (go down), rendre (give back).

finir vendre Endings je finis vends -is / -s tu finis vends -is / -s il / elle / on finit vend -it / — nous finissons vendons -issons / -ons vous finissez vendez -issez / -ez ils / elles finissent vendent -issent / -ent
  • Je finis à six heures. — I finish at six. [zhuh fee-NEE a see-ZUHR]
  • Les enfants grandissent vite. — Children grow up fast. [lay-zã-FÃ grã-DEES VEET]
  • Vous choisissez quel menu ? — Which menu are you choosing? [voo shwa-zee-SAY kel muh-NEW]
  • J’attends le bus. — I’m waiting for the bus. (attendre = wait for, no “pour”) [zha-TÃ luh BEWS]
  • Il répond au téléphone. — He answers the phone. (répondre à) [eel ray-PÕ oh tay-lay-FON]
  • Ils vendent des fruits au marché. — They sell fruit at the market. [eel VÃD day FRWEE]

Here you can hear the plural

With most of these verbs the ils form sounds different: il vend [VÃ] / ils vendent [VÃD], il finit [fee-NEE] / ils finissent [fee-NEES].

docs.title: 11.2 Aller and faire — go and do
docs.text:
aller (go) faire (do, make) je vais fais tu vas fais il / elle / on va fait nous allons faisons [fuh-ZÕ] vous allez faites [FET] ils / elles vont font

Aller is the only irregular -er verb. It also builds the near future: je vais partir = I’m going to leave (see The future).

  • Je vais au bureau en métro. — I go to the office by metro. [zhuh VAY oh bew-ROH ã may-TROH]
  • Comment allez-vous ? — Ça va bien, merci. — How are you? — I’m fine, thanks. [ko-mã-ta-lay-VOO … sa va BYɛ̃]
  • Ils vont visiter Paris demain. — They are going to visit Paris tomorrow. [eel VÕ vee-zee-TAY]
  • Qu’est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ? — What are you doing this weekend? [kes-kuh tew FEH suh wee-KEND]
  • Nous faisons du yoga le matin. — We do yoga in the morning. (faire du / de la + activity) [noo fuh-ZÕ dew yo-GA]
  • Il fait beau aujourd’hui. — The weather is nice today. (weather = il fait) [eel feh BOH oh-zhoor-DWEE]
  • Qu’est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ? — What do you do (for a living)? [kes-kuh voo FET dã la VEE]

docs.title: 11.3 Venir and tenir — come and hold
docs.text:
venir (come) tenir (hold) je viens tiens tu viens tiens il / elle / on vient tient nous venons tenons vous venez tenez ils / elles viennent tiennent

Same pattern: revenir (come back), devenir (become), obtenir (obtain), appartenir (belong).

  • Je viens de Chennai. — I come from Chennai. [zhuh VYɛ̃ duh shuh-NAÏ]
  • Tu viens avec nous ? — Are you coming with us? [tew VYɛ̃ a-vek NOO]
  • Ils viennent dîner samedi. — They’re coming to dinner on Saturday. [eel VYEN dee-NAY]
  • Je viens d’arriver. — I have just arrived. (venir de + infinitive = to have just done) [zhuh VYɛ̃ da-ree-VAY]
  • Tiens, voilà ton café ! — Here, there’s your coffee! (tiens / tenez = “here, take it”) [TYɛ̃ vwa-LA tõ ka-FAY]

docs.title: 11.4 Pouvoir, vouloir, devoir — can, want, must
docs.text:
These three are followed directly by an infinitive, with no “to”: je peux venir = I can come.

pouvoir (can) vouloir (want) devoir (must) je peux veux dois tu peux veux dois il / elle / on peut veut doit nous pouvons voulons devons vous pouvez voulez devez ils / elles peuvent veulent doivent
  • Je peux entrer ? — Can I come in? [zhuh PUH ã-TRAY]
  • Vous pouvez répéter, s’il vous plaît ? — Can you repeat, please? (the learner’s best friend) [voo poo-VAY ray-pay-TAY]
  • Elle veut apprendre le français. — She wants to learn French. [el VUH a-PRÃDR]
  • Les enfants veulent une glace. — The children want an ice cream. [lay-zã-FÃ VUHL ewn GLAS]
  • Je dois partir à cinq heures. — I have to leave at five. [zhuh DWA par-TEER a sɛ̃-KUHR]
  • Nous devons payer maintenant ? — Do we have to pay now? [noo duh-VÕ peh-YAY mɛ̃t-NÃ]
  • Je te dois combien ? — How much do I owe you? (devoir + noun = to owe)

Polite: je voudrais

Je veux (I want) can sound rude in a shop. Say je voudrais (I would like) — the conditional of vouloir, explained in Conditional & si clauses.

docs.title: 11.5 Savoir or connaître? Two ways to “know”
docs.text:
savoir connaître je sais connais tu sais connais il / elle / on sait connaît (also connait) nous savons connaissons vous savez connaissez ils / elles savent connaissent Figure 11.1. Hindi makes a similar split: pata hona (to know a fact) versus jaanna / pehchaanna (to know a person).
  • Tu sais nager ? — Can you swim? (know how to) [tew SEH na-ZHAY]
  • Je ne sais pas où est la gare. — I don’t know where the station is. [zhuh nuh seh PA oo eh la GAR]
  • Vous connaissez un bon restaurant indien ? — Do you know a good Indian restaurant? [voo ko-neh-SAY ɛ̃ bõ res-to-RÃ ɛ̃-DYɛ̃]
  • Elle connaît bien Marseille. — She knows Marseille well. [el ko-NEH byɛ̃ mar-SEY]

savoir vs connaître

savoir + infinitive / que / question word / fact (je sais nager); connaître + person, place or thing (je connais Paul).

docs.title: 11.6 Prendre, mettre, dire, voir
docs.text:
prendre (take) mettre (put) je prends mets tu prends mets il / elle / on prend met nous prenons mettons vous prenez mettez ils / elles prennent mettent

Family: apprendre (learn), comprendre (understand); promettre (promise), permettre (allow).

  • Je prends le train de 8 heures. — I take the 8 o’clock train. [zhuh PRÃ luh TRɛ̃]
  • Qu’est-ce que vous prenez ? — Je prends un thé. — What will you have? — I’ll have a tea. (prendre = to have food or drink)
  • Pardon, je ne comprends pas. — Sorry, I don’t understand. [par-DÕ zhuh nuh kõ-PRÃ PA]
  • Ils apprennent le hindi. — They are learning Hindi. (double n: apprennent) [eel-za-PREN]
  • Je mets mon manteau. — I’m putting on my coat. [zhuh MEH mõ mã-TOH]
dire (say) voir (see) je dis vois tu dis vois il / elle / on dit voit nous disons voyons vous dites voyez ils / elles disent voient

croire (believe) works like voir: je crois, nous croyons, ils croient. Careful: vous dites, but its family says vous interdisez, vous contredisez.

  • Qu’est-ce que tu dis ? — What are you saying? [kes-kuh tew DEE]
  • Comment dit-on « thank you » en français ? — How do you say “thank you” in French? [ko-mã dee-TÕ]
  • Vous dites toujours la vérité. — You always tell the truth. [voo DEET too-ZHOOR la vay-ree-TAY]
  • Je vois la tour Eiffel d’ici ! — I can see the Eiffel Tower from here! (French often drops “can” with see/hear) [zhuh VWA la toor eh-FEL dee-SEE]
  • On se voit demain ? — See you tomorrow? (lit. “we see each other tomorrow?”) [õ suh VWA duh-Mɛ̃]

docs.title: 11.7 Partir, sortir, dormir — drop a consonant
docs.text:
These verbs lose the last consonant of the stem in the singular: part-ir → je pars, dorm-ir → je dors. The consonant comes back in the plural. Also: sentir (je sens), servir (je sers), mentir (je mens).

partir (leave) sortir (go out) dormir (sleep) je pars sors dors tu pars sors dors il / elle / on part sort dort nous partons sortons dormons vous partez sortez dormez ils / elles partent sortent dorment
  • Le train part dans dix minutes. — The train leaves in ten minutes. [luh TRɛ̃ PAR dã dee mee-NEWT]
  • Vous sortez ce soir ? — Are you going out tonight? [voo sor-TAY suh SWAR]
  • Je dors mal quand il fait chaud. — I sleep badly when it’s hot. [zhuh DOR MAL kã-teel feh SHOH]
  • Les enfants dorment déjà. — The children are already asleep. (the m is back) [lay-zã-FÃ DORM day-ZHA]

docs.title: 11.8 The patterns that tame them all
docs.text:
Figure 11.2. Four rules cover nearly every irregular present. Learn the “famous few” as a chant: sont, ont, vont, font — êtes, faites, dites.

The famous few

Only sont, ont, vont, font end in -ont; only êtes, faites, dites are vous forms without -ez.

Learn three forms, not six

For each irregular verb, memorise je, nous and ils (je viens, nous venons, ils viennent). The other three follow from these.

docs.title: 11.9 Mistakes learners really make
docs.text:
Irregular verb traps

  • Wrong: Vous faisez du sport ?
  • Right: Vous faites du sport ?

  • Why: One of the three vous forms without -ez: êtes, faites, dites.

  • Wrong: Ils allent au cinéma.

  • Right: Ils vont au cinéma.

  • Why: aller is the one irregular -er verb: ils vont.

  • Wrong: Je connais nager.

  • Right: Je sais nager.

  • Why: Before an infinitive (a skill), use savoir.

  • Wrong: Je sais ta sœur.

  • Right: Je connais ta sœur.

  • Why: A person → connaître.

  • Wrong: Je veux à partir. / Je peux de venir.

  • Right: Je veux partir. / Je peux venir.

  • Why: pouvoir, vouloir, devoir are followed directly by the infinitive.

  • Wrong: Ils prenent le bus.

  • Right: Ils prennent le bus.

  • Why: Double n in the ils form: prennent, apprennent, comprennent (like viennent).

  • Wrong: Il partit demain.

  • Right: Il part demain.
  • Why: partir is not like finir: il part, not “partit”. Only finir-type verbs add -it.

Real-life lines you will hear constantly:

  • — On va au cinéma ? Tu veux venir ? — Shall we go to the cinema? Do you want to come?
  • — Je ne peux pas, je dois finir un rapport. Mais je connais un bon film pour samedi ! — I can’t, I have to finish a report. But I know a good film for Saturday!

À retenir

  • Most non -er verbs end in -s, -s, -t in the singular and -ons, -ez, -ent in the plural; what changes is the stem.
  • With most of these verbs the ils form sounds different: il vend [VÃ] / ils vendent [VÃD], il finit [fee-NEE] / ils finissent [fee-NEES].
  • Je veux (I want) can sound rude in a shop. Say je voudrais (I would like) — the conditional of vouloir, explained in Conditional & si clauses.
  • savoir + infinitive / que / question word / fact (je sais nager); connaître + person, place or thing (je connais Paul).
  • Only sont, ont, vont, font end in -ont; only êtes, faites, dites are vous forms without -ez.
  • For each irregular verb, memorise je, nous and ils (je viens, nous venons, ils viennent). The other three follow from these.

docs.title: 11.10 Practice — Irregular present
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Vous ___ (faire) quoi ce soir ?

  • faisez
  • faites
  • faisons
  • font
Answer

faites

vous faites — one of the three vous forms without -ez.

Exercise 2

Ils ___ (aller) à la plage.

  • allent
  • vont
  • vas
  • allons
Answer

vont

aller: ils vont.

Exercise 3

Je ___ jouer du piano.

  • connais
  • sais
  • sait
  • connaît

Hint: a skill + infinitive

Answer

sais

savoir + infinitive = know how to.

Exercise 4

Tu ___ mon frère ?

  • sais
  • connais
  • sait
  • savez

Hint: a person

Answer

connais

connaître + person.

Exercise 5

Ils ___ (pouvoir) venir demain.

  • peuvent
  • pouvent
  • peut
  • pouvez
Answer

peuvent

pouvoir: ils peuvent (strong stem peu- + v).

Exercise 6

Je ___ (venir) de finir.

  • viens
  • vient
  • venons
  • vais

Hint: I have just finished.

Answer

viens

venir de + infinitive: je viens de finir = I've just finished.

Exercise 7

Nous ___ (finir) à cinq heures.

Hint: -iss-

Answer

finissons

finir-type verbs add -iss- in the plural: finissons.

Exercise 8

Elle ___ (attendre) le bus.

Hint: -re verb, il/elle

Answer

attend

-re verbs: il/elle + stem with no ending: elle attend.

Exercise 9

Ils ___ (prendre) le métro.

Hint: double n

Answer

prennent

prendre: ils prennent.

Exercise 10

Je ___ (dormir) huit heures par nuit.

Hint: drop the m

Answer

dors

dormir: je dors (stem consonant dropped in the singular).

Exercise 11

Vous ___ (dire) la vérité ?

Answer

dites

vous dites — no -ez.

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

Nous devons de partir maintenant.

Answer

Wrong word: de.

Corrected: Nous devons partir maintenant.

devoir + infinitive directly, no de.

Exercise 13

Pick the wrong word.

Elles veulent prenent un taxi.

Answer

Wrong word: prenent.

Corrected: Elles veulent prendre un taxi.

After vouloir, the second verb stays in the infinitive: prendre.

Exercise 14

Match the infinitive to its ils form.

A B venir ils veulent devoir ils font vouloir ils viennent faire ils doivent Answer

venir — ils viennent; devoir — ils doivent; vouloir — ils veulent; faire — ils font

Learn the ils form of each irregular verb by heart.

Exercise 15

Put the words in order.

Words: s'il / vous / Vous / plaît / répéter / pouvez

Answer

Vous pouvez répéter s'il vous plaît

pouvoir + infinitive: vous pouvez répéter.

Exercise 16

Put the words in order.

Words: cette / Je / ne / connais / pas / ville

Answer

Je ne connais pas cette ville

connaître + a place.

Exercise 17

Say it aloud.

Pardon je ne comprends pas

Answer

comprendre: je comprends [kõ-PRÃ].

Exercise 18

Say it aloud — chant the famous few.

Ils sont ils ont ils vont ils font

Answer

The only four verbs ending in -ont.

Next step

You can now conjugate almost any verb in the present. Next, learn to turn every sentence negative in Saying no. Daily drill: pick one verb from this chapter and say je / nous / ils aloud five times.

docs.title: Chapter 34: Pronunciation clinic
docs.text:
Atelier de prononciation

In The sounds of French you met every sound once. This chapter is the gym. We drill minimal pairs — two words that differ by one sound only, like dessus (on top) and dessous (underneath). If you mix them up, you say the opposite of what you mean. Then we work on the music of French: stress, melody and rhythm.

The clinic method

Listen → say → contrast. Play word A, then word B, then say both, A–B–A–B, until your mouth feels the difference. One pair, five minutes, every day.

docs.title: 34.1 u vs ou — the lip pair
docs.text:
This is the pair that matters most. ou [oo] is like English "food". u [ew] has no English equivalent: say "ee", keep your tongue exactly there, and push your lips forward into a tight round "kiss". Tongue front, lips round.

u = 'ee' with kissing lips

For u, the tongue stays forward as for "ee"; only the lips round. For ou, the tongue pulls back. In a mirror the lips look the same — the difference is inside.

u [ew] ou [oo] Meanings dessus dessous on top / underneath tu tout you / all vu vous seen / you (formal) la rue la roue the street / the wheel pur pour pure / for lu loup read (past) / wolf su sous known / under

Now the pair inside sentences. Say each one three times, slowly, then at normal speed.

  • Le chat est dessus, pas dessous. — The cat is on top, not underneath. [luh sha ay duh-SEW, pa duh-SOO]
  • Tu as tout vu ? — Did you see everything? [tew a too VEW]
  • Vous avez vu la roue dans la rue ? — Did you see the wheel in the street?
  • C’est pour toi, c’est du jus pur. — It’s for you, it’s pure juice.
  • Je ne savais pas où tu étais. — I didn’t know where you were.

Careful

  • Wrong: Le livre est dessous la table.
  • Right: Le livre est sous la table. / Il est dessous.
  • Why: Sur and sous come before a noun. Dessus and dessous stand alone, with no noun after them.

Hindi helps here

Hindi "ऊ" (as in phool) is a good French ou. For u, say "ई" (ee) and round your lips without moving the tongue. English "you" is not French u — it slides from "ee" to "oo".

docs.title: 34.2 e, é and è — small vowels, big meaning
docs.text: Three different "e" sounds. e [uh] is short and relaxed, lips slightly round. é [ay] is closed and tight — smile, and do not let it slide into "ay-ee". è / ê [eh] is open, like "e" in English "bed".

docs.title: e vs é: singular vs plural
docs.text:
In speech, the final -s of a plural is silent. Often the only sound that tells you "one" or "many" is the vowel of the little word in front.

e [uh] é [ay] Meanings le livre les livres the book / the books de des of / some (plural) ce sac ces sacs this bag / these bags je fais j’ai fait I do / I did me mes me / my (plural)

le / les is a meaning switch

le [luh] = one thing; les [lay] = several. The noun sounds the same, so this vowel carries the whole difference. Never blur it.

  • Je prends le livre, pas les livres. — I’m taking the book, not the books.
  • Je fais mes devoirs ; hier, j’ai fait les courses. — I’m doing my homework; yesterday I did the shopping.

docs.title: é vs è: closed vs open
docs.text:
The open è appears almost always when a consonant is pronounced after the vowel in the same syllable: mère, belle, fête, elle, mer. The closed é appears at the end of a syllable: été, café, parlé.

é [ay] è / ai [eh] Meanings les lait the (pl.) / milk été était been, summer / was une fée un fait a fairy / a fact thé tête tea / head

Don’t panic about é/è at the end of words

Many French speakers, especially in Paris and the south, no longer separate j’ai/j’aimais or parlé/parlais at the end of a word. Context does the work. Focus on two things: le/les, and the open è before a consonant (mère, fête).

Careful

  • Wrong: café said "ka-FAY-ee", like English "cafe"
  • Right: café [ka-FAY] — one pure, tight vowel
  • Why: English "ay" glides to "ee". French é is frozen: smile and hold the vowel still until it ends.

docs.title: 34.3 The nasal triplet — bon, banc, bain
docs.text:
Standard French has three nasal vowels you must keep apart. Air goes through the nose and the mouth, and the n is not pronounced. The three words below differ only in the vowel — and they mean "good", "bench" and "bath".

Figure 34.1. The pink outline is the shape of your lips. Round → open → spread. If two of your nasals sound the same, exaggerate the lip shape first. on [õ] an / en [ã] in / ain [ɛ̃] bon banc bain son sans saint long lent lin ils vont le vent le vin
  • Un bon vin blanc. — A good white wine — the classic drill: four nasals in four words. [ɛ̃ bõ vɛ̃ BLÃ]
  • Il prend un bain sur un banc ? C’est bon ! — He’s taking a bath on a bench? Fine!
  • Le vent est lent, le vin est long. — The wind is slow, the wine is long (has a long finish).

docs.title: beau vs bon — oral vs nasal
docs.text:
Close the nose and you get the oral partner. These pairs train the switch:

Oral Nasal Meanings beau bon beautiful / good bas banc low / bench mot mon word / my

docs.title: Nasal vs vowel + n: the gender switch
docs.text:
Add an -e (or double the n) and the nasal disappears: the vowel becomes oral and you now hear the n. This is how many feminine adjectives sound different.

  • bon → bonne — good (m → f) [bõ → BON]
  • fin → fine — fine, thin (m → f) [fɛ̃ → FEEN]
  • plein → pleine — full (m → f) [plɛ̃ → PLEN]
  • un an → Anne — a year / Anne (a name)

Careful

  • Wrong: bon said "bonn", with a real n
  • Right: bon [bõ] — the n only colours the vowel
  • Why: Your tongue must not touch the roof of your mouth. If it does, you are saying bonne.

Hindi already has nasal vowels

The chandrabindu sound in हाँ (hãa) or माँ (mãa) is a nasal vowel with no n — exactly the French idea. an [ã] is very close to that "ãa".

docs.title: 34.4 The French R — drills that work
docs.text:
The French R is made at the back of the throat, where you make "g" and "k". The tip of the tongue does nothing: keep it resting behind the bottom teeth. It is a soft friction, like gently clearing the throat — not a rolled "r" and not an English "r".

Tongue tip down, back of the tongue up

Say "g", then let air rub through the narrow gap at the back. That soft rubbing sound is the French R.

docs.title: Four steps
docs.text:
• Step 1 — from "g": ga… gra… ra — "g" puts the tongue in the right place; slide from it into the R.
  • Step 2 — between vowels: a-ra, é-ré, o-ro — Easy position: the R is soft between two vowels.
  • Step 3 — clusters: gris, grand, très, trois, crêpe — After g, k, t the R almost makes itself.

  • Step 4 — start and end of a word: rouge, rue, Paris, mer, sœur — The hardest: no help from neighbours. Keep it light at the end of a word.

  • Je rentre à Paris mercredi. — I’m going back to Paris on Wednesday. [zhuh RÃTR a pa-REE mer-kruh-DEE]

  • La rue est très large. — The street is very wide.
  • Mon frère préfère le rouge. — My brother prefers red.

Careful

  • Wrong: Paris with a rolled Hindi "र" or an English "r"
  • Right: Paris [pa-REE], R from the throat
  • Why: A rolled r is understood (some rural regions still use it), but it marks you as foreign. The tongue tip should not move.

Hindi/Urdu shortcut: ग़

If you know the Urdu sound ग़ (as in ग़लत, ग़ज़ल), you already have the French R — it is almost the same sound. Use it, just softer.

docs.title: 34.5 Stress and melody — the end of the group wins
docs.text:
English stresses a different syllable in each word (PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy). French does not. In French, the stress falls on the last syllable of a word — or, in a sentence, the last syllable of each group of words. It is a little longer, not much louder.

  • université — university [ew-nee-vehr-see-TAY]
  • photographie — photography — all syllables even, the last a bit longer [fo-to-gra-FEE]
  • restaurant — restaurant — not "RES-trant" [res-to-RÃ]

docs.title: Intonation: the melody carries the meaning
docs.text:
In everyday French, a question is often just a statement with a rising melody. Same words, different music: Tu viens. (You’re coming.) / Tu viens ? (Are you coming?)

Figure 34.2. Blue = falling, pink = rising. The rises in the middle of a sentence (5) say wait, I’m not finished . Only the final fall says done .
  • Tu viens demain. — You’re coming tomorrow. (statement, falls)
  • Tu viens demain ? — Are you coming tomorrow? (rises)
  • Où est-ce que tu vas ? — Where are you going? (question word first, falls)
  • Tu vas où ? — Where are you going? (spoken style, rises on où)
  • Le matin, avant le travail, je bois un café. — In the morning, before work, I drink a coffee.
  • J’ai acheté du pain, du fromage et des pommes. — I bought bread, cheese and apples. (rise, rise, fall)

Rise = more is coming. Fall = finished.

Yes/no questions rise at the end. Statements fall. Inside a long sentence, each group ends with a small rise. Questions that start with a question word usually fall.

docs.title: 34.6 Rhythm groups and linking
docs.text:
French cuts a sentence into rhythm groups (groupes rythmiques) of about 3–7 syllables — usually a noun with its little words, or a verb with its object. Inside a group every syllable is even, like a drum roll: ta-ta-ta-TAAA. Only the last one stretches.

Figure 34.3. Three groups, three stresses: mon FRÈRE / habite à LYON / depuis deux ANS. Words melt into syllables: “habite à” becomes “a-bi-ta”.

docs.title: Enchaînement: the consonant jumps forward
docs.text:
A pronounced final consonant attaches to the next word if it starts with a vowel. You don’t pause between words — you speak in one smooth line. (For liaison of normally silent letters, see Silent letters & liaison.)

  • Il‿arrive à onze heures. — He arrives at eleven. [ee-la-REEV a õ-ZUHR]
  • Elle‿habite avec une‿amie. — She lives with a friend. [eh-la-BEET a-veh-kew-na-MEE]
  • Pour‿une semaine. — For one week. [poo-rewn suh-MEN]

Careful

  • Wrong: Je – voudrais – un – café. (four separate words, each stressed)
  • Right: Je voudrais un caFÉ. (one group, one stress)
  • Why: Word-by-word French sounds robotic and is harder to understand. Glue the group together and stress only its end.
  • Je voudrais un café. — I’d like a coffee. [zhuh-voo-dreh-zɛ̃-ka-FAY]
  • Ma sœur travaille / dans une banque / à Bordeaux. — My sister works in a bank in Bordeaux. (three groups)

docs.title: 34.7 Tongue-twisters — virelangues
docs.text:
French children train with virelangues. Speed up only when your version is clean. Each one targets a sound.

  • Les chaussettes de l’archiduchesse sont-elles sèches ou archi-sèches ? — Are the archduchess’s socks dry or extra-dry? — target: s vs ch
  • Un chasseur sachant chasser doit savoir chasser sans son chien. — A hunter who knows how to hunt must be able to hunt without his dog. — s vs ch, nasals
  • Trois gros rats gris dans trois gros trous ronds rongent trois gros croûtons ronds. — Three big grey rats in three big round holes gnaw three big round croutons. — the R
  • Tu t’entêtes à tout tenter, tu t’uses et tu te tues à tant t’entêter. — You insist on trying everything; you wear yourself out and kill yourself being so stubborn. — u vs ou, t
  • Ton thé t’a-t-il ôté ta toux ? — Did your tea get rid of your cough? — t with no puff of air
  • Si six scies scient six cyprès, six cents scies scient six cents cyprès. — If six saws saw six cypresses, six hundred saws saw six hundred cypresses. — s and "ee"
  • Je veux et j’exige d’exquises excuses. — I want and demand exquisite apologies. — x as [gz] and [ks]

Twister technique

Say it in rhythm groups, not word by word. Whisper it once (whispering shows you the mouth positions), then say it at half speed, then at normal speed. Stop when it breaks.

docs.title: 34.8 Accent fixes for English and Hindi speakers
docs.text:
You do not need to lose your accent. You need to remove the few habits that confuse listeners. Here are the most common ones, with the fix.

English-speaker habits

  • Wrong: Paris said "PA-ris" (stress on the first syllable)
  • Right: [pa-REE] — the last syllable gets the length

  • Why: English pulls stress to the front. French puts it at the end of the group.

  • Wrong: petit with a puff of air on p and t

  • Right: [puh-TEE] — p, t, k with no puff

  • Why: Hold a sheet of paper in front of your mouth: it should not move on p. (Hindi speakers: your प, त, क are already right.)

  • Wrong: beaucoup said "boh-KOOP", final p pronounced

  • Right: [boh-KOO] — the final consonant is silent
  • Why: Most final consonants are silent. Remember CaReFuL: c, r, f, l at the end are often heard; most others are not.

Hindi-speaker habits

  • Wrong: je said with ज (as in jaana)
  • Right: [zhuh] — like the "s" in English "measure"

  • Why: French j and soft g are a buzzing sound with no "d" at the start — the sound in the middle of "measure" or "television", not ज.

  • Wrong: chat said with च ("chaa")

  • Right: [sha] — French ch = श

  • Why: French ch is (almost) always "sh": chocolat = sho-ko-LA.

  • Wrong: station said "is-ta-syõ"

  • Right: [sta-SYÕ] — no extra vowel before s

  • Why: Many Hindi speakers add a vowel before st-, sp-, sk- (as in "iskool"). Start directly with the hiss: spécial, structure, stylo.

  • Wrong: table with a retroflex ट

  • Right: table with the dental त, tongue touching the teeth
  • Why: French t and d are dental, like Hindi त and द — not like English t or Hindi ट/ड.
  • Je joue avec le chat de Jean. — I’m playing with Jean’s cat. — j vs ch
  • Le stylo spécial est à la station. — The special pen is at the station. — no vowel before st, sp
  • Ta tante a des dattes douces. — Your aunt has sweet dates. — dental t and d
Problem Quick test Drill u sounds like ou Do tu and tout sound different? "ee" + lip kiss, §1 le = les Can a friend hear singular vs plural? le/les table, §2 nasals merge Are bon / banc / bain distinct? lip shapes, §3 English or rolled r Does your tongue tip move? ga–gra–ra, §4 wrong stress Is the last syllable the longest? rhythm groups, §6

Record yourself

Once a week, record the same short text on your phone and compare with last week. Your ear improves before your mouth — hearing your own mistakes is real progress.

À retenir

  • Listen → say → contrast. Play word A, then word B, then say both, A–B–A–B, until your mouth feels the difference. One pair, five minutes, every day.
  • For u, the tongue stays forward as for "ee"; only the lips round. For ou, the tongue pulls back. In a mirror the lips look the same — the difference is inside.
  • Hindi "ऊ" (as in phool) is a good French ou. For u, say "ई" (ee) and round your lips without moving the tongue. English "you" is not French u — it slides from "ee" to "oo".
  • le [luh] = one thing; les [lay] = several. The noun sounds the same, so this vowel carries the whole difference. Never blur it.
  • The chandrabindu sound in हाँ (hãa) or माँ (mãa) is a nasal vowel with no n — exactly the French idea. an [ã] is very close to that "ãa".
  • Say "g", then let air rub through the narrow gap at the back. That soft rubbing sound is the French R.

docs.title: 34.9 Practice — Pronunciation clinic
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which word has the ou [oo] sound?

  • dessus
  • dessous
  • tu
  • vu

Hint: Tongue pulled back.

Answer

dessous

dessous = underneath, with ou [oo]. The others have u [ew].

Exercise 2

In speech, what tells you that 'les livres' is plural?

  • the final s of livres
  • the vowel of les [lay]
  • a longer i in livres
  • nothing at all

Hint: The final -s is silent.

Answer

the vowel of les [lay]

livre and livres sound the same; le [luh] vs les [lay] carries the difference.

Exercise 3

Where is the stress in 'université'?

  • first syllable
  • second syllable
  • last syllable
  • no syllable
Answer

last syllable

French stress falls on the last syllable: u-ni-ver-si-TÉ.

Exercise 4

The melody of 'Tu viens demain ?' (yes/no question) usually…

  • falls at the end
  • rises at the end
  • stays completely flat
  • starts high and falls
Answer

rises at the end

A yes/no question asked by intonation rises at the end.

Exercise 5

Match each word to its meaning.

A B bon bath banc beautiful bain good beau bench Answer

bon — good; banc — bench; bain — bath; beau — beautiful

on [õ], an [ã], in/ain [ɛ̃] — and beau is the oral partner of bon.

Exercise 6

Match the minimal pairs to their meanings.

A B dessus the street dessous the wheel la rue on top la roue underneath Answer

dessus — on top; dessous — underneath; la rue — the street; la roue — the wheel

u [ew] vs ou [oo] changes the meaning completely.

Exercise 7

Il prend un ___ chaud. (bath)

Hint: The in/ain nasal.

Answer

bain

bain [bɛ̃] = bath. Don't confuse it with banc (bench) or bon (good).

Exercise 8

un bon gâteau → une ___ tarte

Hint: Feminine: the n becomes audible.

Answer

bonne

bon [bõ] → bonne [bon]: the nasal disappears and you hear the n.

Exercise 9

Pick the wrong word.

Le chat dort dessous la table.

Answer

Wrong word: dessous.

Corrected: Le chat dort sous la table.

Before a noun use sous/sur. Dessous/dessus stand alone.

Exercise 10

Pick the wrong word.

Hier, j'ai acheté le livres pour mes enfants.

Answer

Wrong word: le.

Corrected: Hier, j'ai acheté les livres pour mes enfants.

Plural needs les [lay] — and in speech, that vowel is the only plural signal.

Exercise 11

Put the rhythm groups in order.

Words: habite / frère / Mon / deux / à / depuis / ans / Lyon

Answer

Mon frère habite à Lyon depuis deux ans

mon FRÈRE / habite à LYON / depuis deux ANS — three groups, three stresses.

Exercise 12

Put the words in order.

Words: je / un / bois / matin / Le / café

Answer

Le matin je bois un café

Rise on matin (not finished), fall on café (finished).

Exercise 13

Say it aloud — keep u and ou apart.

Le chat est dessus pas dessous

Answer

dessus [duh-SEW] with kissing lips; dessous [duh-SOO] with the tongue back.

Exercise 14

Say the nasal drill.

Un bon vin blanc

Answer

Four nasals: un, bon, vin, blanc. No n is pronounced.

Exercise 15

Say it — u, ou, u.

Tu as tout vu

Answer

tu [tew], tout [too], vu [vew].

Exercise 16

Say it — make le and les clear.

Je prends le livre pas les livres

Answer

le [luh] vs les [lay]: the only spoken difference.

Exercise 17

Say it with a throat R.

Trois gros rats gris

Answer

Tongue tip down, back of the tongue up. The R after t and g is the easiest.

Exercise 18

Say the famous tongue-twister.

Les chaussettes de l'archiduchesse sont sèches

Answer

s vs ch: chaussettes, archiduchesse, sèches.

Exercise 19

Ask the question with a rising melody.

Tu viens demain

Answer

Same words as a statement — the rise at the end makes it a question.

Next step

docs.title: Chapter 38: Real spoken French
docs.text:
Le français parlé

You studied Je ne sais pas. Then you arrive in France and hear "chais pas". This is not slang and it is not bad French — it is how almost everyone speaks, every day. The grammar in your book is the written code; this chapter is the spoken one. First learn to understand it, then use the parts that feel natural to you.

Two Frenches, one language

Written French keeps every little word. Everyday spoken French drops, squeezes and reorders them. Both are correct in their place — you need both.

docs.title: 38.1 The disappearing ne
docs.text:
In conversation, the ne of the negative is dropped almost all the time. The pas (or rien, jamais, personne, plus) carries the negative alone. The full ne… pas is still used in writing, speeches, news and careful speech.

  • Je sais pas. — I don’t know. (written: Je ne sais pas.)
  • C’est pas grave. — It doesn’t matter. / No worries.
  • J’ai rien compris. — I didn’t understand a thing.
  • Il y a personne. — There’s nobody here.
  • Je fume plus. — I don’t smoke any more. (here plus is said "plu", no s)
  • T’inquiète ! — Don’t worry! — even pas has gone: Ne t’inquiète pas → T’inquiète.
Figure 38.1. The more relaxed the situation, the less you hear ne . Keeping it everywhere is never wrong — it just sounds a bit formal among friends.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je ne sais. (pas dropped)
  • Right: Je sais pas. / Je ne sais pas.
  • Why: Spoken French drops ne, never pas. Pas is the word that really means "not".

docs.title: 38.2 On instead of nous
docs.text:
In speech, on has almost replaced nous for "we". It takes the il/elle form of the verb — which is easier anyway. To insist, people say nous, on…

Written Spoken Nous allons au cinéma. On va au ciné. Nous avons mangé. On a mangé. Nous partons ? On y va ? Nous, nous restons. Nous, on reste. Nous nous voyons demain. On se voit demain.

Careful

  • Wrong: On allons au parc.
  • Right: On va au parc.
  • Why: On means "we" but conjugates like il: on va, on fait, on est. (Adjectives may still agree: On est fatigués.)

on = we, people, someone

On also means "people in general" (En France, on mange tard.) or "someone" (On m’a volé mon vélo.). Context tells you which.

docs.title: 38.3 Squeezed words — elisions and reductions
docs.text:
In fast speech, the short unstressed vowels vanish: the e of je, ne, le, de, que, the u of tu, the l of il. Consonants then crash into each other and change. You don’t write these forms (except in texts and comics), but you hear them all day.

Figure 38.2. Each step drops or merges a sound. The meaning never changes — only the setting does. Full form You hear tu es / tu as t’es / t’as il y a y a il faut faut je suis j’suis / chuis il dit / elle dit i’ dit / è dit peut-être p’têt parce que pa’ce que qu’est-ce que qu’est-c’que [kes-kuh] quelque chose quèque chose puis pis

t’es ≠ tes, t’as ≠ ta

T’es (you are) sounds like tes (your, plural), and t’as (you have) like ta (your). Meaning comes from what follows: T’as vu tes clés ? = Have you seen your keys?

docs.title: 38.4 Questions, the spoken way
docs.text:
In writing you meet three question forms (see Asking questions). In speech, one dominates: the plain statement with a rising voice. Question words like où, quoi, quand, combien often go to the end. Inversion (Où vas-tu ?) survives mostly in fixed phrases and formal talk.

Formal / written Everyday spoken Où vas-tu ? Tu vas où ? Qu’est-ce que c’est ? C’est quoi ? Que fais-tu ce soir ? Tu fais quoi ce soir ? Quand arrive-t-il ? Il arrive quand ? Combien cela coûte-t-il ? Ça coûte combien ? Qui est-ce ? C’est qui ? Pourquoi pars-tu ? Pourquoi tu pars ?

Quoi ? and Hein ? are blunt

Friends say Quoi ? or Hein ? when they didn’t hear. With strangers or at work, use Pardon ? or Comment ? — otherwise you sound rude.

docs.title: 38.5 Fillers and little words
docs.text:
Fillers give the speaker time and colour the sentence. They are the first thing that makes a learner sound natural — and the first thing that makes them sound silly if overused. Learn to recognise all of these; pick two or three to use.

Filler What it does Example euh… thinking (English "um") C’était, euh… mardi. ben / bah "well", obvious answer Ben oui ! bon "right", moving on Bon, on y va ? du coup "so / as a result" Il pleuvait, du coup on est restés. en fait "actually", correcting En fait, c’est pas loin. genre "like" (young speakers) Il était genre super énervé. … quoi end tag: "you know" C’était nul, quoi. voilà "that’s it", closing a point Et voilà, c’est fini. bref "anyway", cutting short Bref, on a raté le train. tu vois / tu sais checking you follow Le petit café, tu vois ? enfin "I mean", self-correcting Lundi, enfin, mardi.

Careful

  • Wrong: Du coup, j’ai, genre, du coup, réservé, quoi, du coup.
  • Right: Du coup, j’ai réservé.
  • Why: Du coup is so overused that even the French make fun of it. One filler per sentence, at most.

Hinglish has the same thing

Du coup works a lot like "toh" or "so basically", and quoi at the end like "na" or "yaar". You already know how fillers feel — you just need the French ones.

docs.title: 38.6 Social codes: tu, ouais and friends
docs.text:
Among young people, and increasingly in start-ups and creative jobs, tu is the default from the first second. With older people or in traditional settings, wait for them to offer it (see Hello, please, thank you). Everyday yes/no and greetings also have relaxed versions. (For true slang and verlan, see Registers & slang.)

Careful Relaxed Meaning Oui / Non Ouais / Nan yeah / nah Bonjour Salut / Coucou hi / hiya (coucou: friends, family) Au revoir Salut / À plus / À toute bye / see you / see you later D’accord OK / Ça marche OK / sounds good Il n’y a pas de problème. Pas de souci ! no problem Vous voulez qu’on se tutoie ? On se tutoie ? shall we use tu?

Ouais ouais… = I don’t believe you

A single ouais is a relaxed yes. A slow, falling ouais, ouais… or mouais means doubt — like a sarcastic "yeah, right".

docs.title: 38.7 Side by side: written vs spoken
docs.text:
Here is the same content in both codes. Read the left column, then listen to the right one — this is what you will actually hear.

Written / careful Everyday spoken Je ne sais pas où il est. Chais pas où il est. Est-ce que tu as vu ce film ? T’as vu ce film ? Il n’y a plus de pain. Y a plus de pain. Nous ne sommes pas prêts. On est pas prêts. Il faut que nous partions. Faut qu’on y aille. Cela ne fait rien. Ça fait rien. Ce n’est pas la peine. Pas la peine. Tu es très fatigué ? T’es crevé ? Je ne comprends rien. J’comprends rien.

Mini-dialogue — two friends, real speed

The gloss gives the careful French, then the English.

  • Inès : Salut ! T’es où, là ? — = Où es-tu en ce moment ? — Hi! Where are you right now?
  • Karim : Bah chuis encore au boulot. Y a eu un problème, du coup j’suis en retard. — = Eh bien, je suis encore au travail. Il y a eu un problème, donc je suis en retard. — Well, I’m still at work. There was a problem, so I’m late.
  • Inès : C’est pas grave. On se retrouve au ciné à huit heures ? — = Ce n’est pas grave. Nous nous retrouvons au cinéma… — No problem. Shall we meet at the cinema at eight?
  • Karim : Ouais, ça marche. T’as pris les places ? — = Oui, d’accord. As-tu pris les billets ? — Yeah, sounds good. Did you get the tickets?
  • Inès : Ben non, j’attendais de savoir si tu venais, quoi. — = Eh bien non, j’attendais de savoir si tu venais. — Well no, I was waiting to know if you were coming, you know.
  • Karim : OK, j’m’en occupe. Allez, à toute ! — = Je m’en occupe. À tout à l’heure ! — OK, I’ll take care of it. Right, see you later!

docs.title: 38.8 Training your ear
docs.text:
Spoken French is fast because the rhythm groups (see Pronunciation clinic) glue words together. You don’t hear words — you hear blocks. Train yourself to catch the blocks.

  • Chunks, not words: Qu’est-ce que t’en penses ? — You hear one block: "kes-kuh-tã-PÃS". Learn it as one unit — What do you think of it?
  • Catch the stressed end: Je crois qu’il est parti à la gare. — Listen for the long syllables: …par-TI… la GARE. — I think he’s left for the station.
  • Shadow it: Ah ouais, c’est clair, j’suis d’accord. — Play, then speak at the same time as the voice. Yeah, totally, I agree.

Understand everything, imitate selectively

Dropping ne, using on and asking Tu fais quoi ? are safe for you to use at once. Leave heavy reductions (chuis, chais pas) and fillers like genre until they come out by themselves.

A daily listening routine

Ten minutes a day: a French street-interview video or a podcast for learners. Watch French series with French subtitles, not English ones. Note one spoken form a day (y a, t’as, faut…) and listen for it until you catch it every time.

À retenir

  • Written French keeps every little word. Everyday spoken French drops, squeezes and reorders them. Both are correct in their place — you need both.
  • On also means "people in general" (En France, on mange tard.) or "someone" (On m’a volé mon vélo.). Context tells you which.
  • Du coup works a lot like "toh" or "so basically", and quoi at the end like "na" or "yaar". You already know how fillers feel — you just need the French ones.
  • Dropping ne, using on and asking Tu fais quoi ? are safe for you to use at once. Leave heavy reductions (chuis, chais pas) and fillers like genre until they come out by themselves.
  • Ten minutes a day: a French street-interview video or a podcast for learners. Watch French series with French subtitles, not English ones. Note one spoken form a day (y a, t’as, faut…) and listen for it until you catch it…
  • Now switch codes. At work, French gets more careful again: Work, phone & interviews gives you phone calls, meetings and job interviews — with vous and the full ne.

docs.title: 38.9 Practice — Real spoken French
docs.text:
Exercise 1

In everyday speech, 'Je ne sais pas' usually becomes…

  • Je ne sais.
  • Je sais pas.
  • Ne sais pas.
  • Je pas sais.
Answer

Je sais pas.

Spoken French drops ne, never pas.

Exercise 2

'On va au ciné ?' — what does 'on' mean here?

  • one (formal)
  • we
  • they
  • you (plural)
Answer

we

In speech, on almost always replaces nous for 'we'.

Exercise 3

'T'as vu ?' is a reduction of…

  • Ta vue ?
  • Tu as vu ?
  • Tu es vu ?
  • T'avais vu ?
Answer

Tu as vu ?

tu as → t'as.

Exercise 4

You didn't hear your boss. Best word?

  • Quoi ?
  • Hein ?
  • Pardon ?
  • Bah ?
Answer

Pardon ?

Quoi ? and Hein ? are fine with friends but blunt with strangers or at work.

Exercise 5

On ___ (aller) au parc cet après-midi.

Hint: on conjugates like il.

Answer

va

on va — the il/elle form.

Exercise 6

Spoken: 'Y ___ du monde.' (= Il y a du monde.)

Answer

a

il y a → y a.

Exercise 7

Pick the wrong word.

On allons au restaurant ce soir.

Answer

Wrong word: allons.

Corrected: On va au restaurant ce soir.

on takes the il form: on va.

Exercise 8

You are speaking to a shop assistant you don't know. Tap the word that sounds rude.

Quoi ? Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

Answer

Wrong word: Quoi.

Corrected: Pardon ? Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

Quoi ? is fine with friends, but blunt with strangers. Use Pardon ? or Comment ?

Exercise 9

Match the filler to its job.

A B du coup anyway, to cut it short en fait you know bref so, as a result quoi (at the end) actually Answer

du coup — so, as a result; en fait — actually; bref — anyway, to cut it short; quoi (at the end) — you know

Recognise them all; use two or three yourself.

Exercise 10

Match the spoken question to the formal one.

A B Tu vas où ? Quand arrive-t-il ? C'est quoi ? Qui est-ce ? Il arrive quand ? Où vas-tu ? C'est qui ? Qu'est-ce que c'est ? Answer

Tu vas où ? — Où vas-tu ?; C'est quoi ? — Qu'est-ce que c'est ?; Il arrive quand ? — Quand arrive-t-il ?; C'est qui ? — Qui est-ce ?

In speech, question words often move to the end.

Exercise 11

Put the words in order (spoken style).

Words: quoi / fais / Tu / ce / soir

Answer

Tu fais quoi ce soir

Spoken style: statement order + question word at the end.

Exercise 12

Put the words in order.

Words: du / Il / coup / restés / pleuvait / est / on

Answer

Il pleuvait du coup on est restés

du coup = so, as a result.

Exercise 13

Say 'I don't know' the everyday way.

Je sais pas

Answer

No ne in normal speech.

Exercise 14

Ask where your friend is.

T'es où

Answer

tu es → t'es; question word at the end.

Exercise 15

Say 'It doesn't matter' (spoken).

C'est pas grave

Answer

Ce n'est pas grave → C'est pas grave.

Exercise 16

Suggest leaving.

On y va

Answer

on = we. On y va ? = Shall we go?

Exercise 17

Say 'There's no more bread' (spoken).

Y a plus de pain

Answer

Il n'y a plus → Y a plus.

Exercise 18

Say 'No problem!' the relaxed way.

Pas de souci

Answer

Pas de souci ! is everywhere in everyday French.

Next step

Now switch codes. At work, French gets more careful again: Work, phone & interviews gives you phone calls, meetings and job interviews — with vous and the full ne.

docs.title: Chapter 20: Reflexive verbs
docs.text:
les verbes pronominaux

In English you “get up”, “wash”, “get dressed”. In French you raise yourself (se lever), wash yourself (se laver), dress yourself (s’habiller). These verbs with se are everywhere — even your name is one: je m’appelle… This chapter shows how they work, what else se can mean, and how to use them in every kind of sentence.

In one line

A pronominal verb carries a pronoun that matches the subject: je me lève, tu te lèves, il se lève. The pronoun goes before the verb.

  • Je m’appelle Priya. — My name is Priya. (literally: I call myself Priya) [zhuh ma-PɛL]
  • Je me lève à six heures. — I get up at six. [zhuhm LɛV]
  • On se voit demain ? — Shall we see each other tomorrow? / See you tomorrow? [õ suh vwa duh-Mɛ̃]

docs.title: 20.1 How they work: verb + matching pronoun
docs.text:
In the dictionary these verbs are listed with se (or s’ before a vowel): se laver, s’appeler. When you conjugate, se changes to match the subject. The verb itself is conjugated normally.

Subject se lever (get up) s’habiller (get dressed) je je me lève je m’habille tu tu te lèves tu t’habilles il / elle / on il se lève elle s’habille nous nous nous levons nous nous habillons vous vous vous levez vous vous habillez ils / elles ils se lèvent elles s’habillent

Yes, nous nous and vous vous look strange — the first is the subject, the second is the reflexive pronoun. In speech, people often avoid nous nous by using on: on se lève.

  • Comment tu t’appelles ? — What’s your name? [ko-mã tew ta-PɛL]
  • Nous nous habillons vite le lundi. — We get dressed quickly on Mondays. [noo noo‿za-bee-YÕ]
  • Vous vous appelez comment ? — What is your name? (polite)

Careful

  • Wrong: Je se lève à sept heures.
  • Right: Je me lève à sept heures.
  • Why: Se is only the dictionary form (and the form for il/elle/ils). With je, the pronoun is me.

docs.title: 20.2 The daily routine
docs.text:
Most everyday-routine verbs are reflexive in French. This is the best set to learn first, because you can practise it every single morning.

Figure 20.1. A whole day of reflexive verbs. Say each one with je me / je m’ as you do it tomorrow morning.
  • Je me réveille à six heures et demie. — I wake up at half past six. [zhuhm ray-VAY]
  • Il se douche et il se rase. — He showers and shaves. [eel suh DOOSH]
  • Dépêche-toi, on est en retard ! — Hurry up, we’re late! [day-pɛsh-TWA]
  • Les enfants se couchent à neuf heures. — The children go to bed at nine. [suh KOOSH]
  • Je me brosse les dents après le petit-déjeuner. — I brush my teeth after breakfast.
  • Elle se lave les mains. — She washes her hands.

Body parts take le / la / les

With a reflexive verb, the body part takes the article, not “my/her”: je me brosse les dents, elle se coupe les cheveux. The me / se already says whose.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je me lave mes mains.
  • Right: Je me lave les mains.
  • Why: Saying “whose” twice (me + mes) sounds wrong in French. English and Hindi both say “my hands / apne haath”; French says “the hands to myself”.

docs.title: 20.3 With or without se: the meaning changes
docs.text:
Many verbs exist in both forms. Without se, you do the action to someone or something else. With se, the action comes back to you.

Without se With se Je lave la voiture.I wash the car. Je me lave.I wash (myself). Il couche le bébé.He puts the baby to bed. Il se couche.He goes to bed. Elle appelle sa mère.She calls her mother. Elle s’appelle Anne.Her name is Anne. Je promène le chien.I walk the dog. Je me promène.I go for a walk. Le film m’ennuie.The film bores me. Je m’ennuie.I’m bored. Il arrête la voiture.He stops the car. La voiture s’arrête.The car stops.
  • Le dimanche, on se promène au parc. — On Sundays we go for a walk in the park. [suh pro-MɛN]
  • Je m’ennuie ici. On s’en va ? — I’m bored here. Shall we leave? [zhuh mã-NWEE]

Careful

  • Wrong: Je suis ennuyé. (meaning “I’m bored”)
  • Right: Je m’ennuie.
  • Why: English “I’m bored” is an adjective; French uses the reflexive verb. Je suis ennuyé means “I’m bothered / embarrassed”.

docs.title: 20.4 Each other: the reciprocal meaning
docs.text:
With a plural subject (nous, vous, ils, on), se can mean each other. The verb is the same; the context tells you which meaning.

Figure 20.2. One form, two meanings. With a plural subject, se usually means “each other” when that makes sense.
  • Ils s’aiment depuis le lycée. — They have loved each other since high school. [eel SɛM]
  • On s’écrit tous les jours. — We write to each other every day.
  • Mes frères se disputent tout le temps. — My brothers argue (with each other) all the time.
  • Vous vous connaissez ? — Do you know each other?
  • On se tutoie ? — Shall we say “tu” to each other? — the moment you switch from vous to tu [õ suh tew-TWA]

To remove any doubt, add l’un l’autre (“one another”): Ils se regardent l’un l’autre.

docs.title: 20.5 Idiomatic pronominal verbs: learn them as new words
docs.text:
Some verbs change meaning completely with se, or exist only with it. There is no “myself” here — just learn them as vocabulary.

Pronominal verb Meaning Compare s’en aller to leave, go away aller = to go se rendre compte (de) to realise rendre = to give back se souvenir de to remember only pronominal se tromper to be wrong, make a mistake tromper = to deceive se passer to happen passer = to pass s’entendre (avec) to get along (with) entendre = to hear se débrouiller to manage, cope only pronominal (in this sense) s’occuper de to take care of occuper = to occupy se mettre à to start (doing) mettre = to put s’inquiéter to worry inquiéter = to worry sb se servir de to use servir = to serve
  • Qu’est-ce qui se passe ? — What’s happening? / What’s going on? [kɛs-kee suh PAS]
  • Je ne me souviens pas de son nom. — I don’t remember his/her name.
  • Tu te rends compte ? Il a tout oublié ! — Can you believe it? (lit. do you realise?) He forgot everything!
  • Pardon, je me suis trompé de numéro. — Sorry, I dialled the wrong number.
  • Ne t’inquiète pas, je me débrouille. — Don’t worry, I can manage.
  • Je m’entends très bien avec ma belle-sœur. — I get on very well with my sister-in-law.

Learn them with se

Always learn these verbs in the se form and with their preposition: se souvenir de, s’occuper de, se mettre à. Dropping se often gives a different verb.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je souviens de toi.
  • Right: Je me souviens de toi.
  • Why: Souvenir alone is a noun (a memory, a souvenir). The verb only exists as se souvenir de. (Synonym without se: je me rappelle ton nom / careful: se rappeler takes no de.)

docs.title: 20.6 Ça se dit: the passive meaning
docs.text:
With a thing as subject, se often has a passive meaning: “it is said”, “it is done”, “it is eaten”. This is very common for rules, habits and instructions — where English uses a passive or “you”.

  • Ça ne se dit pas. — You don’t say that. / That isn’t said. [sa nuh suh dee PA]
  • Ça ne se fait pas ! — That isn’t done! / That’s not acceptable!
  • Comment ça s’écrit ? — How do you spell that? (lit. how is it written?) [ko-mã sa say-KREE]
  • Le français se parle sur cinq continents. — French is spoken on five continents.
  • Ce vin se boit frais. — This wine is drunk chilled.
  • Ça se voit ! — It shows! / That’s obvious!

Thing + se = passive

When the subject is a thing, se + verb usually means “is done”: ça se mange = it can be eaten, ça se dit = people say it.

docs.title: 20.7 In negatives, questions and with infinitives
Negative: ne + pronoun + verb + pas
docs.text:
The pronoun stays glued to the verb; ne … pas wraps around both.

  • Je ne me lève pas tôt le week-end. — I don’t get up early at the weekend.
  • Ils ne s’entendent plus. — They don’t get on any more.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je me ne lève pas.
  • Right: Je ne me lève pas.
  • Why: Ne comes first, then the whole pronoun + verb block. Nothing goes between me and lève.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
• Tu te couches à quelle heure ? — What time do you go to bed? (everyday)
  • Est-ce que vous vous souvenez de moi ? — Do you remember me?
  • À quelle heure vous levez-vous ? — What time do you get up? (formal inversion: the reflexive pronoun stays in front)

docs.title: With an infinitive: the pronoun still matches the subject
docs.text:
• Je vais me coucher. — I’m going to bed.
  • Nous devons nous dépêcher. — We must hurry.
  • Tu veux t’asseoir ? — Do you want to sit down? [tew vuh ta-SWAR]

Careful

  • Wrong: Je vais se reposer.
  • Right: Je vais me reposer.
  • Why: The infinitive keeps a pronoun that matches the subject je. Only the dictionary form says se.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Positive commands put the pronoun after the verb, and te becomes toi: Lève-toi ! Asseyez-vous. Dépêchons-nous ! Negative commands keep it in front: Ne te lève pas ! Ne vous inquiétez pas. More in Giving instructions.

docs.title: 20.8 In the past: always with être (a preview)
docs.text:
In the passé composé, every pronominal verb uses être, never avoir. The pronoun goes before être, and the participle usually agrees with the subject.

Subject se lever — passé composé je je me suis levé(e) tu tu t’es levé(e) il / elle il s’est levé / elle s’est levée nous nous nous sommes levé(e)s vous vous vous êtes levé(e)(s) ils / elles ils se sont levés / elles se sont levées
  • Ce matin, elle s’est réveillée en retard. — This morning she woke up late.
  • On s’est bien amusés hier soir ! — We had a great time last night!
  • Je ne me suis pas rendu compte de l’heure. — I didn’t realise what time it was.

Careful

  • Wrong: Je m’ai levé à sept heures.
  • Right: Je me suis levé à sept heures.
  • Why: Pronominal verbs always take être in compound tenses.

One trap for later

If a direct object comes after the verb, there is no agreement: Elle s’est lavée. but Elle s’est lavé les mains. The full rules are in The past: passé composé.

docs.title: 20.9 In real life: a morning at home
docs.text:
• — Arjun, lève-toi ! Il est sept heures et quart ! — — Arjun, get up! It’s quarter past seven!
  • — Oui, oui… je me lève. Je me suis couché tard. — — Yes, yes… I’m getting up. I went to bed late.
  • — Dépêche-toi, le bus passe à huit heures. Tu te douches maintenant ? — — Hurry up, the bus comes at eight. Are you showering now?
  • — Non, je me suis douché hier soir. Je m’habille et j’arrive. — — No, I showered last night. I’ll get dressed and I’m coming.
  • — Et ne t’en va pas sans ton déjeuner ! — — And don’t leave without your lunch!

À retenir

  • A pronominal verb carries a pronoun that matches the subject: je me lève, tu te lèves, il se lève. The pronoun goes before the verb.
  • With a reflexive verb, the body part takes the article, not “my/her”: je me brosse les dents, elle se coupe les cheveux. The me / se already says whose.
  • Always learn these verbs in the se form and with their preposition: se souvenir de, s’occuper de, se mettre à. Dropping se often gives a different verb.
  • When the subject is a thing, se + verb usually means “is done”: ça se mange = it can be eaten, ça se dit = people say it.
  • Tomorrow morning, narrate your routine out loud as you do it: je me réveille, je me lève, je me douche… Tonight, tell it in the past: je me suis réveillé(e)… — and then read The past: passé composé.

docs.title: 20.10 Practice — Reflexive verbs
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Tu ___ appelles comment ?

  • te
  • t'
  • se
  • s'
Answer

t'

tu → te, and te before a vowel → t'.

Exercise 2

Nous ___ levons à six heures.

  • se
  • nous
  • nos
  • vous
Answer

nous

nous + nous + verb: nous nous levons.

Exercise 3

Which sentence means 'I'm bored'?

  • Je suis ennuyé.
  • Je m'ennuie.
  • J'ennuie.
  • Je suis ennui.
Answer

Je m'ennuie.

'I'm bored' = the reflexive verb s'ennuyer: je m'ennuie.

Exercise 4

Ils s'écrivent tous les jours. This means:

  • They write to themselves.
  • They write to each other.
  • They are written.
  • They write a lot.
Answer

They write to each other.

With a plural subject, se often means 'each other' (reciprocal).

Exercise 5

Ça ne se fait pas means:

  • It doesn't work.
  • That isn't done / not acceptable.
  • He doesn't do it.
  • It's not finished.
Answer

That isn't done / not acceptable.

Thing + se = passive: 'that is not done'.

Exercise 6

Je vais ___ coucher. (I'm going to bed.)

Hint: match the subject

Answer

me

With an infinitive the pronoun still matches je → me.

Exercise 7

Elle se brosse ___ dents.

Hint: body part

Answer

les

Body parts take the article: les dents, not ses dents.

Exercise 8

Hier, elle s'est ___ (réveiller) à six heures.

Hint: être + agreement

Answer

réveillée / reveillee

Pronominal verbs use être; the participle agrees with elle: réveillée.

Exercise 9

Je ne ___ souviens pas de son adresse.

Answer

me

se souvenir de → je me souviens; ne before the pronoun.

Exercise 10

Pick the wrong word.

Je se lève tôt le lundi.

Answer

Wrong word: se.

Corrected: Je me lève tôt le lundi.

With je the pronoun is me.

Exercise 11

Pick the wrong word.

Hier je m'ai couché à minuit.

Answer

Wrong word: m'ai.

Corrected: Hier je me suis couché à minuit.

Pronominal verbs always take être: je me suis couché.

Exercise 12

Pick the wrong word.

Je me lave mes mains.

Answer

Wrong word: mes.

Corrected: Je me lave les mains.

With a reflexive verb, body parts take les, not mes.

Exercise 13

Put the words in order: I don't get up early.

Words: tôt / Je / me / ne / pas / lève

Answer

Je ne me lève pas tôt

ne + pronoun + verb + pas.

Exercise 14

Put the words in order: What's going on?

Words: qui / Qu'est-ce / se / passe

Answer

Qu'est-ce qui se passe

se passer = to happen.

Exercise 15

Match the verb to its meaning.

A B se rendre compte to leave se tromper to manage s'en aller to realise se débrouiller to be wrong Answer

se rendre compte — to realise; se tromper — to be wrong; s'en aller — to leave; se débrouiller — to manage

Idiomatic pronominal verbs must be learned as new words.

Exercise 16

Say it aloud.

Je me lève à six heures tous les jours

Answer

je me lève: zhuhm LɛV — the e of me almost disappears.

Exercise 17

Say it aloud.

Ne t'inquiète pas je me débrouille

Answer

A very useful reassuring line.

Next step

Tomorrow morning, narrate your routine out loud as you do it: je me réveille, je me lève, je me douche… Tonight, tell it in the past: je me suis réveillé(e)… — and then read The past: passé composé.

docs.title: Chapter 48: Registers & slang
docs.text:
Registres, argot et verlan

French has several words for the same thing, and each one tells people who you think you are talking to. A car can be un véhicule, une voiture, une bagnole or une caisse. In this chapter you climb the ladder of registers, learn how verlan flips words inside out, decode text-message French — and, just as important, learn when to keep all of it out of your mouth and your emails.

In one line

A register (un registre de langue) is a level of formality: soutenu (formal) → courant (standard) → familier (casual) → argotique / populaire (slang).

  • Je n’ai plus d’argent. — I have no more money. (courant — safe everywhere)
  • J’ai plus de fric. — I’m out of cash. (familier — friends, family)
  • J’ai plus une thune. — I’m totally broke. (argot — very casual slang)

docs.title: 48.1 The register ladder
docs.text:
Think of registers as the steps of a ladder. The middle step, courant, is standard French: correct, neutral, safe with anyone. Go up and you get soutenu, the French of formal letters, speeches and literature. Go down and you get familier, the relaxed French of friends, and below it argotique (slang) or populaire, the French of in-groups, teenagers and the street.

Hindi speakers already know this idea: aap / tum / tu or bhojan / khaana carry different levels of respect. French does the same with whole vocabularies.

Figure 48.1. Same meaning, four social signals. The highlighted middle step — courant — is the one to use when you are not sure. Register Where you meet it Typical features Soutenu Formal letters, speeches, literature, the news at its most careful Rare words, full negation, inversion: Puis-je… ? Courant Work, shops, teachers, strangers, most books Standard words, vous with strangers Familier Friends, family, relaxed colleagues, social media Short words, tu, dropped ne Argotique / populaire Youth, songs, films, the street, closed groups Verlan, borrowed words, words that change fast

Learn up, understand down

Actively use courant (and some soutenu for writing). Learn to understand familier and argot — but use them only with people who use them with you.

Grammar changes with register too — dropped ne, on instead of nous, chais pas — but those belong to the chapter Real spoken French. Here we focus on words. For tu vs vous basics, see Hello, please, thank you.

docs.title: 48.2 Familier: the words of everyday friends
docs.text:
Familier words are not "bad French". French people of every age use them at home, with friends and often at work over coffee. Many are just shorter or punchier versions of standard words. Here are the ones you will hear constantly.

Courant Familier Argot / note un homme un mec, un type un keum (verlan) une femme une nana une meuf (verlan) un enfant un gosse, un môme, un gamin — (see the Québec warning below) un ami un copain, un pote un poto la police les flics les keufs (verlan) manger bouffer (la bouffe = food) travailler bosser (le boulot, le taf = the job) se dépêcher se grouiller, se magner — regarder mater can sound like "ogling" people comprendre piger capter avoir peur flipper, avoir la trouille — fatigué crevé, naze — ennuyeux chiant (slightly vulgar) relou = annoying (verlan) un livre un bouquin — les vêtements les fringues — les chaussures les godasses, les pompes — très vachement, super grave, trop (youth)
  • Mon pote s’est acheté une nouvelle bagnole. — My mate bought himself a new car.
  • On bouffe où ce soir ? — Where are we eating tonight?
  • Grouille-toi, le film commence ! — Hurry up, the film is starting!
  • Je bosse tout le week-end, c’est chiant. — I’m working all weekend, it’s a pain. (chiant is mildly vulgar)
  • T’as pigé ce qu’il a dit ? — Did you get what he said?
  • J’ai flippé pendant tout le film. — I was scared during the whole film.
  • Les gosses sont crevés, ils dorment déjà. — The kids are exhausted, they’re already asleep.
  • Il est sympa, ce mec. — He’s nice, that guy.

Québec trap: gosses

In France les gosses = the kids. In Québec, gosses is a vulgar word for testicles. With Canadians, just say les enfants or les jeunes.
